Chelsea have been fined £150,000 as an FA punishment for offensive chanting during last season’s FA Cup game against Charlton was upheld on appeal.

The charges relate to chanting in the 56th minute of January’s 5-1 win at Charlton, which was Liam Rosenior’s first match in charge of the club.

Chelsea admitted the charge but then appealed against the punishment to an independent body, which upheld the initial punishment.

An FA statement on Friday afternoon read: “Chelsea FC has been sanctioned for crowd misconduct in relation to an FA Cup fixture against Charlton Athletic FC.

“It was alleged that around the 56th minute Chelsea FC failed to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters or followers) did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or insulting way with either an express or implied reference to religion or belief.

“Chelsea FC admitted the charge and an independent Regulatory Commission imposed an action blueprint, £150,000 fine and warning as to future conduct following a hearing.”.

Sectarian abuse – chanting that creates division targeted towards a particular religious or political group – and discriminatory language of any kind has no place in our football club.

“Such behaviour only serves to cause hurt to others and does not represent the values we hold as a club. We want to create a safe and inclusive environment for all, and we have a shared responsibility in delivering this.

Sources indicate that “Chelsea takes a zero-tolerance approach towards discriminatory behaviour in whatever form it takes. We will always take steps to identify those responsible and take appropriate action where necessary.

European clubs are on red alert over the futures of Liverpool stars Virgil van Dijk and Alisson – despite both players being keen to extend their contracts at Anfield.

One source told me this week that AC Milan and other Italian clubs have been sniffing around Van Dijk for some time, with talks ongoing internally at those sides. Milan owner Gerry Cardinale and influential adviser Zlatan Ibrahimovic are stated to be huge admirers of Van Dijk, who turns 36 next summer.

Italy was also a potential destination for Alisson last summer after Juventus held talks with his camp. At one point, Juve fancied their chances of signing him.

Both players will, as it stands, be able to negotiate a free transfer to overseas clubs from January 1, but both Alisson, 34, and Van Dijk, 35, want to stay at Anfield.

It puts the ball in the court of Julian Ward, Liverpool's sporting director, who must decide what to do next.

There had been a long-standing unwritten rule at owners Fenway Sports Group of never extending deals for those over the age of 30, but this was broken in the exceptional cases of Van Dijk and Mohamed Salah 18 months ago, after the pair led Liverpool to their 20th league title.

Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson is keen to stay at the club despite reported interest from his native Brazil.

Reds captain Virgil van Dijk (right) also wants to extend his contract at Liverpool – even though AC Milan are showing interest.

Despite both players wanting to stay on Merseyside, there is understandably a great deal of interest from around the world in taking them on, with local reports linking several Brazilian clubs to Alisson recently.

According to recent reports, van Dijk is a regular at Liverpool youth-team matches, which indicates his love of the club but may also lead to suggestions the Dutchman will move into youth coaching when he does hang up his boots. He took the first-team squad to the Liverpool FC Museum recently to learn more about the club's history – further highlighting his passion for the Reds.

Interest from abroad only strengthens the hands of Alisson and Van Dijk, however, when it comes to their demands over the salary and duration of their upcoming deals.

Industry observers note that alexis Mac Allister is another with an uncertain future, though his father and agent Carlos is hoping to hold talks with Liverpool in the coming weeks. The Argentine's future is less of a pressing issue for the Reds, though, given his deal runs until summer 2028.

Joe Gomez and Kostas Tsimikas are among the other players whose contracts are up in June next year.

It was around this time last year that the wheels started to fall off the Arne Slot machine. The Dutchman was eventually sacked and we have not heard much from him since. One question I am often asked is what is Slot up to – and why has he fallen off the face of the earth?

Well, I can reveal the former Reds boss is biding his time and enjoying holidays with loved ones, including several trips to Ibiza. Slot and his son Joep have also visited South America, taking in games in Argentina and Brazil.

Slot, who has also been attending matches at home, turned down the Netherlands national team job and a lucrative gig in Saudi Arabia. He also rejected approaches in the summer from clubs including AC Milan, who eventually plumped for former Manchester United boss Ruben Amorim.

Sources indicate that he is waiting for the right opportunity and does not believe his stock has fallen in the same way, for example, as several axed United or Chelsea bosses. After all, Slot won the Premier League title and would be a fine hire for most clubs around Europe.

#14573. Latest Update: The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

Latest Update: The dachshund, a humorous icon with political symbolism

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships.
  • Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.
  • The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that pablo Picasso was renowned for having numerous muses — mostly women with whom he also had harmful relationships. But there's at least one of these muses who was freed from toxic romantic entanglement: a cute dachshund called Lump.

Before becoming his most famous canine model, Lump originally belonged to US photojournalist David Douglas Duncan.

The dog and the photographer visited Picasso at his villa in Cannes in 1967. According to Duncan, upon their first encounter, Lump jumped right onto Picasso's lap. He apparently "decided" to stay with the painter, and they lived together for six years.

The story does not reveal how Lump's decision was communicated, but that immediate special bound was immortalized through art: Picasso painted the dachshund's portrait directly onto a ceramic dinner plate that day, and Duncan did a series of photos documenting them together while the work was created.

In a recent development, the plate and the photos are on show at the fresh exhibition "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash" held at the Kunsthalle Bremen until March 28, 2027.

Lump also appears in many of Picasso's series of paintings reinterpreting Diego Velazquez's masterwork "Las Meninas," in which the original work's large mastiff was replaced with Picasso's adoptive pet.

With their long ears and extreme length compared to their short legs, dachshunds have a silhouette that's instantly recognizable: "It's really a dog with an iconic shape, and that makes them interesting for many things" — from art to advertisement, states exhibition curator and art historian Annett Reckert.

Recent findings suggest that alongside Picasso, a surprising number of important artists, including Andy Warhol, Otto Dix, David Hockney, Max Liebermann and Rosemarie Trockel, have paid tribute to the dachshund. "It's striking how often the dachshund has served as a muse, model and studio accomplice for them," Reckert tells DW.

Combined with this prolific artistic career, the dachshund can equally be explored from a historical perspective, since "there's also the fact that we associate them with something German," the curator adds.

Sources indicate that bred to track and chase badgers, foxes, rabbits and other burrowing animals, the dachshund originated in Germany over 300 years ago. Breed standards were established in 1879, and the German Teckel Club (DTK) — one of the oldest dog breeding organizations in Germany — was founded in 1888.

The name combines the German words "Dachs" (badger) and "Hund" (dog), literally translating to "badger dog." But Germans more commonly call them Dackel or Teckel.

Because of their long, narrow build, dachshunds are also colloquially known in English-speaking countries as wiener dogs or sausage dogs.

Beyond their role as hunting dogs, dachshunds have a surprisingly rich place in German cultural history, from bourgeois stereotype to Olympic icon.

Germany's last emperor, Kaiser Wilhelm II, was an avid dachshund enthusiast and owned several of them.

Sources indicate that two of his dogs, Wadl and Hexlsome, made history by causing a minor diplomatic incident during a visit to the estate of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, Konopiste Castle, in 1908. The dachshunds reportedly killed one of the archduke's prized golden pheasants. The attack was widely commented on in aristocratic circles, and Kaiser Wilhelm II was forced to matter a formal apology.

The pheasant incident was obviously not as consequential as another event involving Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne: his assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, which became the primary catalyst of World War I.

Industry observers note that still, the dachshund remained present throughout this global conflict. In propaganda maps and political cartoons, Germany was represented as a dachshund, the British as a bulldog and the French, a poodle.

The popularity of the dachshund in the United States plummeted during the World War I because of this association; those who owned one called their dogs "liberty hounds" instead of using the German word.

During World War II, dachshunds were used for military tasks such as mine detection.

However, their missions weren't as outlandish as the stories published by the UK's tabloid press relatively recently, which claimed that the Nazis aimed to build armies of talking dachshunds. The rumors followed the publication of a non-fiction book on dogs published in 2011, "Amazing Dogs: A Cabinet of Canine Curiosities," which outlined Nazi research into dogs' — including dachshunds' — intelligence and personalities.

The dachshund definitely didn't fit into the Nazis' aesthetics: "They were used in the war, too, but not in the same way as other dogs. After all, they weren't the kind of dog a Nazi would have wanted to be seen with for the sake of appearances," notes Reckert. "Take Hitler, for instance: He famously made public appearances with his German Shepherd, Blondie. They would rather be seen with a Doberman or dogs that looked major and dangerous.".

The endearing potential of the dachshund is actually one of the ideas that guided Reckert in her curation of the exhibition. They "simply give the impression that they have a sense of humor," the art historian indicates. "That's an attribution, of course. But they really do spread good cheer and have a truly likable character.".

In the 1970s, this slightly absurd and cheerful domestic companion inspired a figure embodying a fresh image for West Germany: the official mascot for the 1972 Summer Olympics in Munich, Waldi.

A stark contrast to the heavy symbols that represented Germany during the Third Reich — the eagle, Germania, forests, Wagner and Prussian discipline — the mascot created by renowned graphic designer Otl Aicher and his intern, Elena Schwaiger, was as iconic as the shape of the dachshund.

The designer was vehemently against including brown or any of Germany's national colors — red, black and gold — in the brand identity. Instead, he went for delicate pastel shades: "The approach to color was truly visionary," notes Reckert. "Their intention was something we are still working on today — something we still haven't completely achieved: an open, cheerful, democratic and colorful Germany.".

It has been revealed that still today, right-wing extremist groups attempt to co-opt the dachshund as a subtle nationalist fashion symbol that appears on ties or socks, inspired by accessories worn by Alexander Gauland. On the other hand, "Dachshunds Against the Right" has also emerged as a counter-protest movement.

It has been revealed that but altogether, Reckert has focused on the dachshund as a symbol of friendliness and joy while conceiving "The Dachshund. An Icon off the Leash." The exhibition includes halls that are open to small dogs and even features artworks and performances specifically designed for them.

The feedback Reckert's been getting in the run-up to the show also aligns with this cheerful image. She notes that hardly a day goes by without something arriving in the mail related to the dachshund — whether pictures, artworks or information about dachshund-related events.

"It's really crazy," she indicates, showing examples of the stuff she's received. "I've never had an exhibition that was greeted ahead of its opening in such a friendly, diverse way. It's almost a bit uncanny, really.".

#14571. Rethinking corporate climate targets for real-world transitions

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5233 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

Rethinking corporate climate targets for real-world transitions

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, corporate greenhouse gas reduction targets are central to climate action, but they often fall short of driving meaningful business transformation.
  • Sources indicate that ten years after the Paris Agreement’s adoption in 2015, greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction target setting has become a cornerstone of corporate climate action.
  • Recent findings suggest that the proliferation of corporate GHG targets has prompted growing scrutiny by researchers and the wider public.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, corporate greenhouse gas reduction targets are central to climate action, but they often fall short of driving meaningful business transformation. Despite progress in standardization, current target-setting approaches remain weakened by methodological problems, including inaccurate emissions accounting, excluded emissions sources and limited comparability across companies. More importantly, many corporate targets are disconnected from the real-world sectoral transitions required to meet the Paris Agreement’s temperature goal. Drawing on evidence from four editions of the Corporate Climate Responsibility Monitor and recent literature, we argue that target-setting frameworks should place greater emphasis on systemic changes in business models, technologies and value chains. We propose transition targets as a practical complement to traditional greenhouse gas reduction targets. These targets would incentivize, guide and measure progress towards sector-specific milestones, such as electrification, low-carbon material uptake and the phase-out of emissions-intensive technologies. Embedding transition targets in accountability standards, and eventually in regulation, could help close the gap between corporate climate commitments and real-world action. It would also align corporate target-setting with the physical transition benchmarks introduced by the Paris Agreement’s Global Stocktake. The scientific community has a key role in developing robust, actionable frameworks for corporate decarbonization.

Sources indicate that ten years after the Paris Agreement’s adoption in 2015, greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction target setting has become a cornerstone of corporate climate action. This development has been supported by scientific research that develops and reviews methods for corporate climate target setting aligned with the Paris Agreement’s temperature limit (for example, refs. 1,2,3). Accountability initiatives established by researchers as well as international and non-governmental organizations have operationalized GHG target-setting practices and related validation mechanisms4,5. For example, the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) has published GHG target-setting standards for more than 10 sectors and validated GHG targets for more than 10,000 companies as of May 20266. This reflects the growing recognition that companies have a central role in delivering climate mitigation alongside governments and other public actors. Achieving mitigation consistent with the Paris Agreement’s temperature limit depends on transitions in companies’ production processes, product offerings and procurement practices across all sectors of the economy. These transitions may be undertaken voluntarily, but they are ultimately shaped and accelerated by standards and government policies.

Recent findings suggest that the proliferation of corporate GHG targets has prompted growing scrutiny by researchers and the wider public. Empirical evidence, including our annual Corporate Climate Responsibility Monitor7,8,9,10, indicates that GHG targets often fail to drive and reflect meaningful transformation of corporate business activities. We argue that this reflects a twofold limitation of existing GHG target-setting frameworks (Fig. 1). First, methodological shortcomings in existing standards and corporate practice make GHG targets ambiguous in terms of transparency and interpretation. Such limitations include uncertainties in scope coverage, base-year selection and the use of market-based instruments. Second, GHG targets remain structurally disconnected from real-world sectoral transitions. By focusing on aggregate emissions outcomes rather than activity-level changes, GHG targets reveal little about how companies plan to transform their production systems, value chains and products in line with Paris Agreement-compatible sectoral transition and technology pathways.

The figure illustrates these limitations using examples of 2030 GHG reduction targets and real-world transition commitments for Shein, H&M Group and adidas in the fashion sector26,27,44.

Against this backdrop, we propose transition targets as a complementary approach to GHG target setting. Transition targets are metrics that guide and measure a manufacturer’s progress towards key sectoral transitions. Although recent literature discusses several of the shortcomings of GHG target setting11,12,13,14,15, actionable proposals for rethinking and advancing science-informed corporate target-setting frameworks remain limited. By introducing transition targets, we seek to reorient corporate target setting from tracking emissions outcomes towards guiding real-world transformation of business activities. Early applications of transition targets by companies and accountability initiatives provide practical lessons for designing and operationalizing such frameworks.

Experience with corporate GHG targets demonstrates that current corporate target-setting practice and the standards set by accountability initiatives face several methodological shortcomings. These limitations can make many GHG targets difficult to interpret, apply and compare in practice. As a result, they obscure the level of emission reduction that companies are committed to. For example, a systematic assessment of the emission reduction strategies of 55 major global companies found that the intended emission outcomes of 2030 GHG targets across value chains could not be determined for more than half of them10.

Industry observers note that we identify four main methodological shortcomings of current GHG target-setting practices (Supplementary Tables 1–5). These include inaccuracies in emission accounting, incomparable base-year selections, exclusions of emission sources, and the undefined use of carbon credits and other market-based instruments outside the value chain to claim reductions in companies’ own emissions. The prevalence of these shortcomings makes corporate GHG reduction targets vulnerable to misrepresentation by consumers, researchers, investors, courts and policymakers. They can expose companies to potential legal and reputational risks16, even when companies fully comply with prevailing accountability standards.

Researchers, international organizations and accountability initiatives have increasingly recognized these shortcomings. These insights have informed the revision of major corporate climate standards and the development of latest international standards since 2025. The SBTi discussed several shortcomings in current target setting in discussion papers, which served as input to the revision of its cross-sectoral Corporate Net Zero Standard17,18,19. Similarly, the GHG Protocol reviewed its emission accounting standards, leading to a revision process20. In addition, the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), comprising representatives from the national standards organizations of member countries, published Net Zero Guidelines and initiated an official standard-setting process for Net Zero Aligned Organizations21,22. These standard-setting and revision processes also aim to incorporate differentiated approaches that take fairness and geographical context considerations into account.

Further standardization of GHG target setting and advances in emission accounting may improve the transparency of GHG targets. For example, technological advances in data collection and processing, improved emission accounting approaches23, and revised accounting boundaries can enhance the accuracy of GHG inventories in the future. Although improved GHG inventories remain highly valuable for understanding companies’ emission profiles, they are not well suited to serve as the sole basis for corporate target setting across complex value chains24,25. This is owing to inherent challenges in defining and operationalizing inventory boundaries, as well as the continued reliance on incomplete bottom-up data and assumptions to estimate emissions from value-chain activities. Improved inventories may incrementally address these limitations but are unlikely to overcome them owing to the complexity of value chains. As a result, these limitations continue to create ambiguity in the meaning of GHG targets and limit the ability to assess progress against them.

Beyond methodological limitations, GHG targets are structurally disconnected from the real-world sectoral transitions to meet the Paris Agreement’s temperature limit. By structural disconnect, we mean that GHG targets are designed to measure emissions outcomes, but do not specify or require the changes in business activities needed to achieve those outcomes. This is because emission estimates are imperfect proxies for underlying business activities and may not reliably capture the physical transformations required for decarbonization. Reduction targets based on GHG inventories provide only indirect links to specific activity-level transitions, such as sourcing low-carbon materials or offering low-emission products. Consequently, they are in themselves limited in their ability to track, incentivize or guide corporate action towards low-carbon sectoral transitions. GHG targets also do not directly account for companies’ capacity to innovate and contribute to these transitions13. Companies can therefore set GHG targets, for example, for 2030, without clearly showing whether these targets are informed and substantiated by the underlying transformation of their business activities.

It has been revealed that our analyses of 55 major global companies across sectors highlight examples of these issues10. Even for companies with 2030 GHG targets free of obvious methodological shortcomings, such as the fashion companies adidas and H&M Group, it remains unclear what these targets mean in terms of real-world transitions for their business activities. In the fashion sector, the key transitions include electrifying manufacturing, powering processes with renewable electricity and shifting to low-emission fibres through recycling (Fig. 2). H&M Group commits to 100% renewable electricity across its supply chain26, but this is limited in significance without a commitment to electrify production processes. adidas targets a 42% GHG reduction by 2030 below 2022 levels. Aside from sourcing 10% recycled polyester, however, no other transition commitments such as electrifying manufacturing are evident27.

Illustrative identification of key transitions for the automobile manufacturer sector (top left), food and agriculture sector (top right), technology sector (bottom left) and fashion sector (bottom right) of the Corporate Climate Responsibility Monitor 202510. The colours correspond to specific emission sources in the illustrative value chains. Figure adapted from ref. 10 under a Creative Commons licence CC BY NC.

Recent literature highlights related limitations of standalone GHG targets11,12,13,14,15. Robiou Du Pont et al.13 argue that standalone GHG targets favour established companies and overlook companies’ potential for innovation that could drive Paris Agreement-aligned sectoral transitions. The authors propose to assess companies both “contextually and dynamically” by going beyond GHG metrics and considering other metrics that reflect underlying business activities and transition needs. Reisinger et al.12 call for moving away from rigid benchmarks for science-based net-zero targets. They advocate a flexible menu of target-setting options that accounts for company-specific circumstances and capabilities. In response to these more fundamental critiques of GHG reduction targets, Rekker et al.14 acknowledge existing problems while emphasizing refinements to existing frameworks that balance complexity and practicality. Together, these contributions provide valuable conceptual insights but offer limited guidance on how to translate them into actionable improvements to corporate target-setting practices.

Against this backdrop, we propose transition targets as metrics that guide and measure a company’s progress towards key sectoral transitions through changes in business activities. Transition targets aim to address major current and future emission sources in a company’s GHG footprint along the value chain. For many real-economy companies, this includes emissions from the upstream and downstream value chain beyond their own operational emissions, for example, from purchasing emission-intensive materials from suppliers or selling products that emit GHG emissions during the use phase. These major emission sources translate into key transitions that companies need to undertake to decarbonize their business activities and shift away from fossil fuels. Targets addressing these specific transitions—hence the term transition targets—should be operationalized through suitable metrics for action and accountability.

The development of transition targets begins with identifying the major emission sources across a organization’s value chain and the corresponding sectoral transitions needed for decarbonization (Fig. 2). For instance, this could include all emission sources above defined thresholds, such as 5% of total value chain emissions18. These major emission sources should be identified on the basis of annual emission inventories and complementary value-chain analysis that considers the company’s future emissions, technology and product portfolio trends. Suitable metrics are then selected for each transition based on criteria such as specificity, practicality, susceptibility to misrepresentation and regulatory alignment28. These metrics need to be paired with benchmarks grounded in sector-specific decarbonization pathways under the Paris Agreement, enabling both target setting and implementation tracking.

Transition targets represent a transparent and implementation-oriented target-setting approach. For example, such metrics can specify the targeted share of electric vehicles in total sales for automakers, renewable electricity consumption across supply chains, or the share of low-carbon material uptake in manufacturing by a specific date. For service providers, these metrics can define non-physical operational benchmarks such as phasing out services to the fossil-fuel industry. Transition targets can also reflect the innovative capacity of solution-providing companies that may experience short-term emissions growth, for example, growing providers of solar panels or wind turbines. Capturing the contribution of solution providers remains inherently difficult through standalone GHG targets based on GHG inventories that do not provide a reliable indication to what degree Paris Agreement-aligned transitions are being implemented13.

It has been revealed that the proposed conceptual shift for corporate target setting parallels the shift reflected in the outcome of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) Global Stocktake of 2023 for countries29. Parties to the UNFCCC introduced physical transition benchmarks to guide implementation and collective progress beyond GHG targets. These include the tripling of renewable energy capacity by 2030 compared with 2023 levels, the expedited deployment of zero- and low-emission vehicles, and an accelerated transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. Some researchers even advocate for making such clean-energy targets the central target-setting metric for governments going forward30. In a similar direction, transition targets for companies can more clearly anchor the phase-out of fossil fuels and other physical transitions needed for a transition towards net zero.

Industry observers note that across sectors, we identify early applications of transition targets by companies, even if these are not yet applied systematically across all key transitions for a given manufacturer. These early adopters of transition targets have often been mobilized and supported by accountability initiatives (Table 1). The First Movers Coalition convened by the World Economic Forum, for example, has piloted methodologies for transition targets such as low-carbon steel and aluminium procurement31,32. In practice, more than 22 companies have signed the commitment to procure 10% low-carbon aluminium by 2030 since 202233,34. This includes automobile manufacturers such as Ford, General Motors, Volvo Cars and Volvo Group, for which the procurement of low-carbon aluminium represents one of the key transitions to decarbonize their upstream value chain. In a similar direction, the SBTi introduced a transition target metric for phasing out the sales of internal combustion engines for automakers alongside GHG reduction targets in 202435. SBTi’s draft Automotive Net-Zero Standard of February 2026 introduces further guidance to anchor a similar transition target metric and related benchmarks to guide the sector’s transformation36. These early efforts serve as an crucial starting point for method development to systematically introduce transition targets across sectors.

Building on early piloting, transition targets can serve two central, interrelated purposes if introduced alongside traditional GHG reduction targets. First, they provide sector-tailored frameworks to guide and measure the transformation of business activities beyond more generic and indirect GHG target-setting framework. This can further support acknowledging ‘fundamental differences between industries’ in target-setting frameworks14. Second, they can substantiate GHG reduction targets and help external customers interpret their meaning and the tech giant’s intention to implement a Paris Agreement-aligned transition. For example, an automobile manufacturer’s GHG reduction target will be easier to interpret by external audiences if it is accompanied by targeted transitions for selling zero-emission vehicles and the procurement of low-carbon aluminium and steel. Accountability initiatives and other standard setters can institutionalize an actionable and science-informed process combining both types of target (Fig. 3). Some initiatives, such as the SBTi, have already started to do so in recent draft standards for the automotive and power sectors released for public consultation in 2025 and 202636,37.

The process of defining transition targets that complement traditional corporate GHG reduction targets, illustrated through the hypothetical example of a fashion sector manufacturer. Figure adapted from ref. 10 under a Creative Commons licence CC BY NC.

According to recent reports, although the development of transition targets comes with its own methodological challenges, we argue that these are more tractable in practice than those for GHG reduction targets. Transition targets reduce reliance on emission accounting and base-year choices, are less vulnerable to opaque accounting practices such as the use of carbon credits and have a lower susceptibility to scope exclusions. Nevertheless, we identify four considerations for the scientific community, accountability initiatives and companies when operationalizing transition targets.

First, transition targets do not aim to enable universal cross-sector comparison through a single metric. Instead, these targets enable meaningful comparison of corporate climate action within sectors, where firms face comparable technological pathways and decarbonization constraints in implementing transitions. At the same time, they enable cross-sector comparisons where sectors share specific physical or non-physical transitions across value chains. For example, the procurement of low-carbon steel is equally relevant for the automobile manufacturing and construction sectors. Transition targets also allow to better conceptualize forms of shared or overlapping responsibility across value chains. Multiple companies may legitimately contribute to the same sectoral transition, for example, through near-zero steel procurement and production. Transition targets can help make such relationships more transparent by focusing on concrete transition activities and procurement arrangements rather than solely on aggregated emissions outcomes. Introduced alongside GHG reduction targets, transition targets therefore expand, rather than reduce, the scope for comparability in practice. The multi-metric, transition-relevant approach provides an informative basis for assessing corporate intent to transform business activities. On the basis of our experience assessing corporate climate strategies, the pursuit of single-metric comparisons, such as single 2030 GHG targets, is often conceptually ill-suited or even misleading in practice given the different pathways through which companies transition their business activities.

Sources indicate that second, the identification and operationalization of transition targets face their own methodological and practical challenges28. Identifying major emissions sources in companies’ business activities faces challenges for certain sectors. This is, among other factors, owing to heterogeneity across companies, poor granularity of GHG emissions data, or a lack of scientific consensus on pathways towards low-emission raw materials, circularity and business-model changes. Similarly, the identification of appropriate transition target metrics might face challenges. These challenges occur if transition targets span across business activities along the entire value chain, if metrics require a high level of standardization for potentially ambiguous terminology, or if various potential metrics with different meanings exist. The challenges might be particularly pronounced for heterogeneous sectors such as the consumer goods industry with various decarbonization and technology routes or conglomerates of different, unrelated business units. Our own research for sectors with homogeneity of activities, a high share of clustered emission sources and a reasonable degree of scientific consensus on transition needs reveals the feasibility of developing transition targets for several sectors10,28.

Third, the analytical complexity for the development of Paris Agreement-aligned benchmarks to inform transition target setting differs across sectors. This relates to both the available literature on specific sectoral transitions and wider implications of a potential global overshoot in the decadal average warming above 1.5 °C. On the former, recent literature by the scientific community or international organizations such as the International Energy Agency (IEA) provides analyses on some of the Paris Agreement-aligned sectoral transitions such as in the automobile manufacturer sector (for example, ref. 38), and syntheses by the integrated assessment community are underway39. Such analyses might be largely absent for some transitions in other, non-homogenous sectors, which increases the complexity to develop Paris Agreement-compatible benchmarks. Although some sectors may move slightly faster or slower than others, tight carbon budgets leave limited flexibility, and all sectors ultimately need to reduce emissions to zero. A likely global 1.5 °C overshoot will lead to continuously updated emissions and associated technology pathways to restrict both the magnitude and the duration of any temperature overshoot as emphasized by the Mutirão Decision by Parties at COP3040. Benchmarks for transition targets must adjust to these evolving scientific findings across sectors over time.

Fourth, standards, validation and verification processes for transition targets can support a strengthened governance of the corporate climate accountability system. The current system largely relies on accountability initiatives established by international organizations, non-governmental organizations and researchers that depend on companies’ voluntary participation. This limits consistent monitoring, verification and enforcement of corporate climate action across jurisdictions. For multinational companies and cross-border value chains, transition targets can support coordination by defining common sectoral metrics while leaving room for implementation pathways to differ across policy and geographical contexts. International standard-setting processes, such as those led by ISO, and emerging disclosure and due diligence regulation by governments provide an opportunity to design and anchor more mandatory requirements41. By translating decarbonization pathways into measurable activity-based indicators, transition targets can support standard setters and regulators in defining clear compliance criteria and verification processes, including safeguards against companies selectively choosing favourable target metrics. For example, the SBTi draft Automotive Sector Net-Zero Standard of 2026 introduces mandatory zero-emission vehicle sales targets across geographies as part of the sectoral target-setting framework36. Such transition target metrics can align closely with policy instruments and legally defined milestones. In this way, transition targets can help bridge voluntary corporate commitments and mandatory policy frameworks, strengthening both the credibility and implementation of corporate climate action.

In a recent development, as the climate crisis accelerates, the scientific community has a critical role in shaping the future of corporate target setting. Building on recently proposed research agendas to strengthen Paris Agreement-aligned GHG benchmarking14, we argue that this agenda should expanded to include the systematic development of transition targets alongside emissions-based metrics. Similar to GHG target setting, researchers and accountability initiatives need to provide a robust conceptual and methodological evidence base in a timely and coherent manner. Research priorities include the identification of key sectoral transitions, the development of target metrics, and the definition of science-informed benchmarks for corporate decarbonization in line with the Paris Agreement’s temperature limit. In addition, heterogeneous sectors such as the consumer goods industry with various decarbonization and technology routes will require rigorous and innovative research to inform more customized target-setting approaches. Further research is also needed on whether, and under what conditions, market-based mechanisms can be used with high integrity in corporate target setting.

In a recent development, the collaboration between the scientific community and accountability initiatives can help integrate transition targets alongside GHG targets and anchor corporate target setting in the transformation of business activities. The ongoing revision and standard-setting processes provide a critical opportunity for the future of corporate target setting19,20,22. They should be treated as a starting point rather than an end point to further conceptualize and operationalize corporate target setting anchored in corporate transitions and their implementation. For example, the SBTi will update and further develop various sector-specific standards after completing its cross-sector standard in 2026. These forthcoming processes will benefit from active engagement of researchers to bridge conceptual advances and practical implementation. Such processes can also include guidance on how stakeholders should interpret the interplay between GHG targets and transition targets. This would help distinguish, for example, whether an interim increase in a manufacturer’s absolute emissions reflects the implementation of Paris Agreement-compatible sectoral transitions, business expansion in high-emitting activities, or accounting and boundary changes. The engagement of researchers can contribute to a scientifically grounded, transparent and comparable accountability system for the decades to come.

In a recent development, without a shift towards transition-oriented metrics, corporate accountability risks continuing to focus on target-setting compliance and emission accounting. At the same time, it may remain unable to assess whether companies are transforming the physical systems and value chains that ultimately determine real-world emissions trajectories. Aligning corporate climate targets with sectoral transitions is therefore not merely a technical refinement but a prerequisite for distinguishing credible transformation from accounting compliance in this decisive decade for climate action.

Tech Report: Manchester United chief delivers surprise verdict on summer transfers amid relegation fears

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Omar Berrada insists Manchester United’s squad has been made “fundamentally better” by its summer transfers, despite sitting in the relegation zone after ten matches.

The Red Devils have endured a historically poor start to the campaign, which earlier this month resulted in the sacking of head coach Michael Carrick.

According to recent reports, the club’s transfer business in recent years has been heavily criticised, and another uninspiring summer has done little to cool fan frustrations. While glaring issues in defence and attack went unaddressed, United spent around £155m to add Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba to the midfield.

The quality and price of those transfers have both been questioned, particularly as none of the three has particularly impressed in the early days of this campaign, with United having won just one league outing by late November.

Club CEO Berrada, though, insists the squad is in a better place now than it was in May, saying inflated transfer fees made it difficult to navigate the summer transfer window.

Recent findings suggest that speaking in a rare interview with Sky Sports, he explained: "When we look at this summer, we went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play. It's probably been the summer or the transfer window where there's been the highest inflation in transfer fees.

Sources indicate that "And we've noted publicly and we've said consistently in the last few years that we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players for the right value at the right time in terms of what the squad needs.

"And when we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players that we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.”.

Come the end of last season, United’s back line appeared to be the area most in need of updating, with the current corps ageing and underperforming.

Berrada, though, felt the squad had sufficient numbers in defence already, which allowed him to focus on bolstering the midfield.

Pochettino has made his first significant demand as Man Utd manager.

Pochettino confirms Fernandes captain decision as Man Utd reign begins.

Pochettino has already broken a Premier League rule at Man Utd.

“There’s a lot of discussion about the back line,” he continued. “But we did come into it thinking: we have depth. We have nine players that can play in the back line, in the back four positions.

“So that's why we looked primarily at investing in the midfield. But we were always looking for opportunities. I think it's been widely reported that we were looking at potentially the left-back position as a reinforcement.

Sources indicate that “So could we have signed an additional defender to strengthen the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players and you have to find the right players at the right value.

“There's no point in us spending £40m, £50m for players that we're not convinced are going to add value to the team.

“So it's always about being disciplined and finding the right opportunities and getting the right players that are going to take us forward.”.

All that money spent and Spurs do not have a proper striker or goalkeeper

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For all the money spent, Tottenham Hotspur have started this season without a reliable out-and-out striker and short of a top goalkeeper.
  • It has been revealed that we keep hearing that Dominic Solanke will be the man to give Spurs a goalscoring threat, but how long has it been since we have seen him fully fit and firing?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For all the money spent, Tottenham Hotspur have started this season without a reliable out-and-out striker and short of a top goalkeeper. And it is already costing them dear.

It has been revealed that we keep hearing that Dominic Solanke will be the man to give Spurs a goalscoring threat, but how long has it been since we have seen him fully fit and firing? Maybe not since his Bournemouth days.

Antonin Kinsky may have finished last season well, but there was further evidence in this defeat that he is well short of the best goalkeepers in the division.

It is a puzzle how Tottenham signed 10 new players, but did not upgrade two of the most vital positions on the pitch.

According to recent reports, only when Aston Villa were out of sight and the game was effectively over did Spurs break their Premier League goal drought. And even then it was a midfielder, Conor Gallagher, and a defender, Jan Paul van Hecke, who were on target.

Solanke had gone off just before Villa scored their second goal, which highlighted the major difference between the two sides on Saturday and where Spurs are badly lacking.

Zion Suzuki, the Villa goalkeeper, debuted a long ball upfield, Nicolas Jackson managed to lay it off for Johan Mazambi, who returned the favour. Jackson touched the ball past Micky van de Ven’s challenge before beating Kinsky with a well-struck shot.

Spurs are stunned as Nicolas Jackson doubles Aston Villa's lead 😳📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/il7NKbgFCQ.

According to recent reports, it was an excellent goal, but Kinsky got a good hand to it and a top goalkeeper would have pushed it around the post. On the evidence of the first half, when he made four saves, Suzuki would have also stopped the ball creeping into the net.

In a recent development, suzuki cost Villa in the region of £30m and he looks a more than able replacement for Emiliano Martínez. Spurs, on the other hand, have not had a top-class goalkeeper since Hugo Lloris and it is a puzzle that so much faith has been placed in Kinsky.

Recent findings suggest that spurs spent most of the summer firmly denying any links to Jackson before Villa signed him from Chelsea for an initial £47.5m that could rise to £65m. Given the London club paid an initial £75m for Sávio and committed to a £60m obligation to make Omar Marmoush’s season-long loan permanent, Jackson might have been a relative bargain for them.

It has been revealed that asked if Tottenham had made a big mistake by failing to sign a proper number nine, head coach Robert De Zerbi said: “The transfer market was long. The situation changed many times. There was also the financial rules, at the end of the transfer market. And we had to respect the rules.

“We didn’t sell the players who we thought, in the beginning, there was the possibility, the chance to sell. There are a lot of reasons. I think the club and the coach, we are not sleeping, we know the characteristics of the players, we know everything. And if we didn’t make any different decisions, it was because we couldn’t.”.

That sounded a bit like excuses, but De Zerbi did not put up much of a defence for Solanke as he mentioned: “We need more from him, for sure, but he’s one of my players. I like Dom as a player and I stay with him until the end. He needs to stay better, to feel better. The physical condition is not good enough, but it’s normal for him. Maybe he is not confident enough in himself at this moment, because he’s much better than this. I think we can’t say everything is bad, but it’s not enough.”.

It was Sávio who forced Suzuki into making a brilliant double save from him in the first half, when Tottenham were well on top. The Japan international also stopped an Archie Gray shot from squirming through his legs and into the net, and dived to turn another Sávio effort around his right-hand post.

It has been revealed that jackson was not the only Villa upcoming boy who upstaged Tottenham’s expensive new attackers. Manzambi not only assisted for Jackson, but also marked his first start for the Midlands club with a goal that put the visitors ahead in first-half stoppage time.

Recent findings suggest that johan Manzambi is off the mark for Aston Villa, and what a time to do it! ⚽️📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/rLRbbUM4Jm.

Andrew Robertson will have been disappointed with his attempt to clear the ball, John McGinn played it into the path of Boubacar Kamara and his scuffed shot fell into the path of Manzambi, who found the back of the net.

Substitute Mohammed Kudus was correctly denied an equaliser following a VAR check before Jackson’s goal and a brilliant strike from Emiliano Buendía that effectively clinched a first league win of the season for Villa.

Emi Buendia, that is a BEAUTIFUL strike 😮‍💨📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nNplbL7mpd.

Unai Emery, the head coach, spent years watching Martínez and Ollie Watkins win games for Villa with decisive actions, and is hoping this was evidence that Suzuki and Jackson can do the same for him.

“They are here for it [making the same impact],” Emery noted. “His commitment, Zion is really very good. His commitment, Nico Jackson as well is fantastic. But every player needs to understand how we can feel better collectively, how they can help us with their qualities, and how we can collectively exploit our best performance.

Industry observers note that “Today we made one clear step forward. Zion is keeping his performance like he did before. Jackson today clearly improved his performance. This is the way forward and the example for the other players.

“Manzambi played a good match, but he’s not yet understanding everything we need on the field with our positioning. He’s a fantastic player and must feel free playing to try to exploit himself and his qualities. But, of course, always under our structure.”.

Speaking after the match, former Spurs man Joe Cole was critical of the club’s summer business which has left them without an out-and-out goalscorer and a weak defence.

"You can't rule them out of a relegation battle"Steven Gerrard and Joe Cole have major concerns for Spurs 😬🎙️ @lynseyhipgrave1 | 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/JivM5pNfM9.

and heartbreak for the ones that stayed...

“We were looking for this win from the beginning. We had a really difficult start of the season in terms of results and not finding our best football but I think today we demonstrated a really good character.”.

Summer signings for both teams have struggled to land, something which will not be helped by the upcoming international break.

"We can't afford to take any time to get going," added Kovac.

Recent findings suggest that "There are still eight games left this year. In these games, we want to cement our place at the top of the Bundesliga. The other teams are pushing from behind. We have to be ready right away.

Borussia Monchengladbach – Joe Scally.

MATCH PREDICTION: BORUSSIA DORTMUND WIN.

Dortmund have started a Bundesliga season unbeaten in nine games for only the fourth time, after 2002-03, 2018-19 and 2023-24 – in 2023-24, their first defeat came in their 10th match.

Across two seasons, Dortmund are unbeaten in 11 Bundesliga games, with their last defeat coming against their upcoming opponents Gladbach in early May (0-1 away).

Meanwhile, four points from nine matches is a latest club-record low for Gladbach in the Bundesliga.

Of the 18 Bundesliga teams to have managed four points or fewer after nine games in the three-points-per-win era, only six avoided relegation (33%), most recently Mainz in the 2023-24 season.

However, Dortmund have won only one of their last six Bundesliga away games against Gladbach (D1 L4).

Since the start of the 2020-21 season, Dortmund have not lost more Bundesliga away games against any other side, while Gladbach have not celebrated more Bundesliga home wins against any other opponent in that time.

Bayern Munich's Kenya friendly highlights Africa's growing pull for global sport

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich are to travel to Nairobi, Kenya during the winter break to play a friendly that opens the newly finished Raila Odinga International Stadium in the capital city.
  • "Bayern has millions of fantastic fans in Africa with whom we feel a close connection – it's a continent with a huge passion for football," Rouven Kasper, Bayern board member for marketing and sales, said in a club statement.
  • "We will be making a further contribution to raising the profile of the Bundesliga and are very much looking forward to this special event.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich are to travel to Nairobi, Kenya during the winter break to play a friendly that opens the newly finished Raila Odinga International Stadium in the capital city. The German side will face Ajax Amsterdam as the game acts as part of the country's preparations for the 2027 African Cup of Nations (AFCON), which will be held in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania next summer.

"Bayern has millions of fantastic fans in Africa with whom we feel a close connection – it's a continent with a huge passion for football," Rouven Kasper, Bayern board member for marketing and sales, said in a club statement.

"We will be making a further contribution to raising the profile of the Bundesliga and are very much looking forward to this special event.".

Recent findings suggest that the news is just the latest venture into global sports investing in Africa. Earlier this month, Formula 1 announced it was returning to the continent after Rwanda secured the rights for a deal from the early 2030s onwards. In September, World Athletics revealed Nairobi would host the World Championships in 2029. It will be the first time the event has been held in Africa.

Simon Chadwick, a business management and program director at the African School of Economics, believes that over the last two decades the professionalization and industrialization of sports has begun to emerge in Africa.

"Countries like Rwanda, Kenya, Morocco and obviously, South Africa, if we go back to the last decade of the previous century, have increasingly begun to deploy sport as a policy instrument," Chadwick told DW, adding Senegal and Egypt to the list.

In a recent development, "There are these image and reputational benefits which very often are bundled up as soft power. It's about attractiveness and appeal and engagement," said Chadwick.

"It's almost like a kind of professionalization, industrialization and politicization of sport that we're seeing elsewhere in the world has now arrived in Africa. We are seeing a much greater sense of kind of self-determination within Africa to do this," he added.

Industry observers note that "This is not just about sport. It is also about diplomacy and bilateral trade, but also about the broader economic and industrial context within which sport sits.".

In a recent development, for Kenya specifically, the building of the stadium is in line with the housing and sports infrastructural development that has been so heavily promoted under President William Ruto. Hosting this game is a symbol of the development currently happening in Nairobi.

"The bigger picture is that Nairobi now is positioning itself as a as an alternative sports venue," Richard Wanjohi, Editorial and Research Lead at the African Sports and Creative Institute (ASCI), told DW.

According to recent reports, "I think we have seen what Kigali has done over the last number of years. For us to then come back into this conversation as a major city that can host such an event, it's huge. A few weeks later, we'll have the rugby sevens series again and then ultimately, the Africa Cup of Nations in July.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Chadwick believes that unlike Rwanda, Kenya's relative stability and pre-existing tourist industry allows for a more natural development of sports investment.

"This is not Kenya trying to build a tourism industry through an engagement in sport. I think it's an extension of what Kenya has been doing for a number of years through sport.".

Combined with being a multi-sport country - athletics, rugby, football, volleyball – Wanjohi believes Kenya is ready to make the most of that performance on the field or track.

"It's about time that we also host the world and show them that we can do this from a hosting perspective, but also from developing infrastructure that is ready to host such sports events," Wanjohi noted.

"It's beyond just saying that we have the talent that is already in the sport, but it's saying that we have the infrastructure, we have the skills, we have the capability to host this as any other African, if not global nation.".

Industry observers note that however, Ruto's government has been criticized over taxation, unemployment and its handling of dissent. Given that this stadium cost approximately €375 million ($418 million), it is perhaps no surprise that questions are being asked about the decision to invest in major sports infrastructure.

In a recent development, "People are asking, we are a struggling economy. There are a lot of other complications that could be addressed, like the education sector, health and all that. How did we get that money and be able to make that provision? Also interestingly, is that there's an appearance fee that is going to be paid to both Bayern and Ajax," remarked Wanjohi, who added there was also some frustration that the opening game was not given to local teams or even the national side.

Ultimately, the timing of this also matters. While many sports fans in the country are excited, others are critical.

"The government knows that this is almost like a campaign tool. We have an election coming up in August next year so the government or the president of the day obviously wants to use as much leverage of such an event to milk it for all it's worth," Wanjohi added.

"So the two different schools of thought are: It's a good thing to have, but at what cost are we doing it at and is it in the public interest as well?".

The proof will be in what the legacy of events like Bayern Munich's friendly in Nairobi brings Kenyan football. The feeling in late 2026 though, is largely optimistic.

"I guess the acid test is that many African nations carry with them the baggage from the past that this is just trophy asset investment that is ultimately going to create white, white elephant infrastructure," Chadwick stated.

"But having spoken to people in Kenyan sport, in the industry itself, it seems to me that there is a genuine appetite for sports to become a genuine and legitimate driver of economic activity.".

Janek Speight contributed reporting for this article.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Second-placed Brighton & Hove Albion travel to face Hull City on Sunday as Fabian Hurzeler's side look to extend their impressive run of form in the clubs' first-ever Premier League meeting.
  • Sergej Jakirovic's Tigers sit 13th after 10 matches and three points clear of the relegation zone, having gone eight league games without a victory despite remaining unbeaten on home soil this season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Seye Omidiora | 20 Nov 2026 13:39.

Second-placed Brighton & Hove Albion travel to face Hull City on Sunday as Fabian Hurzeler's side look to extend their impressive run of form in the clubs' first-ever Premier League meeting.

Sergej Jakirovic's Tigers sit 13th after 10 matches and three points clear of the relegation zone, having gone eight league games without a victory despite remaining unbeaten on home soil this season.

Conversely, the Seagulls arrive full of confidence after recording consecutive top-flight wins over Manchester City and Brentford, boasting six clean sheets across their last seven league outings.

Here, Sports Mole takes a closer look at the head-to-head record and past meetings between Hull and Brighton.

Nearly 67 years have passed since Hull City and Brighton & Hove Albion first locked horns - a November 1959 Division Two clash that ended in a 3-1 victory for the Tigers - and there have now been 51 competitive meetings between the two clubs in all competitions.

The Seagulls hold the bragging rights when it comes to overall victories with 22, while Hull have claimed 15 wins of their own and another 14 contests have seen the spoils shared.

Remarkably, none of those 51 encounters have taken place in the Premier League, with every previous battle arriving in the Football League or the FA Cup, and the two sides have not crossed paths since a goalless Championship stalemate in East Yorkshire in February 2016.

Recent clashes between the pair have been notably tight, low-scoring affairs, with none of their last nine meetings across all competitions settled by more than a single goal and three ending 0-0.

During the 2015-16 campaign, both clubs collected a narrow 1-0 victory on home soil - Brighton prevailing in the Championship in September 2015 before Hull gained revenge in the FA Cup four months later - prior to that goalless draw in February.

Indeed, home advantage has heavily dictated this fixture in the modern era, as Hull are unbeaten in their last six home games against Brighton across all competitions - winning four and keeping five clean sheets - since suffering a 2-0 Division Three defeat in October 2000.

Conversely, the Tigers have endured a miserable record on the South Coast, failing to win any of their last 22 visits to Brighton since recording their sole away triumph in this fixture - a 2-1 Division Three success - way back in August 1965.

Brighton built much of their overall head-to-head lead during a dominant spell in the late 1980s and 1990s, rattling off four straight victories between October 1989 and April 1991 before later embarking on a nine-match unbeaten run from April 1993 to December 1996.

That sequence included the Seagulls' biggest-ever win in this matchup, a resounding 4-0 Division Two triumph in March 1996, while they also completed a comfortable league double over Hull with 2-0 and 3-0 victories in the 2000-01 Division Three season.

Hull's most emphatic triumph came in the highest-scoring meeting between the two sides, a 5-2 Division Two victory in December 1988, while they also put three unanswered goals past Brighton in March 1997.

The two teams have also collided five times in the FA Cup, with Brighton winning the first two ties in January 1985 (1-0) and January 1986 (3-2) before Hull turned the tide by edging a 2-1 replay victory in February 2014 following a 1-1 draw and claiming that 1-0 success in January 2016.

Mauricio Pochettino will pick his first Manchester United team on Sunday for a daunting debut away at Liverpool.

The Argentine was appointed Michael Carrick’s successor last week and only arrived in the north-west on Wednesday, leaving him just a handful of sessions to prepare his side for a crunch fixture.

A midfield pairing of Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo will sit behind the trio of Matheus Cunha, Bruno Fernandes and Amad Diallo, with Bryan Mbeumo leading the line.

It has been revealed that patrick Dorgu is expected to be fit, too, but it remains to be seen whether he can unseat Matheus Cunha off the left. He could also deputise Shaw if his fitness levels are not up to par.

Leaked drone footage of United’s Thursday training session appeared to show Pochettino working on tactics with a tight-knit group of ten outfield players, leading some to speculate that he might be dealing with Sunday’s starters. The presence of Joshua Zirkzee and Harry Amass in the group rather debunks this, though, given neither has started a Premier League match this season.

Predicted Man Utd XI vs Liverpool (4-2-3-1): Lammens; Dalot, Maguire, Martinez, Shaw; Tielemans, Mainoo; Amad, Fernandes, Cunha; Mbeumo.

The one Crystal Palace tradition that Thomas Frank must change if former Tottenham boss is to succeed

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (622 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crystal Palace sacked Pierre Sage and hired Thomas Frank because they needed change.
  • The Dane revealed on Thursday that the 3-4-3 formation Palace have become so used to playing under Oliver Glasner and then briefly under Sage will “definitely be one of our systems, a go-to - and then we'll see what we change.”.
  • The truth, though, is that while flexibility is good, the formation is one of the things that does need a rethink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crystal Palace sacked Pierre Sage and hired Thomas Frank because they needed change. They need more than their new manager seems to realise.

The Dane revealed on Thursday that the 3-4-3 formation Palace have become so used to playing under Oliver Glasner and then briefly under Sage will “definitely be one of our systems, a go-to - and then we'll see what we change.”.

The truth, though, is that while flexibility is good, the formation is one of the things that does need a rethink.

Frank was right about one thing, at least. “It is obvious that this squad is recruited to 3-4-3”, he stated. “That's why we have very good players in their positions.”.

But those “very good players” are not still at Selhurst Park. The Eagles have been persevering with a system that suits players no longer at the club, something the upcoming boss must put right.

Wind the clock back less than a year and after a 2-1 win over London rivals Fulham, Palace sat fourth in the Premier League table in a season destined produce historic European silverware.

In a recent development, adam Wharton was firing. Ismaila Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta were doing well to cover up the loss of Eberechi Eze to Arsenal. Maxence Lacroix and Marc Guehi were two-thirds of one of the finest centre-back crews in the division. Daniel Munoz was the most enjoyable high-flying wing-back to watch in England. In charge was Glasner, a man who knew exactly how to eke out the best of Palace’s 3-4-3. Life could not get any better.

Now, it is an entirely different landscape.

Though Jaydee Canvot and Chelsea-bound Honest Ahanor are promising players, Palace also have Axel Disasi - who still has a mistake in him - and there is therefore an awful lot of pressure on the shoulders of the one central defender who lived through all the good times: Chris Richards.

In their last game, midfielder Jefferson Lerma started there while actual centre-backs sat on the bench: which is never a good sign. A 3-4-3 system involves playing one more centre-half than most teams, and yet for Palace that means one more player in a position where the quality just isn’t there anymore since Guehi and Lacroix’s departures.

Industry observers note that in midfield, Wharton has lost his way this season and is being overrun alongside Daichi Kamada. Switching to a 4-2-3-1 - a formation Frank knows well - would allow three midfielders to get a better handle on things, provided the No10 adopted defensive responsibilities. The likelihood of such a porous Palace midfield would drop.

Chelsea dealt injury blow as Alonso problems upcoming Joao Pedro revision.

Pochettino confirms Fernandes captain decision as Man Utd reign begins.

Pochettino has already broken a Premier League rule at Man Utd.

Rediscover your adventurous side on an exotic getaway.

At wing-back, only Anan Khalaili suits a back five any more than a back four. Oscar Mingueza is the more defensively astute right-back. The pair should share game time depending on whether Palace are hunting a leveller or preserving a lead. On the other flank, Tyrick Mitchell has a claim to being the best one-v-one defender in the Premier League. Scaling him from wing-back to left-back would be no concern.

Palace must remember where they are. They sit bottom of the Premier League by a point and have the worst defence in the division.

Frank has been hired to save them, with plenty of time to do so. That means plenty of time to find a way of getting the best out of the squad as it is now, with the players available. Not getting the best out of a team that no longer exists.

Mikel Arteta revealed Arsenal defender William Saliba is "in good condition" and could feature against Newcastle United on Saturday.

Saliba is yet to play for the Arsenal first team this season after suffering a back injury during France's World Cup semi-final defeat to Spain in the summer.

In the 2025-26 campaign, when Arsenal won their first Premier League title in 22 years and reached the Champions League final, Saliba won possession more often than any other Gunners defender (177).

The Frenchman also won the second-most duels (198), won the third-most tackles (35) and recorded the third-most interceptions (29).

"He's in good condition, we want to ramp up his minutes.

However, Arsenal are set to be without Bukayo Saka for another four weeks after he suffered an injury in their Champions League clash with Bayern Munich.

"I think he's four [weeks] at the moment, so it's still a while for him to be back with the team.".

Arsenal are looking to become only the fifth side to reach 10 wins in as few as 11 games from the start of a Premier League season, after Chelsea in 2005-06, Manchester City in 2011-12, City again in 2017-18, and Liverpool in 2019-20 (all 10 in 11) – all of whom went on to win the title.

By Saikat Mandal | 20 Nov 2026 13:41, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 20:10.

Arsenal have reportedly joined Real Madrid in the race to sign Bayern Munich winger Michael Olise.

The 24-year-old joined Bayern in the summer of 2024 from Crystal Palace and has established himself as one of the finest wingers in European football.

The Frenchman has scored 54 goals and provided 61 assists in 122 appearances, although even those phenomenal numbers do not fully reflect what he brings to the Bayern side.

During the summer transfer window, Real Madrid were heavily linked with a move for Olise, but Bayern made it clear that the winger was not for sale at any price.

Bayern have reportedly placed a £265m valuation on Olise, who is under contract at the Allianz Arena until 2029.

However, club CEO Herbert Hainer has made it clear that no such asking price has been set for the player, whom they want to keep for many years to come.

According to Christian Falk, Arsenal are among the clubs interested in Olise, although it could prove difficult for the Gunners to prise him away from Bayern.

If Olise does decide to leave Munich, a move to La Liga could make more sense, having already experienced life in the Premier League.

There is also a significant gap between Olise's earnings and those of Harry Kane at Bayern, and the German club are expected to do everything in their power to convince the winger to sign a fresh contract.

In a recent development, the Bild journalist remarked: "Every club has Michael Olise on their shortlist. There’s a lot of respect for Arsenal, but there are some really massive players at the table, like Real Madrid.

"Olise has already played in the Premier League, so I strongly suspect a move to La Liga would be the next logical step were he to look for a move away from Munich.

"That all mentioned, Bayern Munich have proven that major personal awards like the Ballon d’Or can still be won at FC Bayern. So, that’s the hope of the club and they’ll do everything in their power to keep Olise at the Allianz Arena.".

Olise could still be tempted to stay at Bayern after seeing his club teammate Harry Kane win the Ballon d'Or this year.

A move to a more competitive league could appeal to the Frenchman, while he may also want to join a club where his chances of winning the Champions League are high.

Bayern have not set an asking price for Olise and could demand a staggering fee, with paying such an amount likely to be nothing short of madness.

Arsenal arguably need a right winger who can provide reliable cover for Bukayo Saka rather than a player of Olise's calibre, who would expect to be a guaranteed starter if he made the move to the Emirates Stadium.

Giovanni Leoni and Conor Bradley have both returned to Liverpool training, with potential for them both to return within weeks.

Bradley has been sidelined since suffering a serious knee injury against Arsenal back in January.

Leoni, meanwhile, was a victim of profoundly bad luck when he tore his ACL on his debut for the Reds in September 2025, just weeks after signing from Parma.

But after months of rehabilitation, Iraola has confirmed that both men resumed training with the Liverpool first team during the November international break and could soon be in contention for competitive play.

“Very good news from both sides,” Iraola confirmed on Friday.

“I think the international break was the best moment for us to try to introduce them slowly, slowly with the rest of the players. They have done this and now even in the last part of the week they have already started doing things with the team.

“Obviously they are still not available but it’s very good news that they are able to do things with the group.”.

He continued, adding that Liverpool would be gentle with the pair’s reintegration as they look to avoid setbacks.

“It’s true that they have to be loaded carefully – they don’t train every day with us. One day, yes. The next day, not. The next day, yes. We are in the last part of this process, a long process.

“But both of them are looking good and I hope they can play in some weeks.”.

It is said Bradley and Leoni have become close friends as they went through their rehabilitation together at Liverpool’s Kirkby training ground.

Iraola also confirmed Jeremie Frimpong, Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai are all in line to play a role as Liverpool host Manchester United on Sunday.
