📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that andoni Iraola spun on his heels, turned his back to the action and began to bite his nails. Managers often envisage the worst outcome when the clock ticks down, and here, in the 93rd minute, Bournemouth had a corner.

According to recent reports, he needn’t have worried. As the set-piece was swung in, Alisson Becker moved powerfully off his line and plucked the ball from the air, a catch that essentially confirmed Liverpool would leave Dorset with three points. It was a catch, too, that put the gloss on another impeccable personal afternoon.

When Iraola took charge at Anfield, one question he had to answer – given Bournemouth had conceded 167 goals in his three years in charge – was whether he could make Liverpool defensively resilient. This dour 1-0 success, though, proves he is taking them in the right direction: he is the first Liverpool manager since Joe Fagan in 1983 to start with five unbeaten league games.

Alexander Isak might have scored the goal that leaves Bournemouth winless in the Premier League but this success owed everything to Alisson’s enduring brilliance – a comment that also applies to Virgil van Dijk – the enormous promise of Jérémy Jacquet and the grit of Ronaldo Araújo.

You go to top level football matches hoping to see something that will take your breath away and how Alisson did that in the 17th minute with a reflex save from an Evanilson backheel, the shape of his body resembling a fielder in the slips diving to prevent a boundary.

Sources indicate that it proved to be the foundation stone from which Liverpool were able to build and inflict Bournemouth’s first home defeat since January. There are plenty of [valid] questions to ask of Liverpool’s attack at present but, defensively, it is starting to come together.

In a recent development, “It was a really good fight,” Alisson remarked, in that self-effacing way of his. “But we have to improve a lot – on the ball and sometimes off the ball as well but we improved in the second half. We adapted to the opponent and that’s what we are doing.”.

According to recent reports, any manager with a well-drilled defence stands a chance of improving and that is what Liverpool are doing. Only four weeks ago the discussion was about how easy it was for teams to play through their middle – remember that chaotic afternoon at Newcastle to start? – but that is changing swiftly.

Since Iraola replaced Jeremie Frimpong with Araújo at right-back, three consecutive Premier League clean sheets have followed. Araújo, the Uruguayan on loan from Barcelona, revels in doing the dirty work while Jacquet, the £60m signing from Rennes, oozes quality.

Recent findings suggest that “He’s [Jacquet] very young and adapted really well to the Premier League,” Iraola said. “The first games, he was physically feeling the change of rhythm and I had to sub him. This was a step forward. He looked solid until the end. He’s in a good place physically and I hope he can continue his development.”.

Don’t confuse positivity about one aspect of the team as being a guide to its collective health. There was always a chance this contest would become a cagey affair and, Evanilson’s chance aside, the opening 45 minutes were as flat as you could imagine.

Iraola again played his three £100m+ signings but Bradley Barcola is still adjusting to the physicality of English football and Florian Wirtz is still finding it difficult to impose himself on a game; patience with the German will not be infinite.

He would do worse than to look at Isak, who is now on a run of four goals in four league games and is influencing games in the manner Liverpool envisaged when they broke the British transfer record to sign him last August.

Industry observers note that isak had an unusual afternoon. His only shot in the first half almost took out some low-flying pigeons, a cross early in the second half was sliced so badly that the weekend hackers on the nearby Queens Park golf course would have felt a flood of sympathy but then he got his third opening.

Sources indicate that cody Gakpo, who could have been in Manchester City blue had the cards played out differently earlier this month, wriggled down the right flank and squeezed in a cross that Isak seized upon and turned in from six yards. Liverpool never looked back.

Alexander Isak grabs his fourth Premier League goal of the season! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/5ehwhl1it4.

It has been revealed that “A striker’s job is like this,” Iraola said, who badgered Isak persistently to press Bournemouth’s defence. “He had a couple of crosses that he did not hit properly or control. He has to help us to be closer to the box, to play in the opposition’s half and have more meaningful possession. And then if the team is playing there, he will receive rewards in terms of goals.”.

One, ultimately, was enough to see off Bournemouth, whose start to the campaign is something of a riddle. They shouldn’t be anywhere near the relegation places but that is the reality and Thursday’s historic Europa League win in Real Sociedad couldn’t mask the home crowd’s frustration.

Recent findings suggest that “Our attitude and effort is good,” head coach Marco Rose noted. “But, at this level, small things and little details decide games.”.

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, Iraola said: “I’m obviously happy with the result because I know this is a difficult place to come, very difficult place to get three points. And we could see it, especially in the beginning of the game. In the first 20 minutes we weren’t at the level [required] and it cost us. We finished the first half better and in the second half we played better, but that beginning of the game has surprised us, not surprised us [because] we knew where we were coming but it [was] difficult for us.”.

Sources indicate that jeremy Jacquet has made the kind of quietly authoritative start to his Liverpool career that showed why there was such excitement in February within the club when they completed his deal. So much focus on so many players but Jacquet has never been anything other 7.5/8 out of 10.

According to recent reports, cody Gakpo has been Liverpool’s stand-out forward this term and he was at the heart of Isak’s goal this afternoon. Speaking about the job the Dutchman is doing to fill the void left by Mohamed Salah on the right flank, Ashley Young said on Sky Sports: “Players have to step up when you lose big players and you get the opportunities. I think Cody Gakpo is doing that. He’s a bit fortunate [in the build-up to Liverpool’s goal] but you create your own luck. He gets the ball down the line, that’s what you want to do and he puts the ball in the box. That’s what Isak’s waiting for.”.

Industry observers note that andoni Iraola returns to Bournemouth this weekend knowing what to expect from players he understands so well. Sadly, I do not mean Liverpool’s.

Having built his reputation creating a hard-working, well-drilled team rich in potential, Iraola is responsible for infusing those same characteristics into the most expensively assembled squad in Liverpool history.

Sources indicate that his first six games demonstrate it is no quick fix. The Basque coach is the first Liverpool appointment to work with more than £700m of recent signings while being entitled to feel he has been dealt a bad hand.

In a recent development, everything Iraola has stated and done so far screams that he is searching for the right blend in his starting XI while having to eradicate negative traits, with and without the ball. It was telling that the excellent performance of his youngsters against Tottenham Hotspur in midweek offered the clearest hint of Iraola’s vision than anything we have seen with all the high-priced stars on the pitch.

Industry observers note that there is a reason the Kop stood to acclaim the energy and application of youngsters Lewis Koumas, James McConnell and Trey Nyoni – and why Iraola keeps name-checking them. Iraola is indebted to them for issuing a reminder of the non-negotiables that come with being a Liverpool footballer; regardless of price tag and reputation, leaving everything on the pitch is compulsory. It is a concern that so many of the renowned players need to hear that message.

Jurgen Klopp named Florian Wirtz in his first squad as Germany manager and has stated that fans must refrain from expecting “special moments” from the Liverpool playmaker as a matter of course.

Of Wirtz, he remarked: “I think he’s the player who covered the most ground at Liverpool this season, so the willingness is absolutely there.

Industry observers note that “We have to move away from the idea that we need to see special moments from him. He is there to help us as a team. We have to make sure that Flo feels comfortable with us.”.

Wirtz has delivered seven goals and 11 assists in his 54 Liverpool appearances.

Adam Smith, 35, played for Iraola 81 times and he admitted his former manager’s visit to the Vitality will be a sentimental affair. He said: “It’s going to be an emotional day for everyone I think, [for] our ex-manager and some of our players that have played under him, but we’ll be up for the game for sure.”.

Speaking before his return to the South Coast, Iraola remarked: “I know where we are going [the Vitality], and I know the stats they have there [unbeaten in 12 matches], not only in their stadium, overall, I think if you see the games they’ve lost in a long while, you realise how difficult it is to beat Bournemouth.

“But, I suppose I also have the advantage that I know them very well, they also have the advantage that they know me very well, so you never know who has more advantage in that sense.

He added: “On a personal side, I’m very much looking forward to meet them [his former players], to hug them. It’s players that I love, staff that I’ve been working with who I appreciate so much, and I was pushing for them [against Real Sociedad] when they were playing their first European game. I wish them all the best, but there is another part, which is the most key one right now that we need to go there and win.”.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the Premier League match between Liverpool and Bournemouth as Andoni Iraola returns to the Vitality Stadium for the first time since his significant move up north. The Basque propelled Bournemouth to new heights, guiding the club into Europe and his successor, Marco Rose, ensured they made a winning start to life on the Continent by defeating Real Sociedad in midweek.

Previewing Iraola’s Vitality Stadium return, Craig Beazley, host and creator of the Up The Cherries In All Departments podcast, remarked: “We’ve now got the Andoni Iraola return … Andoni is very much a legend really, there should be a statue of Sir Eddie Howe and Sir Andoni Iraola [outside the ground] as well.”.

Across three seasons, Iraola guided Bournemouth to 12th, ninth and sixth in the Premier League, winning 47 of his 127 matches in charge (37 per cent).

Liverpool are still acclimatising to his exacting style of play and their results suggest as much. They are 10th in the table having drawn three and won one, impressing in flashes but struggling to maintain consistently productive final-third patterns and pressing structures. Deploying Ronald Araújo at right-back has proved effective, though, with Liverpool conceding just two goals in their last four matches.

The Cherries are searching for their first Premier League win of the season and have retained the 4-2-3-1 shape from the Iraola days, with Rose preferring a similarly vertical attacking strategy. They continue to leverage their strengths in transitions and in wide areas as Adrien Truffert rains in crosses for any one of Bournemouth’s exuberant frontline to pounce on.

Bayern Munich's chief executive has confirmed Vincent Kompany is expected to return to the dugout on Friday, less than a month after collapsing at the club's training ground.

Kompany collapsed on October 23 while watching Bayern's Under-23 side and reportedly suffered from seizures.

The 40-year-old, who suffered a dislocated shoulder in the fall, underwent tests in hospital which determined that a 'meningeal irritation' had been the cause of his collapse.

If left untreated meningeal irritation can become meningitis. The meninges are the membranes around the brain and spinal cord.

Kompany was discharged from hospital the following week to continue his recovery at home.

The Belgian coach is now set to return to the dugout when Bayern face Cologne on Friday, with Kompany due to also address the media tomorrow morning.

Vincent Kompany is set to return to the Bayern Munich dugout for their Bundesliga match on Friday.

Kompany's return was officially confirmed by Bayern chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen.

In a recent development, 'Yes, Vincent is in pretty good spirits. I ran into him today,' Dreesen told German outlet Abendzeitung.

According to recent reports, 'The meningeal irritation has healed. He has already undergone shoulder surgery.'.

Kompany had led training for the first time since his collapse earlier this week, with his arm reportedly in a sling following his shoulder injury.

He had missed five matches during his recovery with Bayern winning two and drawing against Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga.

The German champions also beat Atletico Madrid in the Champions League in his absence, as well as progressing in the DFB Cup.

Kompany's assistant Aaron Danks had overseen the first team during his recovery.

Danks previously worked as Kompany's assistant at Anderlecht before deputising for Dean Smith and Steven Gerrard at Aston Villa and Michael Carrick at Middlesbrough.

Kompany has missed five matches following his collapse at Bayern's training ground on October 23.

Bayern had stressed they wanted to give Kompany as much time as required to recover before returning to work.

The German giants play eight matches in the next month, including two matches in the Champions League, before the Bundesliga takes its winter break.

Reports had emerged after Kompany's collapse that club officials had been concerned by his irregular eating habits, as well as barely exercising, drinking excessive amounts of coffee, and taking on too much work.

Bayern sporting director Max Eberl dismissed the claims last month, reiterating that Kompany's illness had been the cause of his collapse rather than his workload.

Germany's annual inflation rate eased to 2.8% in October from 3.3% in September, with economists pointing to the government's fuel tax cut as the main reason.

Preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office revealed energy prices rose 12.2% compared with a year earlier, down from 14.9% in September. Services inflation slowed to 2.5%, while food inflation remained at 0.4%.

Sources indicate that "The decisive factor was the fuel tax cut," said Silke Tober of the Macroeconomic Policy Institute. The reduction took effect in October and runs through December, although rising crude oil prices partly offset the savings at the pump.

According to recent reports, ING bank economist Carsten Brzeski noted higher energy costs had yet to feed through into broader price increases. Unlike during the 2022 energy crisis, consumers were unwilling or unable to absorb substantially higher prices, he said.

Sources indicate that it was a state visit of a kind rarely seen today. For four days, Steinmeier traveled across the country: from Hefei, where the German automaker Volkswagen's China operations are headquartered, through historic villages and the imposing landscapes of the Yellow Mountains. He also visited several points of interest of Chinese history, art, and science, and finally, he headed to Tiananmen Square in the heart of Beijing's political center.

Steinmeier—who is set to leave office in March 2027— spoke as a statesman and diplomat on matters of German and European interest. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Steinmeier have known each other for many years, so in this respect, the president was the right man to address even the most difficult concerns as a European.

This political balancing act between respect and criticism did not trigger any visible outrage in Beijing.

When he spoke with Chinese leaders about their subsidies for exports to Europe and the related issue of the trade deficit, Xi replied: "I am ready to work together to open a newly introduced chapter in the comprehensive strategic partnership between our two countries and to advance the development of global governance.".

Just how much willingness lies behind the push for a strategic partnership will become clear during further negotiations between the EU and China.

Xi Jinping seems to understand that a persistent trade deficit with Europe could also become a problem for his country, as an economic crisis in Europe could further strain China's economy.

According to recent reports, as "the world's second- and third-largest economies," China and Germany also bear "an vital responsibility for the development of relations between China and Europe, as well as for stable growth in the global economy," Xi Jinping said. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.

North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.

In remarks to reporters, Merz recalled Germany's reunification 36 years ago.

"Let us hope that Korea too gets the chance one day to regain state unity," he noted.

A glass cabinet containing memorabilia linked to the 1958 Munich Air Disaster, in which eight Manchester United footballers lost their lives, was smashed and plundered in the Munich suburb of Trudering this week.

The display case on Manchesterplatz forms part of a memorial commemorating the tragedy which occurred when the United team made a refueling stop in Munich while on the way back from a European Cup game in Belgrade, Serbia, on February 6, 1958.

In a recent development, the plane struggled to take off again in the wintery conditions at the old Munich-Riem airport to the east of the city center and, on the third attempt, ploughed off the end of the runway and into a house. Of the 44 people on board, 23 were killed, including eight United players, several journalists and two crew members.

The crash site has become a place of pilgrimage for United supporters and, in 2020, the cabinet was installed on the initiative of the Red Docs Munich – a local Bayern Munich fan club – to house the various memorabilia and tributes left by visitors.

Recent findings suggest that munich police said the cabinet was broken into on Monday morning between 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. local time (07:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. UTC), with the unknown perpetrators making off with a glass sculpture and several medals.

"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ifty Ahmed, chairman of the Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF), told the BBC, adding: "Whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories.".

Recent findings suggest that the Red Docs Munich arranged for replacement glass to be installed on the same day. The MMMF said Manchester United had offered to pay for the repairs but said the foundation had covered the costs itself.

The joint commemoration of the 1958 disaster and the maintenance of the memorial site has produced extensive and friendly relations between Bayern Munich and Manchester United, who will meet in the Champions League in January.

Profits of German luxury car brand Audi for the third quarter came plunged 87% year-on-year to €95 million ($106 million), the Volkswagen subsidiary reported on Friday. This is a drop from €718 million seen in the same quarter last year.

The drop comes amid weak demand in China, and US tariffs.

"Market and competitive conditions have become significantly more difficult in the third quarter," Audi chief financial officer Jürgen Rittersberger told journalists on a call.

"That all shows that we need to intensify measures and set clear priorities," he added.

Overall in the first nine months of 2026, Audi's profits have dropped 41% to €1.22 billion.

The carmaker trimmed its 2026 profit outlook down to 3 to 5% for the year, down from the previous 5 to 7%.

Audi's sluggish numbers represent more bad news for the 10-brand Volkswagen Group, which on Thursday reported its largest quarterly loss in more than a ‌decade, at nearly €6 billion.

A ban on new Stolpersteine ("stumbling stones") to commemorate victims of the Holocaust in the eastern German town of Heidenau will be upheld after five petitions against the measure were thrown out.

Local councilors from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voted together in September to pass the controversial ban on new stones being laid in the town in Saxony, near Dresden.

Petitions against the measure were submitted from across Germany — as well as one from the Netherlands — calling for victims of the Nazi regime to continue to be remembered in Heidenau by way of the small metal plaques embedded in pavements.

"Not everybody has to like the stumbling stones but everyone should have the possibility to lay one in public," one councilor, Michael Schürer, told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), criticizing the rejection of the petitions.

The initiators of the Heidenau ban had argued that, while remembering Holocaust victims remains essential, the placement of Stolpersteine leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring victims at a local cemetery instead.

The decision of the local Heidenau CDU to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion sparked a nationwide scandal and furthered the debate over the conservatives' commitment to the political "firewall" against the far right.

Ahead of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier lauded China's role as a global technological and economic power, while emphasizing the responsibility that comes along with it.

"We both bear responsibility for the ⁠international order ​and for the conditions under which states in this world maintain and shape their relations," Steinmeier said.

President Xi praised what he called an "all-dimensional strategic partnership" between China and Germany, calling for new cooperation based on stability and mutual benefit.

"This latest paradigm sends a positive signal to the world: we favor openness over closure, and cooperation over confrontation," Xi stated during opening remarks, emphasizing the start of a "new chapter" in Germany-China ties.

Xi added that he hopes Germany and the European Union will stick by a "rational, pragmatic and friendly" China policy, adding that cooperation outweighs competition and consensus outweighs differences in China-EU relations.

The EU has a massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.

Brussels has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field. Germany with its export based economy, the EU's largest, is hit hard by China's manufacturing surplus flooding global markets.

Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.

Nonetheless, "differences and problems can always be resolved," the Chinese president said.

According to recent reports, on October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called "guest workers" cannot live from their pensions.

Learn more about how "guest workers" are struggling as they reach retirement age in this in depth report by Oliver Pieper.

While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.

In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.

Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.

At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions.".

Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.

Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.

During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.

Merz mentioned the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.

"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and fresh technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.

Recent findings suggest that "These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe.".

During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.

In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.

The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).

"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he remarked in Seoul on Friday.

"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.

"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions.".

Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.

"There is a fear that we might be facing ‌a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ‌ourselves off from other nations," ‌Merz noted.

"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, ‌but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.

Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference  "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region.".

Observation of tunable superradiant frequency combs

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 52 min read (10348 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~52 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that cavity quantum electrodynamics1 with quantum emitters coupled to resonators provides a powerful platform for engineering light–matter interactions2,3 and exploring many-body phenomena4,5.
  • Industry observers note that the invention of the laser stands among the most transformative technological advances of the twentieth century11.
  • Specifically, from a conceptual perspective, conventional lasers and superradiant light sources represent two complementary limits of light–matter interaction in a cavity-coupled system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cavity quantum electrodynamics1 with quantum emitters coupled to resonators provides a powerful platform for engineering light–matter interactions2,3 and exploring many-body phenomena4,5. In particular, superradiance6—arising from collective quantum interference among emitters—has been explored as a route to ultrastable continuous radiation7. However, engineering superradiance in the time domain to realize periodic pulsed sources or frequency combs remains largely unexplored. Here we investigate the non-equilibrium many-body dynamics of a driven spin ensemble coupled with an on-chip superconducting resonator and uncover a dynamical phase transition from continuous-wave to periodic pulsed superradiant emission. To quantitatively capture the observed dynamical phases, we introduce a driven-dissipative cavity-quantum electrodynamics model that elucidates how the periodic pulsed superradiant phase emerges from collective, periodically repeating spin dynamics stabilized by the interplay of coherence growth, disorder and dissipation. We also find that rare-earth ion spin systems with both optical and microwave transitions enable phase-synchronized, dual-rail superradiant frequency combs in both the microwave and the optical domains. Our results not only open new opportunities for atom-based frequency-comb sources and programmable superradiant generation, but establish a fundamental connection between periodic pulsed superradiance and the emergence of a continuous time crystal8,9,10 as a new non-equilibrium phase in driven open systems.

Industry observers note that the invention of the laser stands among the most transformative technological advances of the twentieth century11. Laser operation relies on stimulated emission, whereby coherent radiation emerges once the gain exceeds loss in a resonant cavity12. By contrast, superradiance, first proposed by Dicke in 195413, can also lead to continuous coherent radiation arising from a collective many-body dissipation process in which emission results from quantum interference among an ensemble of emitters6. Remarkably, compared with conventional lasers, superradiant emission can have exceptional frequency stability due to the long coherence of atomic transitions, along with output power that scales nonlinearly with ensemble size7. Superradiance has been observed across a wide range of platforms in both free space and cavity-coupled systems, including cold atoms14,15,16, atomic gases17,18, artificial atoms19,20,21 and solid-state defects22,23,24.

Specifically, from a conceptual perspective, conventional lasers and superradiant light sources represent two complementary limits of light–matter interaction in a cavity-coupled system. Conventional lasers rely on stimulated emission, where the coherence is governed primarily by the cavity field. Superradiant systems, however, operate in the opposite regime, where coherence resides predominantly in the atomic ensemble, and radiation emerges from collectively synchronized dissipation driven by atom–atom correlations mediated by a lossy (bad) cavity (Fig. 1a–c). In this regime, the dynamics are naturally described within the framework of cavity quantum electrodynamics (QED), where light–matter interactions are treated at the fundamental quantum-mechanical level and different photon emission mechanisms can be individually identified25. This perspective has motivated extensive studies on superradiant dynamics in cavity QED systems1,2,26,27, including superradiant bursts28,29, triggered superradiance30 and ultra-narrow-linewidth superradiant lasers7,31,32.

According to recent reports, a, An ensemble of two-level atoms, \(\{| \uparrow \rangle ,| \downarrow \rangle \}\), coupled with a common cavity field. The cavity output serves simultaneously as a probe of the intracavity dynamics and as an emitted light field generated by the atomic ensemble. b, The frequency–domain picture for a superradiant, bad-cavity regime, where the inhomogeneously broadened atomic linewidth, Γ, is narrower than the cavity linewidth, κ. c, A comparison table between conventional and superradiant light sources. d, Three types of superradiant dynamics: superradiant burst emission under a transient pump (di), steady superradiant emission under a continuous-wave (CW) pump (dii), and periodic pulsed superradiant emission under a continuous-wave pump (diii). In diii, as the cavity coupling strength increases, periodic pulsed emission dynamics emerge due to the spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translation symmetry under a continuous-wave drive. We find that the periodicity, T, of the pulsed emission is set by the ensemble cooperativity, whereas the onset time, t0, of the resulting pulse train relative to the start of the continuous-wave drive is spontaneously random. e, A phase diagram of a cavity QED model showing three distinct phases of no superradiance (SR) (I), continuous-wave superradiance (CW SR) (II) and periodic superradiance (III). These phases are distinguished by the interplay of cavity-mediated collective coupling and dissipation, and disorder due to the frequency inhomogeneity of the emitters. The coutinuous-wave superradiance phase emerges when the ensemble cooperativity exceeds unity (C = 1, black solid line), whereas the periodic superradiance phase is expected to emerge when the normalized cavity–ensemble coupling strength exceeds unity (gnorm = 1, black dashed line). Surprisingly, the phase transition into the periodic superradiance phase occurs at a weaker coupling strength in our experiment due to the presence of disorder, consistent with our theoretical prediction (red solid line). The yellow vertical bar indicates the experimentally probed regime of collective coupling strengths (refer to the main text and Supplementary Information for details).

In a recent development, historically, advances in laser physics have demonstrated that introducing nonlinear elements can drive systems into unstable dynamical regimes33, enabling the development of mode-locked lasers that generate periodic, ultrafast optical pulses34. This periodic emission in the time domain, corresponding to a frequency comb in the spectral domain, dramatically expands the impact of lasers across science and industry35,36. This naturally raises curiosity into whether superradiant systems can support frequency-comb-like emission that produces time-periodic, phase-coherent pulse trains, and if so, what mechanism underlies this behaviour, and whether the resulting time-domain pulsing can be engineered.

In a recent development, although recent theoretical37 and experimental38,39 efforts have begun to explore periodic pulsed superradiant dynamics in driven-dissipative systems, a clear understanding of their physical origin and underlying mechanisms, as well as comprehensive experimental demonstrations, remains elusive. Here we develop a unified theoretical and experimental framework that elucidates how superradiant frequency combs emerge in a driven cavity QED system of quantum emitters through the interplay of atomic coherence, dissipation and disorder, where the nonlinearity is provided by superradiant emission. Building on this framework, we experimentally investigate non-equilibrium superradiant dynamics in a disordered spin ensemble coupled to a superconducting microwave cavity, and show that robust, phase-coherent superradiant pulse trains can be both probed and engineered, with their pulse repetition rate set by the ensemble cooperativity. Unexpectedly, we also observe simultaneous and correlated periodic microwave and optical superradiant emissions that are both time-synchronized and phase-coherent. We refer to this phenomenon as dual-rail superradiant frequency combs, which opens upcoming opportunities for ensemble-based quantum technologies. Furthermore, our results reveal a fundamental connection to a continuous time crystal, that is, a dynamical phase of matter in driven, non-equilibrium cavity QED systems characterized by spontaneously broken continuous time-translation symmetry and the emergence of robust temporal order.

Industry observers note that to develop an intuitive understanding of the physical origin and mechanisms underlying superradiant frequency-comb formation, we consider an ensemble of frequency-inhomogeneous two-level quantum emitters (\(| \downarrow \rangle ,| \uparrow \rangle \)) coupled to a common lossy cavity mode and driven by an external pump. The microscopic dynamics of such cavity–ensemble interactions are imprinted on the cavity output, which serves as the primary experimentally accessible observable of the system’s cavity QED behaviour. Specifically, the photon emission rate, Γph, is governed by three distinct emission processes: Purcell-enhanced spontaneous emission, stimulated emission and superradiant emission25:.

Here g is the single atom-cavity coupling strength; κ is the cavity decay rate; N is the number of quantum emitters; \({\widehat{S}}_{z}=\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{j}{\widehat{\sigma }}_{z,j}\) is the collective spin operator along the z direction, representing the total population imbalance of the ensemble with \({\widehat{\sigma }}_{z,j}={| \downarrow \rangle }_{j}\langle \downarrow | -{| \uparrow \rangle }_{j}\langle \uparrow | \) for the jth spin; \({\widehat{S}}_{\downarrow \uparrow }={\sum }_{j}{\widehat{\sigma }}_{\downarrow \uparrow ,j}\) and \({\widehat{S}}_{\uparrow \downarrow }={\widehat{S}}_{\downarrow \uparrow }^{\dagger }\) represent the collective ensemble coherence obtained from the sum of individual atomic coherences, with \({\widehat{\sigma }}_{\downarrow \uparrow ,j}={| \downarrow \rangle }_{j}\langle \uparrow | \); and \(\widehat{b}\) and \({\widehat{b}}^{\dagger }\) are the cavity annihilation and creation operators, respectively (Methods).

Sources indicate that in contrast to conventional laser systems, where emission is dominated by stimulated emission (second term in equation (1)), superradiant systems are governed by collective spin correlations (third term), with the photon emission rate scaling as \(\langle {\widehat{S}}_{\uparrow \downarrow }{\widehat{S}}_{\downarrow \uparrow }\rangle \propto {N}^{2}\). This collective behaviour acts as an effective nonlinearity, providing the foundation for dynamical phase transitions in superradiance.

It has been revealed that although three different mechanisms contribute to the photon emission rate, the presence of superradiant dynamics can first be identified by monitoring the emission following a transient excitation pump pulse (Fig. 1di). In this case, superradiant ensembles have a delayed burst of emission arising from stochastic quantum fluctuations that initiate synchronized dissipation of individual emitters, providing a clear signature of superradiance14,28.

In a recent development, transitioning from a transient pump to a continuous-wave pump, the superradiant ensemble can support continuous emission by reaching a steady-state condition under the continuous-wave pump (Fig. 1dii). Analogous to a conventional laser, this condition is achieved when the cavity-mediated gain, \(\frac{4N{g}^{2}}{\kappa }\), is greater than the atomic dephasing rate, Γ (here, Γ is the linewidth of the emitter ensemble). Equivalently, defining the ensemble cooperativity as \(C=\frac{4N{g}^{2}}{\kappa \varGamma }\), continuous-wave superradiant emission occurs when C ≥ 1 (Fig. 1e, solid black line).

Crucially, when the coherent cavity–ensemble coupling strength, \(\sqrt{N}g\), exceeds the cavity-induced decoherence rate, κ/2, the steady-state dynamics can break down, turning continuous-wave into periodic pulsed emission (Fig. 1diii and Fig. 1e, dashed black line). In this regime, quantum interference between the strongly dressed cavity–ensemble states drives oscillatory behaviour in the photon emission. Surprisingly, however, we find that the presence of moderate disorder (defined as an extra inhomogeneous contribution to spectral line broadening beyond the homogeneous linewidth) substantially lowers the critical coupling threshold, thereby facilitating the phase transition into the pulsed phase (Fig. 1e, solid red line). Refer to the Supplementary Information for details on the theoretical phase boundary, which is estimated on the basis of a Hopf bifurcation model.

In a recent development, using our driven-dissipative cavity QED model, we elucidate how such periodic pulsed emission directly originates from an emergent, time-periodic trajectory of the spin ensemble, in which collective coherence builds up, collapses through synchronized dissipation, and is then rebuilt under continuous pumping (inset of Fig. 1diii). We find from both our experiment and the theoretical model that this persistent pulsed emission repeats robustly without decay, with a periodicity, T ∝ 1/C, set by the ensemble cooperativity, C. This periodic superradiance phase, arising intrinsically and spontaneously from time-independent cavity QED dynamics, stands in stark contrast to conventional mode-locked lasers, where the periodicity is externally imposed by the cavity round-trip time. Such spontaneously broken time-translation symmetry, leading to the emergence of temporal order, defines a continuous time crystal—a class of non-equilibrium phases of matter that has been explored in a variety of driven-dissipative systems8,9,10,40.

We use rare-earth-ion-doped crystals to experimentally explore superradiant dynamics; such crystals offer highly coherent transitions in both the microwave and optical domains at cryogenic temperatures41,42, and are readily compatible with on-chip cavity QED architectures43,44,45,46. In particular, we use an ensemble of ytterbium-171 ions doped in a yttrium orthovanadate crystal47, whose excited-state spin manifold forms a two-level system, \(\{|\uparrow \rangle ,|\downarrow \rangle \}\), with a microwave transition frequency of ω = 2π × 3.4 GHz and an inhomogeneously broadened linewidth of Γ = 2π × 160 kHz (Fig. 2a). A superconducting microwave resonator with a cavity linewidth of κ = 2π × 3.6 MHz is fabricated on the crystal to couple to the excited-state microwave spin transition. We measured a maximum collective coupling strength of \(\sqrt{N}g\approx 2{\rm{\pi }}\times 1.1\) MHz, corresponding to a normalized coupling strength of \({g}_{{\rm{norm}}}=2\sqrt{N}g/\kappa \approx 0.6\), which lies below the critical threshold necessary for inducing the periodic superradiant phase in the absence of disorder (Extended Data Fig. 1).

a, Schematic of the effective three-level structure, \(\{|\uparrow \rangle ,|\downarrow \rangle ,|g\rangle \}\), of our spin ensemble. A continuous-wave optical pump controls the net population in the two-level microwave spin manifold, \(\{|\downarrow \rangle ,|\uparrow \rangle \}\), by driving optical transitions between \(|g\rangle \) and \(|\uparrow \rangle \). Thus, the collective coupling strength, which scales with N, can be readily tuned by varying the pump power. A superconducting microwave resonator (red) couples the \(|\downarrow \rangle \leftrightarrow |\uparrow \rangle \) transition at around 3.4 GHz. A weak optical Fabry–Pérot mode (yellow) at about 304 THz couples the optical transitions (refer to Fig. 4 for transferred optical superradiance). b, Bloch-sphere representations of superradiant dynamics in three distinct regimes (I, no superradiance (SR); II, continuous-wave superradiance (CW SR); III, periodic superradiance) probed with increasing collective coupling strength. In regime I, the collective coupling is too weak to generate ensemble coherence, resulting in no superradiance. In regime II, a stable balance among cavity-induced coherence growth (red arrows), disorder-induced precession (blue arrows) and dephasing (black arrows) stabilizes continuous superradiant emission for all individual spins. Five spins are depicted representatively. In regime III, the continuous-wave superradiance phase becomes unstable due to increased coupling strength, driving the spin system into a phase characterized by persistent, periodic pulsed emission dynamics. The periodic behaviour originates from a stable limit cycle, characterized by recurring cycles of coherence growth, precession and dephasing. c, Time-domain superradiance emission profiles for the three regimes, as the continuous-wave pump power increases from 0  to 36 μW (refer to the Methods for measurement details). d, Corresponding Fourier spectra for the three regimes. Insets in regimes II and III show linewidths of approximately 30 and 50 Hz, respectively, which are about three orders of magnitude narrower than the spin inhomogeneous linewidth (about 160 kHz). e, Microwave superradiant emission power as a function of continuous-wave pump strength. The corresponding normalized collective coupling strength, gnorm, is shown on the top x axis (Fig. 1e, yellow line, and Extended Data Fig. 1). Black (blue) points denote the total (sideband) spectral power, Atot (Asb). The phase transitions into the continuous-wave and periodic phases are marked by sharp increases in Atot and Asb, respectively. The inset demonstrates the time-crystalline fraction, Asb/Atot, providing a clear distinction between the continuous-wave and periodic superradiance phases as a function of pump power.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, although the total available number of ytterbium ions in the cavity is on the order of Ntot ≈ 4 × 1010, we can control the effective emitter number, N ≤ Ntot, which participates in superradiant dynamics by varying the optical pump power that transfers population to the \(|\uparrow \rangle \) state in the excited-state manifold (Fig. 2a). We experimentally verify that superradiance dominates the dynamics of our dense cavity-coupled spin ensemble by observing that the delay time (τd) of a superradiant burst under a transient pump scales inversely with the effective ensemble size, N, that is, τd ∝ 1/N (Extended Data Fig. 2). Notably, by simply varying the continuous-wave pump power, we can continuously tune the ensemble cooperativity, thereby enabling systematic exploration of superradiant dynamics and phase transitions across three distinct regimes: no superradiance (regime I), continuous-wave superradiance (regime II) and periodic superradiance (regime III) (Fig. 2b; Fig. 1e, yellow line).

We first probe non-equilibrium dynamics under a weak continuous-wave pump at low collective cavity coupling strength. In this regime, the \(|\uparrow \rangle \)-state population is insufficient to establish collective behaviour, and no superradiant emission occurs (Fig. 2c,d, regime I).

According to recent reports, however, as the pump power increases and crosses the critical threshold at which the ensemble cooperativity exceeds unity, a steady-state coherence emerges in this non-equilibrium setting, giving rise to continuous-wave superradiance (regime II). Intuitively, in the Bloch-sphere picture, this can be understood as a balance of competing contributions acting on each spin, where disorder, dephasing and coherence growth terms compensate one another, resulting in a collectively enhanced steady-state coherence (Fig. 2b, regime II). In the Fourier spectrum, we find that the emission linewidth is around 30 Hz—a value that is orders of magnitude narrower than the inhomogeneous ensemble linewidth (Fig. 2d, regime II; Extended Data Fig. 3).

In a recent development, upon further increasing the pump power, and thus the collective coupling strength, we observe that the continuous-wave superradiant emission becomes unstable, leading to a breakdown of the balance, which in turn gives rise to time-periodic pulsed emission dynamics (regime III). Essentially, a stronger pump provides a larger nonlinear perturbation in the collective ensemble coherence, which triggers synchronized dissipation across the entire spin ensemble. The decayed emitters are then repumped into the excited state, forming a closed, repeating cycle that generates a persistent superradiant pulse train (Fig. 2c, regime III). This behaviour can also be understood as a Hopf bifurcation that signals the breakdown of steady-state dynamics and leads to the emergence of a stable limit cycle8. In the spectral domain we observe a frequency-comb structure with a narrow comb linewidth of about 50 Hz, indicating stable phase coherence of the pulses (Fig. 2d, regime III).

We analyse the emission spectrum in detail to systematically determine the phase boundaries across the three distinct superradiant phases (Fig. 2e). Specifically, we define the total emitted spectral power as \({A}_{{\rm{tot}}}={\int }_{-\infty }^{+\infty }S(\omega )d\omega \), and the total sideband power as \({A}_{{\rm{sb}}}={\int }_{-\infty }^{{\omega }_{p}-\Delta \omega /2}S(\omega )d\omega +{\int }_{{\omega }_{p}+\Delta \omega /2}^{+\infty }S(\omega )d\omega \), where S(ω) is the power spectral density of the time-domain emission signal, ωp is the frequency corresponding to the peak spectral density and Δω is a narrow integration window that isolates the central spectral peak. These quantities serve as effective experimental order parameters that distinguish the three phases in our experiment. Concretely, the onset of continuous-wave superradiance (regimes I to II) is marked by a sharp increase in Atot, whereas the transition from the continuous-wave to the pulsed superradiant phase (regimes II to III) is signalled by a sharp increase in Asb. To more clearly characterize the second phase transition, we introduce the normalized sideband fraction, which is defined as the ratio Asb/Atot. This quantity, which has also been used to characterize the crystalline fraction in time-crystal phenomena8,48, provides a clear signature of the transition into the periodic superradiant phase (Fig. 2e, inset).

Sources indicate that crucially, this robust temporal ordering in the superradiant dynamics emerges spontaneously under strictly time-independent continuous-wave pumping, without any externally imposed modulation or timing reference. By repeating the experiment under identical conditions, we find that the onset time of the superradiant pulse train is spontaneously random from experiment to experiment (Extended Data Fig. 4), providing direct evidence of the spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translation symmetry8. Our experimental measurements and numerical simulations consistently indicate that the system satisfies the defining criteria of a time-crystalline phase (Extended Data Table 1).

It has been revealed that A natural follow-up investigation would be to determine what sets the periodicity of the persistent, periodic superradiant phase. According to our theoretical framework, the periodicity of the superradiant bursts is determined by the ensemble cooperativity, which depends on the number of emitters participating in the superradiant dynamics. To probe this experimentally, we selectively excite different spectral subsets of ytterbium ions by intentionally detuning the pump carrier frequency across an optical inhomogeneous linewidth of about 2π × 92 MHz. This allows us to systematically vary the number of emitters excited to the \(|\uparrow \rangle \) state within the microwave superradiant manifold while keeping the pump Rabi frequency unchanged (Fig. 3a).

According to recent reports, a, Optical inhomogeneous broadening profile with a linewidth of about 2π × 92 MHz for Ntot ≈ 4 × 1010 ions in our system. By tuning the continuous-wave pump detuning, Δpump, relative to the ensemble centre frequency, different spectral subsets of spins are selectively pumped into the excited-state manifold, enabling continuous control of the effective ensemble size that participates in superradiance. b, Measured phase diagram showing superradiant emission (red, regimes II and III) and no superradiance (blue, regime I) phases under varying pump detuning and power. The dashed line indicates the calculated phase boundary corresponding to an ensemble cooperativity of 1. c, Time-domain microwave superradiant bursts recorded at various pump detunings under 36 μW pump power. The superradiant burst periodicity, T, varies systematically with pump detuning. d, Numerical simulations of the periodic superradiant phase based on the same experimental conditions used in c, showing good agreement between theory and experiment. e, Detuning-resolved experimental time traces from c at pump detunings of Δpump/2π = 2.4, 12, 18.4, 26.4, 31.2 and 36 MHz, illustrating how periodicity and emission intensity vary with detuning. Darker (fainter) colours correspond to smaller (larger) detuning values. f, Rescaled time traces from e, demonstrating universal data collapse (refer to the main text for details).

It has been revealed that as shown in Fig. 3b, the threshold for the onset of superradiant emission increases as the optical pump is detuned away from the centre of the inhomogeneous linewidth, indicating that pump detuning serves as an effective control knob for tuning the collective cavity–ensemble coupling strength. In regime III we observe that the superradiant burst periodicity, T, also depends sensitively on the pump detuning (Fig. 3c): T increases as the detuning moves away from zero. Numerical simulations show strong quantitative agreement with our experimental observations, further corroborating the effective tuning of the collective coupling strength via pump detuning in our system (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 5).

As our theoretical framework reveals that T scales inversely with the ensemble size N, while the intensity scales quadratically with N, we rescale both the time and intensity axes of all measured superradiant burst profiles, acquired at different detuning values, by their corresponding effective ensemble size. Remarkably, we find that all data collapse onto a single universal curve (Fig. 3e,f). This universal collapse demonstrates that the periodic superradiant phase is governed by collective scaling laws set by the effective size of the driven spin ensemble, independent of the microscopic details of individual emitters.

Sources indicate that collectively, our experimental findings, in agreement with our theoretical model, indicate that the periodic superradiant phase is a robust collective phenomenon representing a non-equilibrium phase of matter in driven open quantum systems. To further substantiate this, we perform extensive numerical simulations addressing the following three key aspects (Extended Data Fig. 6). First, we confirm that, in our experimental regime, the nonlinear superradiant term associated with collective ensemble correlations dominates the conventional stimulated emission term by more than an order of magnitude. Second, we verify that the observed pulsed phase originates from a large atomic ensemble, as it cannot be explained by a single emitter with an artificially enhanced coupling strength. Third, we demonstrate that disorder plays an essential role, as the periodic superradiant phase does not emerge in the absence of disorder for the experimentally measured coupling strength, gnorm ≈ 0.6. This finding implies that inhomogeneous broadening is not merely a source of decoherence, but can instead be harnessed to engineer collective quantum interference, thereby reshaping photon-emission dynamics in the cavity QED system.

Although our experimental results so far have focused on superradiance in the microwave domain, our ytterbium-ion-based system intrinsically comprises a three-level structure that involves both microwave and optical transitions. Direct optical superradiance is not observed due to the low optical cooperativity49 (of about 0.14). However, we find that the periodic superradiant dynamics in the microwave transition is transferred to the optical transition via a coherent Raman scattering process50 (\(|g\rangle \langle \uparrow |\cdot | \uparrow \rangle \langle \downarrow |\Rightarrow |g\rangle \langle \downarrow |\)). Consequently, the transferred optical field coherently inherits the temporal dynamics of the microwave field, giving rise to correlated, dual-rail frequency-comb generation in both the microwave and optical domains (Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8). As shown in Fig. 4a, the optical and microwave signals have temporally synchronized burst sequences, demonstrating that both emissions originate from the same underlying collective dynamics. To quantify the coherence between the two emission channels, we analyse their relative phase difference and observe a zero-phase offset, indicating in-phase locking across the microwave and optical domains (Fig. 4b). We further characterize the spectra of the dual-rail frequency combs and confirm that the narrow comb structures are well matched and have the same repetition rate (Fig. 4c).

It has been revealed that a, Simultaneously recorded microwave and optical superradiant burst emissions under 200-μW pump power over a 500-μs window, showing time-synchronized pulsed superradiance emission. The overlays represent the signal amplitudes after demodulation (Fig. 2a). Mixers with a local oscillator (LO) are used for measurement (Methods; refer to Extended Data Fig. 7 for measurements taken over a 100-ms window, and Extended Data Fig. 8 for phase-stability analysis). b, Relative phase difference between microwave (ϕMW) and optical (ϕOP) superradiant bursts. The phases of individual pulses are analysed using a magnified 20 μs window on each burst within a 2 ms continuous measurement frame, revealing strong in-phase correlation, that is, ϕMW − ϕOP ≈ 0 with a s.d. of about 0.06π, across the two emission channels. c, Emission spectrum of the transferred optical superradiance (yellow), overlaid with that of the microwave superradiance (blue, identical to that shown in Fig. 2d), revealing a spectrally overlapping frequency-comb structure.

In a recent development, our work positions disordered solid-state cavity QED systems as a versatile platform at the intersection of cavity QED, non-equilibrium physics and quantum metrology. A central result is a unified understanding of dynamical phase transitions in a driven cavity QED system, where the periodic pulsed superradiant phase can be identified as a continuous time-crystal phase. We also demonstrate the unexpected observation and tunable engineering of robust dual-rail superradiant frequency combs in both the microwave and optical domains. We believe these results pave the way for stable atom-based frequency comb sources, superradiance-based waveform synthesis and coherent microwave-optical quantum interconnects.

Industry observers note that our platform opens several promising avenues for future exploration. The repetition rate is at the moment limited by the optical pumping rate required to rebuild population inversion. Incorporating a high-cooperativity optical cavity would Purcell-enhance the repumping process, which would increase the transferred optical emission strength and enable higher repetition rates and faster control over ensemble participation, while also allowing direct generation of a tunable optical superradiant frequency comb. In parallel, recent advances in superconducting microwave technology offer fresh opportunities to dynamically engineer the cavity-mediated interactions that govern the collective dynamics. Combined control over ensemble coupling, dissipation and detuning will unlock a powerful route to programmable quantum light sources, enabling on-demand synthesis of tailored emission waveforms and new paradigms in coherent quantum control.

Industry observers note that 171Yb3+:YVO4 crystals are grown by Gamdan Optics and further diced into 6 mm × 6 mm × 0.5 mm chips. The ytterbium-171 concentration is measured to be 340 ppm via secondary ion mass spectrometry. A 150-nm niobium film is sputtered onto the chip surface at 3.5 mTorr. The device patterns are written by an electron beam lithography system (Raith EBPG 5200) with an ma-N 2403 photoresist. A 25-nm aluminium layer was evaporated as a hard mask, followed by further lift-off using remover PG. The niobium was dry-etched in a plasma-reactive ion etcher, and the aluminium mask was removed using a wet-etching process with aluminium etchant and 3.5% hydrofluoric acid. Finally, a 100-nm gold layer is evaporated on the back of the chip to form a reflective coating.

In a recent development, A master laser (Toptica DL Pro) is locked to a stable cavity reference (Stable laser systems) via the Pound–Drever–Hall method, resulting in an approximately 22 kHz locking linewidth. The experimental laser (Moglabs CEL) is offset-locked to the master laser using a Vescent D2-135 servo and TPI 1005-A frequency source for further tuning the locking frequency. This frequency source is frequency-locked to a 10 MHz rubidium frequency standard (SRS FS725) with a specified phase noise below −130 dBc Hz–1 at a 10 Hz offset. The chip is mounted on the mixing-chamber plate of a dilution refrigerator (Bluefors LD250). A total of 70-dB attenuation is distributed along the microwave input lines. The microwave output line is connected to cryogenic circulators (LNF-CIC2.8-4.3A) at the mixing chamber plate and linked to a high-electron-mobility transistor amplifier (LNF-LNC2-6B) at 4 K plate via superconducting coax cables. The microwave signal outside the fridge is measured on a Field Fox N9915A spectrum analyser and an oscilloscope (Tektronix TDS7104). For pulsed measurements, a digitizer (Alazar ATS9130) is used to acquire data after mixing down to 5 MHz with an IQ mixer (Marki Microwave IQ0307 LXP). When analysing the total sideband power Asb, we use Δω = 2π × 10 kHz to fully isolate the central spectral peak from adjacent sidebands. The memory depth of our acquisition instrument for IQ detection limits the longest continuously recorded single-shot trace to 100 ms (Extended Data Fig. 7). However, we observe no discernible decay in the periodic superradiance over several hours of data acquisition each day.

The optical pump is delivered into the device through a pair of aspheric lenses and collected along the same path via the gold layer reflection. The beam is focused on the gold layer with a 4-μm beam waist, resulting in a 20-μm beam waist on the front surface of the chip for the experiment. The collected optical photons are combined with another optical path outside the fridge from the same experiment laser for heterodyne measurements at a 200-MHz offset frequency, which is also frequency-locked to the rubidium frequency standard. The optical heterodyne signal is detected by a high-speed photodiode (ALPHALAS UPD-35-IR-2) and further analysed using Field Fox N9115A spectrum analyser, or down-converted to 5 MHz with an IQ mixer (Marki Microwave IQ0307 LXP) and measured on Tektronix TDS7104 oscilloscope. For pulsed excitations, an acousto-optic modulator (Aerodiode model 6) shapes the optical pump beam with a trigger from Zurich HDAWG. All electronics used in experiments are externally referenced to the 10-MHz rubidium frequency standard. All of the relevant experimental parameters can be found in Extended Data Table 2.

For the phase coherence analysed in Extended Data Fig. 8, we record the IQ traces of the microwave and optical field, I(t) and Q(t), using the four channels of an oscilloscope (Tektronix TDS7104). We reconstruct the complex heterodyne field as Z(t) = I(t) + iQ(t) = A(t)eiϕ(t), where A(t) and ϕ(t) are the amplitude and phase at time t, respectively. By centring each pulse in the time-domain pulse-train traces, we estimate the standard deviation of the pulse-to-pulse phase (normalized amplitude) variations to be 0.03π (0.009) and 0.11π (0.05) for the microwave and optical fields, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 8b,d). We note that the transferred optical superradiant pulse train follows the microwave-domain pulse train as a result of the coherent Raman scattering process. The larger standard deviation of the optical superradiant pulse train is probably dominated by the higher detection noise floor and the phase instability of the optical heterodyne set-up.

To gain an intuitive understanding, we first apply a mean-field approximation to the Heisenberg equation of motion for the spin (\(\widehat{\sigma }\)) and cavity (\(\widehat{b}\)) operators, which are given by:.

Here, κ is the cavity decay rate, Fe(t) represents time-dependent random noise fluctuations in the cavity field, which induce random kicks that drive the population-inverted Bloch spin vectors away from z-axis, ωk is the kth spin transition frequency, γ is the homogeneous spin dephasing rate, D is the incoherent pumping rate into the \(|\uparrow \rangle \) state, and γ1 is the spin relaxation rate. Note that the equations of motion include incoherent processes such as pumping, cavity dissipation and noise terms, thereby capturing the intrinsic openness of cavity QED systems. In particular, the spin inversion or, equivalently, the spin polarization towards the \(|\uparrow \rangle \) state, is determined by the balance between incoherent pumping and the relaxation process.

In the bad cavity regime, where the cavity decay rate, κ, is much greater than the collective coupling strength, \(\sqrt{N}g\), we can adiabatically eliminate the cavity field, which yields a reduced set of equations of motion involving only the spin degrees of freedom:.

Here, \({\widehat{S}}_{z}=\frac{1}{2}{\sum }_{k}{\widehat{\sigma }}_{z,k}\) is the collective spin polarization along the z-axis with \({\widehat{\sigma }}_{z,k}={\widehat{\sigma }}_{\downarrow \downarrow ,k}-{\widehat{\sigma }}_{\uparrow \uparrow ,k}\); \({F}_{k}(t)=(\frac{-ig\langle {\widehat{\sigma }}_{z,k}\rangle }{i{\Delta }_{e}+\kappa /2}){F}_{e}(t)\) and \({F}_{z}(t)\,=\) \(2\,{\rm{Re}}\,[(\frac{ig\langle {\hat{S}}_{\uparrow \downarrow }\rangle }{i{\Delta }_{e}+\kappa /2}){F}_{e}(t)]\) are the spin noise fluctuations arising from Fe(t); and δk = ωk − ω0 is the detuning of the kth spin relative to the centre of the inhomogeneous ensemble line profile. As, in our experiment, the microwave cavity field is approximately homogeneous inside the beam waist49, we assume that the cavity coupling strength is homogeneous across all spins based on the finite-element simulations of the microwave resonator mode49, that is, gk = g. Note that the rate of change of an individual spin’s coherence, \(\langle {\mathop{\widehat{{\sigma }}}\limits^{.}}_{\downarrow \uparrow ,k}\rangle \), depends on the collective ensemble coherence, \(\langle {\widehat{S}}_{\uparrow \downarrow }\rangle \), as a result of cavity-mediated interaction. In the presence of ensemble coherence, spin inversion (\(\langle {\widehat{\sigma }}_{z,k}\rangle < 0\)), acting in tandem, leads to the growth of individual spin coherence. At the collective level, the ensemble polarization dynamics, \(\langle {\mathop{\widehat{{S}}}\limits^{.}}_{z}\rangle \), depends on \(\langle {\widehat{S}}_{\uparrow \downarrow }\rangle \langle {\widehat{S}}_{\downarrow \uparrow }\rangle \), which is responsible for superradiant decay when this term is dominant. The full theoretical formalism and simulations—including both the optical and microwave cavities and their corresponding mean-field equations—can be found in Supplementary Section 1.

Although the mean-field equations provide a leading-order, intuitive understanding of superradiant cavity QED dynamics with a disordered spin ensemble, the numerically simulated periodicity of pulsed superradiance is inconsistent with the experimental observations (Supplementary Information).

Recent findings suggest that to address this discrepancy, we use a second-order cumulant expansion51 in numerical simulations to more accurately capture the spin–spin correlations responsible for the superradiance process. As random on-site disorder breaks the permutation symmetry among the spins, it prevents us from using collective spin operators for the numerical simulation, thereby requiring full many-body simulations52. Recent findings suggest that where \({\tau }_{{\rm{d}}}\approx \frac{\kappa }{2N{g}^{2}}\log (| \tan (\frac{\theta }{2})| )\) is the delay time of a superradiance burst, where \(\theta ={\cos }^{-1}(2\langle {\widehat{S}}_{z}(0)\rangle /N)\). The duration of the burst, τw, is given by \({\tau }_{{\rm{w}}}=\frac{\kappa }{N{g}^{2}}\log (\sqrt{2}+1)\). Note that both the delay time, τd, and the burst width, τw, scale inversely proportional to the emitter ensemble size, N, that is, τd, τw ∝ 1/N. Experimental results showing good agreement with the theoretical predictions are presented in Extended Data Fig. 2.

Our theoretical framework predicts how the burst periodicity (T), peak power (Ppeak) and average emission power (\({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\)) scale with the number of participating emitters, N (Extended Data Fig. 5a). First, the burst periodicity is governed by the ensemble cooperativity, leading to the scaling of T ∝ 1/N (Extended Data Fig. 5b). Second, each burst originates from the collective emission of an inverted ensemble of N atoms, resulting in the emission of N photons. As the superradiant burst duration, τw, scales inversely with the ensemble size, that is, τw ∝ 1/N, the peak power—proportional to the burst energy divided by its duration—scales quadratically with N, that is, Ppeak ∝ N2 (Extended Data Fig. 5c). Third, the average emission power follows from the burst energy multiplied by the repetition rate, leading to the same quadratic scaling with N, that is, \({\overline{P}}_{{\rm{MW}}}\propto {N}^{2}\) (Extended Data Fig. 5d).

As shown in Extended Data Fig. 5, all of these scaling predictions are in excellent agreement with the experimental data. This agreement enables a universal rescaling of the experimentally observed superradiant pulse trains in terms of the effective ensemble size N, or equivalently, the experimentally tunable cooperativity.

Industry observers note that the emission linewidth of a superradiant atomic ensemble has been studied extensively in the literature, both in the thermal ground-state and finite-temperature regimes54,55. By linearizing the quantum Langevin equations in the frequency domain, one can compute the phase fluctuation correlation function of the emitted field and hence derive the emission linewidth as.

where nc is the intracavity photon number; κc and κa are the linewidths of the cavity mode and atomic ensemble, respectively; nth is the thermal occupancy of the cavity mode; and nsp is the spontaneous emission factor. The linewidth is therefore determined by noise contributions from both the thermal bath of the cavity mode and the imperfect inversion of the atomic ensemble. In the ideal limit of a quantum ground state with perfect population inversion, one recovers the result of ref. 7 by setting nth = nsp = 0. Noting that the emission power P is proportional to the intracavity photon number, that is, P ∝ nc, the linewidth correspondingly narrows as ΔfST ∝ 1/P.

By fitting equation (13) to the data shown in Extended Data Fig. 3, we extract a total noise contribution of nth + nsp = 5.8 quanta. From numerical simulations, the spontaneous emission factor is estimated to be nsp = 2.6 quanta, leaving nth = 3.2 quanta for the thermal occupancy of the microwave resonator, corresponding to an effective resonator temperature of around 0.6 K.

Recent findings suggest that we also observe a correlation between the microwave and optical transition frequencies, consistent with previous observations56. The laser linewidth is carefully calibrated using the Pound–Drever–Hall error signal, yielding a locking linewidth of 22 kHz. This corresponds to a 27 Hz limit on the microwave emission frequency, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 3b.

Sources indicate that on the optical side, the transferred superradiant emission inherits the linewidth of the optical pump laser due to energy conservation. The data shown in Fig. 4c of the main text correspond to heterodyne detection between the optical emission and the pump laser, which in principle should yield the same linewidth as the microwave comb (about 50 Hz). However, the measured optical comb linewidth is about 1 kHz, probably due to frequency jitter arising from the time delay between the optical path through the dilution refrigerator and the local oscillator path.

We evaluate whether the observed periodic pulsed superradiance can be classified as a continuous time-crystal phase by applying a set of five criteria commonly associated with time-crystalline order8,9,10,40,48.

First, the underlying Hamiltonian should be time-independent, ensuring that any emergent periodic behaviour is not trivially imposed by external driving. Second, the observed dynamics should arise from genuine many-body dynamics, rather than from single-particle effects or externally enforced synchronization. Third, the system should have persistent and well-defined periodic temporal behaviour in its steady state. Fourth, this periodicity should correspond to the spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translation symmetry, meaning that the system evolves with a characteristic frequency that is not explicitly set by the Hamiltonian. Fifth, the observed behaviour should be robust against perturbations such as noise, dissipation and experimental imperfections, indicating the presence of a stable dynamical phase rather than fine-tuned transient dynamics.

We systematically evaluate these criteria across different experimental platforms and summarize the results in Extended Data Table 1. This comparison provides a unified framework for assessing whether periodic superradiant dynamics can be understood within the broader context of continuous time crystals.

To further corroborate that our system spontaneously breaks continuous time-translational symmetry, we apply a transient optical pump for 1 ms and monitor the emergence of the periodic pulsed-emission phase. The temporal phase, θk, of the continuous time crystal is defined from the onset time of the periodic burst oscillations as θk = 2π × τk/T (mod 2π), where k indexes individual experimental realizations and τk is the burst onset time in the kth run. As shown in Extended Data Fig. 4, the system first undergoes superradiant burst dynamics and then relaxes into a long-lived periodic pulsed phase that persists without decay over the observation window. Crucially, the onset time, and hence the phase θk, varies randomly over 2π across repeated experiments, indicating that the phase is not determined by the transient pump. This self-evolved randomness provides evidence that temporal order emerges spontaneously, consistent with the spontaneous breaking of continuous time-translational symmetry.

Sources indicate that furthermore, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 7, the observed periodic superradiance represents a robust dynamical phase in which both microwave superradiance and the transferred optical superradiance exhibit essentially non-decaying oscillations under continuous pumping.
