📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Amazon rainforest is a cornerstone of regional and global carbon cycling1 and is widely regarded and modelled as a perennially evergreen ecosystem2,3. This prevailing view, however, masks substantial fine-scale variation in leaf phenology, limiting our capacity to predict ecosystem responses to climate change. Here by combining 10-m Sentinel-2 observations with machine learning, we uncover pervasive, spatially structured seasonal deciduousness across the basin. In 70.0% of the Amazon, leaf shedding precedes leaf flushing by at least 3 months, creating pronounced asynchrony between deciduousness and greenness seasonality, whereas the remainder highlights near-synchronous phenology. Hydroclimate emerges as the dominant factor associated with this asynchrony across 51.6% of the area, followed by soil properties (33.2%) and light availability (15.2%). Motivated by this widespread decoupling between deciduousness and canopy greenness, we incorporated deciduousness-constrained leaf turnover and the resulting leaf-age demography into ecophysiological models, yielding spatially widespread improvements in the seasonal agreement between simulated gross primary productivity and satellite-derived photosynthetic seasonality across 79.9% of the basin. These findings challenge the conventional view of Amazonian phenology, demonstrating that previously overlooked deciduousness influences Amazonian carbon dynamics. Incorporating these insights into process-based models is essential for refining projections of climate–forest feedbacks in the Amazon and for understanding its ecological functions under accelerating global change.

The Amazon rainforest accounts for about 16% of global terrestrial carbon fixation through photosynthesis1, hosts nearly a third of known terrestrial biodiversity4 and is a critical yet vulnerable component of the climate system of Earth5,6. Its role as a carbon sink, driven by ecophysiological processes such as photosynthesis, is increasingly threatened by climate change7,8, yet the impacts of climate on these processes remain uncertain, particularly related to tropical leaf phenology9. Leaf phenology, the rhythm of leaf shedding and flushing, substantially influences carbon cycling and other ecological processes10,11. Because photosynthetic capacity develops after leaf expansion, typically peaks in mature leaves and declines with leaf ageing12,13, shifts in phenological synchrony between leaf shedding and flushing could substantially change leaf-age composition, influencing the carbon balance of the Amazon11,14. Understanding these phenological dynamics is therefore pivotal for forecasting rainforest–climate feedbacks and guiding conservation in a warming world.

According to recent reports, the warm, humid climate and extraordinary tree diversity in the Amazon support diverse phenological strategies across species and landscapes15,16,17 (Fig. 1). Field and satellite studies show that these strategies generate widespread and regionally variable seasonality in canopy greenness18, leaf demography11,19 and photosynthetic activity20,21. Yet, variation in these strategies remains poorly resolved at the basin scale because commonly used satellite products, such as those derived from the Moderate-Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS; greater than or equal to 500 m), are vulnerable to subpixel cloud contamination18 and average over crowns with different phenological states, blurring fine-scale phenological dynamics22. Field measurements11,16, proximate remote sensing15,17,23 and high-resolution satellite imagery24 instead show local mosaics of deciduous and evergreen phenological strategies (Fig. 1a,b). Deciduous species seasonally shed and regrow leaves16,25, producing marked fluctuations in leafless-canopy fraction (deciduousness), whereas evergreen species show smaller changes in foliage cover but can exhibit seasonal variation in photosynthetic activity through near-synchronous leaf turnover11,26. This functional diversity creates spatiotemporal heterogeneity in canopy status, as species follow distinct phenological trajectories. In particular, temporal lags between leaf shedding and flushing (increasing greenness) cause asynchrony, further increasing heterogeneity in canopy status over time (Fig. 1b). This phenological asynchrony shapes ecosystem carbon, water and nutrient cycles in the Amazon19,27, yet its basin-wide distribution remains poorly understood. Advances in 10-m Sentinel-2 observations and machine learning now enable mapping of this variability across the Amazon22,28.

a, Coarse-resolution satellite imagery (greater than or equal to 500 m) portrays Amazonia as largely evergreen, despite the coexistence of deciduous and evergreen species in individual tropical rainforest stands. b, Variation in the temporal lag between seasonal leafless-canopy exposure and canopy greenness defines phenological asynchrony and reflects dynamic leaf-demographic states in tropical rainforests. Several leaf-transition processes, including mature to old (M → O), old to deciduous (O → D), deciduous to young (D → Y) and young to mature (Y → M), may occur simultaneously in forest stands. Newly flushed leaves are classified as young during the first 1–2 months, mature during months 3–5 and old from month 6 onwards, following ref. 11. For example, a cohort flushed in January becomes mature in March and old in June. Low asynchrony occurs when leaf shedding and leaf flushing are closely coupled in time, producing weak temporal separation between seasonal changes in deciduousness and greenness. High asynchrony occurs when leaf shedding precedes leaf flushing by a substantial interval, producing a stronger temporal offset between peaks in deciduousness and greenness. c, Potential drivers of phenological asynchrony, including hydroclimatic constraints, light availability, soil nutrient status and herbivory pressure.

In a recent development, the drivers of Amazonian phenological asynchrony are also poorly understood (Fig. 1c), with seasonal differences in leaf shedding and flushing traditionally attributed to distinct climatic niches. Leaf shedding peaks under seasonal water limitation25, whereas flushing peaks with dry-season solar radiation in less water-restricted regions29,30. However, across much of the Amazon, high solar radiation and low rainfall are seasonally coupled31, complicating efforts to disentangle the roles of light and water in phenology. Soil texture32, nutrient availability33 and herbivory pressure34 may also modulate these dynamics by shaping leaf traits and leafing strategies (for example, deciduous versus evergreen). For instance, sandy soils may amplify water stress, favouring deciduousness, whereas nutrient-poor soils favour longer leaf lifespans35. The incomplete mechanistic understanding of phenological asynchrony hinders predictions of how climate change will alter phenological patterns and their cascading impacts on carbon cycling.

To bridge these gaps, we use 10-m Sentinel-2 observations (2019–2021) to map monthly deciduousness across the Amazon. We validate these maps against independent ground and high-resolution satellite observations (Extended Data Figs. 1–3) and quantify asynchrony between deciduousness and canopy greenness represented by the MODIS enhanced vegetation index (EVI)36. We then assess the environmental and biotic factors associated with this asynchrony. Finally, we incorporate deciduousness-constrained leaf turnover and the resulting leaf-age demography into photosynthetic models and evaluate the consequences for gross primary productivity (GPP) seasonality using independent solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) and eddy-covariance (EC) observations (Methods).

Our Sentinel-2 mapping uncovers strong spatial heterogeneity in Amazon forest canopy phenology (Fig. 2a). Using a 10% amplitude threshold in leafless-canopy fraction to indicate moderate seasonality, we estimate that 75.4% of the basin exhibits seasonal deciduousness (Fig. 2a), whereas 32.8% exceeds a stricter 20% threshold (sensitivity to alternative thresholds is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1). When we repeated the same analysis after aggregating Sentinel-2 reflectance data to 500 m, these fractions declined to 54.5% and 24.5%, respectively, corresponding to relative reductions of about 28% and about 25% (Supplementary Fig. 2). This scale dependence indicates that fine spatial resolution is critical for detecting canopy deciduousness, because crown-scale differences in leaf state and phenological timing are progressively averaged in coarser pixels. The largest amplitudes occur in the Southern Amazon (particularly the southwest and central-south) and in the Guiana Shield (northeastern Amazonia), contrasting with little-to-modest variation in the Everwet Amazon (including the wetter western and northwestern basin, where monthly precipitation remains greater than or equal to 100 mm year-round37) (Fig. 2a). These spatial patterns differ markedly from existing satellite-based representations of Amazon canopy structure and seasonality, including MODIS evergreen forest cover38, MODIS vegetation continuous fields tree cover39, MODIS EVI greenness amplitude and microwave vegetation optical depth (VOD) amplitude from the Vegetation Optical Depth Climate Archive (VODCA)40 (Methods; Extended Data Fig. 4). Although deciduousness amplitude is negatively correlated with MODIS evergreen forest cover (r = −0.38) and tree cover (r = −0.27), substantial amplitudes still occur in areas classified as evergreen and in forests with more than 80% tree cover (Extended Data Fig. 4a–d), indicating that structurally closed-canopy forests can nonetheless exhibit moderate-to-strong seasonal deciduousness. Deciduousness amplitude is positively correlated with EVI amplitude (r = 0.40; Extended Data Fig. 4e,f) and VOD amplitude (r = 0.37; Extended Data Fig. 4g,h), but these products capture different aspects of canopy dynamics. EVI integrates variation in leaf area, leaf age, canopy structure and optical properties15,26, whereas VOD is sensitive to vegetation water content and biomass40,41. Consequently, neither metric uniquely indicates seasonal changes in leafless-canopy fraction, because EVI or VOD may vary as a result of leaf ageing or canopy water dynamics even without substantial leaf shedding. Their divergence from our product therefore reflects the fact that conventional optical- and microwave-based indices capture composite canopy signals. By contrast, our Sentinel-2 product provides a more direct proxy of seasonal deciduousness across Amazon forests.

a, Map of annual deciduousness amplitude, defined as the magnitude of seasonal variation in the fraction of leafless canopy, with black stars marking the ATTO and RJA phenocam sites. b, Map of phenological asynchrony, expressed as the time lag (Δt) between deciduousness and greenness seasonality that yields the strongest correlation between the two metrics. c, Seasonal patterns of satellite-derived deciduousness, MODIS EVI and ERA5-Land precipitation at ATTO (central Amazonia), showing low asynchrony. d, Seasonal patterns of the same metrics at RJA (southern Amazonia), exhibiting high asynchrony. In a and b, inset histograms show the distribution of deciduousness amplitude and asynchrony values, respectively. In c and d, black and green lines represent mean deciduousness and MODIS EVI, respectively, averaged over a 15 × 15 km2 area centred on each site; grey shading denotes the dry season (defined as months with precipitation under 100 mm) and error bars indicate the interannual standard deviation across 3 years (n = 3 years; 2019–2021). Detailed in situ validation against local phenocam observations for these sites is presented in Extended Data Fig. 2.

To examine the temporal relationship between seasonal deciduousness and canopy greenness, we quantified their asynchrony as the time lag (Δt) between the two metrics. Although deciduousness amplitude and Δt were strongly related at the bin-mean level (r2 = 0.96; Supplementary Fig. 3), they were not redundant. Substantial within-bin variation in Δt indicates that similar deciduousness amplitudes can occur under different degrees of temporal coupling between canopy leaf loss and greening. We therefore use Δt as a timing-based metric that complements deciduousness amplitude, which quantifies the magnitude of seasonal change in leafless-canopy fraction. Across the basin, Δt ranges from 0 months to 6 months (Fig. 2b), showing substantial spatial variation in the degree of coupling between leaf shedding and canopy greening. In 70.0% of the Amazon, Δt ≥ 3 months, indicating that peak deciduousness precedes peak greenness by at least 3 months and reflecting pronounced phenological asynchrony between deciduousness and greenness. The remaining area exhibits near-synchronous phenology, with lags of 0–2 months (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Fig. 4a). Spatially, strong asynchrony (Δt ≥ 3 months) is most prevalent in the Southern Amazon (78.9% of the area), followed by the Guiana Shield (63.5%) and the Everwet Amazon (54.0%) (Supplementary Fig. 4b–d). By contrast, low asynchrony is concentrated mainly in the everwet, weakly seasonal parts of the basin, where both deciduousness and greenness show muted seasonality. Site-level observations further illustrate this diversity. At the Amazon Tall Tower Observatory (ATTO) in central Amazonia (mean annual precipitation (MAP) = 2,628 mm yr−1), increased deciduousness coincides with enhanced greenness (Fig. 2c), indicating rapid leaf turnover with minimal delay. Conversely, at Reserva Jaru (RJA) in southern Amazonia (MAP = 1,990 mm yr−1), pronounced dry-season leaf shedding is followed by delayed canopy greening later in the season (Fig. 2d), indicating a more asynchronous phenological regime. At the basin scale, these spatial patterns were robust to the choice of greenness metric and lag definition, with similar results obtained using the kernel normalized difference vegetation index (kNDVI)42 and an alternative peak-to-peak lag defined as the interval between the months of maximum deciduousness and maximum greenness (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6).

According to recent reports, these patterns show a complex mosaic of varied phenological strategies across the Amazon, characterized by the coexistence of near-synchronous and asynchronous regimes. Such diversity highlights the limitations of relying on a single indicator (for example, either deciduousness or greenness) for phenological monitoring in the Amazon and calls for a multimetric framework to capture the full range of phenological behaviours across tropical rainforest landscapes15,16,17. Our findings also align with emerging LiDAR evidence of divergent leaf shedding strategies across the landscape2, underscoring the need for high-resolution, basin-scale characterization to refine global vegetation models.

The striking variability in the degree of asynchrony between deciduousness and greenness across the Amazon (Fig. 2b) prompts us to investigate its underlying mechanisms. We tested four hypotheses (Fig. 1c) focused on: (H1) hydroclimatic constraints (maximum cumulative water deficit (MCWD), MAP and soil moisture)43; (H2) soil property constraints (soil fertility, clay and sand)35; (H3) light optimization (surface downwelling shortwave radiation flux (SR))11,29; and (H4) herbivory pressure34,44. Using an XGBoost model45 with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP)-based interpretation46 (Methods), we find these factors collectively yield a squared correlation coefficient (r²) of 0.67 between predicted and observed asynchrony (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 7). On the basis of normalized SHAP importance, hydroclimatic predictors contribute most strongly (48.4%), followed by soil properties (30.0%) and light (14.4%), whereas herbivory has the least influence (7.2%). SHAP dependence plots show how each predictor contributes to the modelled asynchrony (Extended Data Fig. 5). As an extra sensitivity test, including MODIS-derived land-surface temperature (LST) left the r² unchanged at 0.67 and largely preserved the ranking of the leading predictors, with LST ranking below MCWD, soil fertility and solar radiation (Supplementary Fig. 8). The unchanged predictive performance probably reflects overlap between LST and the hydroclimatic and radiation conditions already represented in the model, supporting the robustness of the broader environmental attribution. Herbivory has long been hypothesized to be a principal driver of tropical phenology34 and its limited contribution here probably reflects the coarse spatial resolution of available proxy data47. Incorporating finer-scale, field-based herbivory observations would help quantify its role across both spatial and temporal scales. Moreover, the hypothesis that herbivory pressure is reduced during the dry season, when light availability and cumulative water deficit are elevated, may still hold, but our spatial analysis may not fully capture this effect. Given the limited contribution of the herbivory proxy, we therefore focus below on hypotheses H1–H3 (Fig. 3a).

Industry observers note that a, Performance and variable importance of the XGBoost model incorporating several variable dimensions: hydroclimate (MCWD, MAP and soil moisture), light availability (SR), soil properties (soil fertility, sand and clay fraction) and herbivory pressure (the proportion of leaf area consumed by herbivores). Variable importance is ranked by mean absolute SHAP value, with inset pie charts showing the fractional contributions of hydroclimate, light, soil properties and herbivory to the total mean absolute SHAP importance. b–d, SHAP dependence plots for the three most vital variables: MCWD (b), soil fertility (c) and SR (d). SHAP values greater than 0 indicate positive effects, whereas SHAP values less than 0 indicate negative effects of the corresponding driver on the degree of phenological asynchrony. In b–d, black fitted lines show the central tendency value of the data points. e, Spatial distribution of the dominant potential drivers (corresponding to the three hypotheses) regulating phenological asynchrony across the Amazon basin. The directional effects shown by the SHAP curves, including the response to herbivory (Extended Data Fig. 5), are consistent with the potential drivers summarized in Fig. 1c and suggest that hydroclimate, light, soil properties and herbivory contribute to variation in phenological asynchrony across Amazonian forests.

It has been revealed that focusing on the top three predictors (MCWD, soil fertility and SR), we further identify complex controls on phenological asynchrony across the Amazon (Fig. 3b–d): H1, H2 and H3. For hydroclimatic constraints (H1), severe water stress promotes high asynchrony, with Δt increasing strongly and linearly with reduced MCWD (Fig. 3b). This aligns with H1 predictions43,48 indicating that prolonged seasonal water deficits promote drought-avoidance through leaf shedding while delaying canopy flushing until water conditions improve. For soil property constraints (H2), below approximately 0.32 cmol(+) kg−1 (corresponding to 10−0.5 on the log-scale axis in Fig. 3c), soil fertility showed limited influence on phenological asynchrony, with SHAP values remaining close to zero. At higher fertility levels, increasing SHAP values indicate a positive association between soil fertility and asynchrony. This pattern is consistent with nutrient-poor soils supporting more evergreen species with longer leaf lifespans, probably because leaf construction costs are high under nutrient limitation33,43. By contrast, fertile soils can support species with shorter leaf lifespans49, allowing leaf shedding during unfavourable environmental conditions and subsequent canopy flushing when conditions improve, thereby contributing to greater temporal separation between the two. This pattern is particularly pronounced in the fertile southwestern Amazon, supporting H2 (Fig. 3e). For light optimization (H3), under low light conditions, SR strongly suppresses asynchrony (reflected by strongly negative SHAP values), but this suppression diminishes linearly with increasing SR and eventually plateaus at high SR (Fig. 3d). In aseasonal regions such as the Everwet Amazon, persistently low and weakly seasonal light availability may favour tightly coupled leaf loss and replacement, as a transient reduction in leaf area would further constrain canopy carbon gain under limited irradiance16,50. By contrast, higher SR may relax this light constraint, allowing leaf replacement to become more temporally separated from leaf loss and thereby contributing to greater deciduousness–greenness asynchrony.

Our subsequent modelling of how hydroclimate, soil properties and light availability interact to shape phenological asynchrony across the Amazon shows that hydroclimate is the dominant driver, influencing 51.6% of the basin area, followed by soil properties (33.2%) and light availability (15.2%) (Fig. 3e). The relative importance of these factors varies regionally: hydroclimate drives phenological asynchrony in 52.8% of the Southern Amazon, 48.6% of the Guiana Shield and 51.1% of the Everwet Amazon, with soil properties acting as the secondary driver in each region (34.1%, 32.2% and 31.9%, respectively) (Extended Data Fig. 6). These Δt-based driver rankings are consistent across low-, intermediate- and high-deciduousness-amplitude classes, with MCWD remaining the top predictor in all classes (Supplementary Fig. 9a–d). A complementary analysis using deciduousness amplitude as the response variable identified MCWD, MAP and soil fertility as the main predictors of seasonal leafless-canopy magnitude (Supplementary Fig. 9e–h), supporting the interpretation that deciduousness amplitude and Δt capture connected but non-redundant dimensions of Amazon canopy phenology. Notably, light ranks third in spatial dominance, contrasting with earlier studies that emphasized light as the primary control of Amazonian (leaf flushing) phenology27,29,31. We propose that light mainly optimizes leaf-age turnover to enhance photosynthetic capacity, whereas water availability governs the timing of leaf shedding, together shaping phenological asynchrony11,51. This reframes the prevailing paradigm of Amazonian phenology from a traditionally light-driven system29,30 to a water-constrained framework, with nutrient and light optimization modulating responses.

In a recent development, to test whether a more realistic representation of canopy phenology improves simulations of Amazon forest photosynthesis, we incorporated satellite-derived seasonal deciduousness and its constraints on canopy leaf-age composition into three established light-use efficiency (LUE) models (Methods). This framework allows us to separate the effects of canopy structure from those of leaf-age regulation by comparing three configurations driven by identical climate forcing: (1) a conventional baseline based on greenness or leaf area index (LAI), (2) a structurally harmonized baseline using deciduousness-constrained canopy input but seasonally fixed photosynthetic capacity and (3) a full leaf-demography-driven framework (LD-LUE), in which canopy photosynthetic capacity varies seasonally with leaf-age composition following the established leaf-age regulation scheme11. Comparisons between LD-LUE and the conventional baseline quantify the combined effect of representing seasonal deciduousness and leaf demography, whereas comparisons between LD-LUE and the structurally harmonized baseline isolate the physiological contribution of leaf-age regulation beyond canopy structure alone. Model performance was evaluated against EC GPP at four contrasting Amazon forest sites and against basin-wide SIF, represented here by the mean of two satellite-derived products (GOSIF52 and CSIF53) as an independent benchmark of seasonal photosynthetic dynamics20.

Explicitly representing seasonal deciduousness and leaf demography substantially improves model performance. Across the basin, LD-LUE improves the seasonal correspondence between modelled GPP and SIF in 79.9% of Amazon forests relative to conventional LUE models (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 11). The magnitude of improvement varied spatially. The basin-wide distribution of Δr, defined as the difference in correlation with SIF between the LD-LUE ensemble and the conventional LUE ensemble, had a median of 0.16 (interquartile range, 0.031–0.37), with the largest gains concentrated in specific regions (Fig. 4a). The spatial pattern is consistent across the two SIF products (GOSIF and CSIF; Supplementary Fig. 10) and across all three LUE formulations (Extended Data Fig. 7), indicating that the improvement is robust to both the choice of SIF benchmark and model structure. Site-level EC validation further supports these results (Fig. 4b–g). EC observations and model simulations are compared in absolute GPP units (gC m−2 d−1), allowing both seasonal phase and amplitude to be evaluated. Because EC records span earlier multiyear tower observation periods and do not fully overlap with the 2019–2021 Sentinel-2 mapping window (Supplementary Table 1), we evaluated the climatological mean seasonal cycle rather than year-specific interannual variability. In humid central and eastern forests, LD-LUE more accurately captures both the phase and magnitude of seasonal GPP variation than do the conventional greenness- or LAI-based formulations (Fig. 4b–d and Extended Data Fig. 8), consistent with the idea that seasonal productivity in these forests is governed less by simple changes in canopy quantity than by coordinated leaf flushing, leaf replacement and age-dependent shifts in photosynthetic capacity11,54. By contrast, improvements relative to the conventional baseline are smaller at the drier southern site in RJA (Fig. 4e), where traditional greenness or LAI metrics already reproduce much of the observed GPP seasonality, in agreement with previous findings9.

The conventional ensemble includes the EC-LUE, two-leaf EC-LUE and MODIS-LUE models, all driven by standard satellite vegetation inputs and the same meteorological forcing. By contrast, the LD-LUE ensemble represents canopy processes that incorporate both seasonal deciduousness and leaf-age demography. Black stars indicate flux-tower sites. b–e, Seasonal cycles of GPP simulated by the Conv-LUE ensemble, the LD-LUE ensemble and EC-derived GPP at K34 (b), K67 (c), CAX (d) and RJA (e). (n = 3 LUE formulations per ensemble). f,g, Site-level agreement with EC-derived GPP, evaluated using correlation coefficient (f) and r.m.s.e. (g).

In a recent development, the structurally harmonized comparison further shows that the performance improvements do not arise from canopy structure alone. When both simulations are forced with the same deciduousness-constrained canopy input, the LD-LUE framework still improves the seasonal correspondence between modelled GPP and SIF relative to the fixed-capacity structural baseline across all three LUE formulations (Extended Data Fig. 9). Because canopy structure is identical in this comparison, the remaining improvement can be attributed to seasonal variation in canopy photosynthetic capacity associated with leaf-age composition. Relative to the broader gains obtained against conventional LUE models (Fig. 4), this physiological contribution is more spatially heterogeneous. The magnitude and spatial prevalence of improvement indicated distinct regional patterns. Across much of the central and western Amazon, improvements become weaker, whereas the largest gains in Δr persist in the northeastern Amazon, suggesting a stronger added role for leaf-age-dependent photosynthetic regulation there. By contrast, positive gains are most spatially extensive in the more seasonal Southern Amazon, where the fraction of pixels with improved seasonal agreement (mean Δr > 0 across three formulations) reached 79.6%, but was much lower in the northwestern Everwet Amazon (35.7%; Extended Data Fig. 9e). The weaker improvement in the northwest probably reflects low phenological seasonality16,55, which may increase uncertainty in detecting deciduousness-constrained leaf demography. At the site level, LD-LUE also better reproduces the seasonal amplitude of GPP than the structural baseline, particularly at three humid forest sites (Extended Data Fig. 10), indicating that leaf demography improves simulation of the magnitude of photosynthetic variation, not only its timing11.

Recent findings suggest that these differences are also consequential for regional carbon accounting. Relative to conventional LUE baselines, LD-LUE changes basin-integrated annual GPP by about 1.42 PgC yr−1 (Supplementary Fig. 11), equivalent to a 9.4% difference from conventional estimates and approximately 10–20% of current global annual anthropogenic CO2 emissions when converted to carbon units56. These results show that incorporating satellite-constrained deciduousness and leaf demography systematically shifts not only the seasonal distribution but also the magnitude of simulated photosynthesis. Together, these findings highlight the importance of explicitly representing canopy phenology and leaf turnover in tropical carbon-cycle models to improve projections of climate–carbon feedbacks.

In a recent development, our study reshapes the understanding of Amazon rainforest dynamics by showing that seasonal deciduousness is both widespread and spatially structured across the basin. We demonstrate that deciduousness and greenness cycles are often asynchronous, and that this asynchrony, shaped by hydroclimate, light and soil nutrient availability, substantially modulates Amazon carbon-cycle dynamics by changing both the seasonal distribution and magnitude of simulated photosynthesis. Incorporating seasonal deciduousness and associated leaf demography into LUE modelling improves the representation of tropical leaf phenology and seasonal GPP estimates, highlighting the importance of explicitly incorporating canopy phenology into process-based models used to project Amazon responses to climate change.

In a recent development, these findings carry three implications for tropical ecology and global change research. First, traditional vegetation monitoring overlooks key phenological variation in tropical forests, highlighting the need to evaluate similar dynamics in other forests presumed to be predominantly evergreen. Emerging monitoring frameworks should integrate multidimensional, high-resolution datasets to capture the full complexity of tropical forest phenology. Species ecophysiological responses manifested in these multidimensional phenological dynamics10,11 can provide early warning signs of ecosystem transition, such as shifts from evergreen- to deciduous-dominated ecosystems. Second, our mechanistic understanding of basin-wide phenological asynchrony provides a basis for predicting carbon–climate feedbacks. As climate change intensifies dry seasons7,8, elevated hydroclimatic stress may expand deciduous-dominated regimes, potentially reducing the carbon sink capacity of the Amazon and altering species composition. Third, current process-based models (including mainstream terrestrial biosphere models9) misrepresent Amazon rainforest phenology, leading to systematic biases in carbon flux simulations3,9. Because phenology underpins many important ecophysiological processes, our results highlight the need to explicitly incorporate deciduousness and its constraint on leaf demography into terrestrial biosphere models. Doing so will improve predictions of: (1) carbon sequestration under present and future climate conditions9,11, (2) evapotranspiration dynamics, which affect regional rainfall patterns10,57 and (3) ecosystem–microclimate interactions that are tightly linked to seasonal canopy changes2. Integrating these advances into next-generation models will refine projections of Amazon rainforest responses to climate change and strengthen our broader understanding of vegetation–climate feedbacks at the global scale.

To elucidate seasonal patterns of greenness and deciduousness in the Amazon rainforest, we integrated multisensor satellite observations. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample size. Experimental randomization and blinding were not applicable to this observational study based on existing datasets.

We assessed canopy greenness dynamics using the EVI derived from daily MODIS data. EVI was selected, as it reduces saturation effects in high-biomass forests compared with the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)36, while demonstrating accuracy in tracking leaf flushing and canopy structural changes in the rainforest36,58,59. Previous studies have also demonstrated that EVI can capture dry-season canopy greening associated with upcoming leaf flushing in the Amazon15,23,26. We accessed daily MCD43A1 bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) model parameters at a 500-m resolution by means of Google Earth Engine (GEE). To minimize cloud and shadow contamination, we conducted stringent cloud filtering following the method described in ref. 24. We then used these BRDF parameters with the RossThick-LiSparse kernel model to reconstruct reflectance at a nadir view and a 45° solar zenith angle, thereby reducing view- and illumination-angle effects. This approach has been extensively validated for tropical forests58,60. Subsequently, BRDF-adjusted, quality-assured daily EVI values from 2019 to 2021 (matching the temporal range of Sentinel-2 data, detailed later) were aggregated into monthly composites. Remaining missing data were gap-filled following ref. 61 to reconstruct complete monthly EVI trajectories for subsequent seasonal analyses24,26. To evaluate the robustness of our results, we repeated the primary greenness-based analyses using kNDVI (Supplementary Fig. 5) and an EVI dataset derived from the MODIS Multi-Angle Implementation of Atmospheric Correction (MAIAC) MCD19A3CMG V061 product62 (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). Both produced closely comparable seasonal patterns.

Sources indicate that to quantify seasonal deciduousness (that is, leafless-canopy fraction in each pixel), we analysed Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface-reflectance imagery at 10-m resolution and a 5-day revisit interval for 2019–2021. This period was selected because systematic global production of Sentinel-2 Level-2A surface-reflectance data became available only in late 2018 (ref. 63) and because it avoids the potentially confounding effects of the severe 2023–2024 El Niño-related Amazon drought64. We used the 10-m visible and near-infrared bands, including blue (B2), green (B3), red (B4) and near-infrared (B8), because these bands have demonstrated effectiveness in differentiating leafless-canopy status from other phenophases26 and the 10-m spatial resolution also provides an appropriate scale for both fine- and ecosystem-scale analyses22,28. Cloud and shadow contamination was minimized using a two-step quality-control procedure. First, pixels with cloud probability values greater than 50% were masked using the Sentinel-2 Cloud Probability product generated by the s2cloudless algorithm65. Second, remaining cloud and shadow artefacts were further screened using the Automatic Cloud and Shadow Screening algorithm66, which is designed for high-resolution satellite imagery. To improve spectral comparability among images acquired under different viewing and illumination geometries, we applied image-specific BRDF correction using coefficients derived from the MCD43A1 product, following ref. 67.

Recent findings suggest that subsequently, we estimated deciduousness from Sentinel-2 data using the Index-Guided, Ecologically Constrained Autoencoder (IG-ECAE)22. The model was implemented using TensorFlow v.2.20.0 in Python v.3.13.5. IG-ECAE is an automated, biophysically grounded spectral-unmixing framework developed for scalable mapping of tropical forest deciduousness22,28. It represents each Sentinel-2 pixel as a linear mixture of three dominant endmembers commonly observed in intact forest canopies: leafy canopy, leafless canopy and shade (equation (1)). The algorithm enables automated endmember extraction specific to each forest landscape by integrating a deep learning method that minimizes the difference between input spectral data and reconstructed spectral output, alongside constraining the reconstruction using ecologically informed spectral relationships among the endmembers. These constraints are based on field-observed spectral patterns, including that near-infrared reflectance is highest for leafy canopy, lower for leafless canopy and lowest for shade26,68 (Supplementary Fig. 14). Reconstruction error was quantified using the mean squared error (m.s.e.) between the input spectral data and the reconstructed output. After endmembers were estimated, the linear mixture model was inverted for every valid Sentinel-2 pixel to obtain leafy, leafless and shade fractions. Further algorithmic details are provided in refs. 22,28. For pixel i, the observed reflectance spectrum is expressed as:.

Recent findings suggest that where xi is the observed reflectance, pki is the fractional abundance of endmember k; ek is the reflectance spectrum of the kth endmember; εi is the residual error and N is the number of valid pixels in a given Sentinel-2 image. Endmember fractions were constrained to be non-negative and to sum to one (equation (2)):.

Sources indicate that in practice, rather than relying on a single Amazon-wide endmember spectral library, we derived endmembers separately for each 10 × 10 km2 tile and updated them annually to account for spatial and temporal variation in endmember spectra associated with illumination conditions, canopy structure and floristic composition69,70. Basin-wide endmember spectra for 2019–2021 are shown in Supplementary Fig. 15 and these spectra were highly consistent across years and closely matched previous field-based biophysical expectations26. Because the shade fraction mainly captures variation in illumination, canopy architecture and within-pixel shadowing, rather than representing an independent phenological state, we retained shade as an auxiliary endmember during spectral unmixing. To test whether explicitly including shade was necessary, we repeated the endmember extraction and unmixing using only leafy and leafless-canopy endmembers. Excluding shade substantially reduced agreement with leafless-canopy fractions derived from high-resolution, 0.5-m Google Earth imagery (GEI) across all 16 validation sites (next section ‘Validation of the deciduousness product’), with a Pearson correlation of r = 0.42 and root mean square error (r.m.s.e.) = 0.59, compared with the three-endmember model showing much stronger agreement with the same GEI reference data (r = 0.87, r.m.s.e. = 0.07; Supplementary Fig. 16). We therefore retained the shade endmember during model inversion to account for illumination-related spectral variability. For the final canopy-composition estimates, however, we redistributed the retrieved shade fraction between the leafy and leafless components in proportion to the retrieved leafy and leafless fractions following ref. 24. This allowed shade to serve as an auxiliary spectral component during inversion without being treated as a separate phenological class. A further sensitivity analysis supported this approach, showing that redistributing shade improved agreement with GEI-derived leafless fractions compared with retaining shade as a separate final component (r = 0.87 versus 0.78; r.m.s.e. = 0.07 versus 0.09; Supplementary Fig. 17). Finally, after unmixing, we applied temporal gap filling following ref. 61 to further reduce residual cloud-related data gaps and reconstruct continuous monthly deciduousness trajectories. These monthly products were then spatially aggregated for subsequent analyses.

According to recent reports, we validated the Sentinel-2-derived deciduousness product using four independent datasets that capture complementary dimensions of forest canopy phenology: phenocam observations, litterfall records, forest inventory data and high-resolution GEI (Extended Data Figs. 1–3 and Supplementary Table 1). Phenocam observations (n = 5) were used to evaluate seasonal changes in monthly leafless-canopy fraction, whereas litterfall records (n = 47) provided an independent proxy for the timing of seasonal leaf shedding. For spatial validation, we compared satellite-derived deciduousness amplitude (that is, seasonal maximum minus minimum in leafless-canopy fraction) with the relative abundance of deciduous tree taxa in forest inventory plots (n = 289). Finally, GEI scenes at 0.5-m resolution and closely matched in acquisition date to Sentinel-2 observations (n = 16) were used for spatially explicit cross-validation of leafless-canopy status across diverse forest sites in the Amazon. Although some reference datasets were not fully contemporaneous with the 2019–2021 Sentinel-2 analysis period, together they provide complementary evidence for the temporal consistency, spatial realism and biological interpretability of the mapped deciduousness patterns.

Recent findings suggest that we compiled phenological observations from five tower-mounted phenocams across tropical American rainforests (Extended Data Fig. 1). Seasonal deciduousness dynamics were evaluated following established phenocam protocols11. An illustrated example of extracting ecosystem-scale deciduousness is provided in Supplementary Fig. 18. Specifically, to reduce artifacts caused by variable illumination and viewing geometry, we selected high-quality red–green–blue (RGB) colour composite images acquired daily between 10:00 and 14:00 local time. In each image, individual, well-illuminated tree crowns were manually delineated and classified as leafless when bare branches constituted more than 50% of the visible crown area. Monthly site-level deciduousness was then calculated as the proportion of leafless crowns among all identified crowns for that month. This procedure was applied consistently across all months and sites. As shown in Extended Data Fig. 2, Sentinel-2-derived monthly deciduousness closely tracked the phenocam observations across the five sites (mean r = 0.92; range 0.87–0.96), indicating that the product captured seasonal variation in canopy deciduousness well.

To assess the timing of seasonal leaf shedding over a broader geographic extent, we compiled and screened litterfall records from 47 sites across the Amazon basin. We used regional and global litterfall compilations71,72 and retained only records that met three criteria: (i) sites were located in our study region; (ii) sampling was monthly or submonthly, enabling seasonal dynamics to be resolved; and (iii) observations were collected after 2000, making them more representative of recent phenological conditions. These filters yielded 47 sites distributed across most of the basin (Extended Data Fig. 1). We used litterfall as an independent proxy for the timing of leaf-shedding activity because seasonal increases in leaf abscission can produce litterfall peaks even when canopy leaf loss is partly offset by rapid leaf flushing15,16. Litterfall was therefore treated primarily as a benchmark for phenological timing rather than as a direct measure of standing leafless-canopy fraction. To emphasize seasonality and account for scale differences between measurements, both litterfall and satellite-deciduousness time series were standardized within each site using Z-score standardization before comparison73. The standardized trajectories demonstrated strong temporal coherence across sites (r = 0.83; Extended Data Fig. 3a), indicating that the Sentinel-2 product reliably captures broad-scale seasonality in canopy leaf shedding.

In a recent development, we assessed the spatial correspondence between mapped deciduousness amplitude and local deciduous tree composition using inventory plots. Candidate plots were obtained from the Botanical Information and Ecology Network (BIEN)74 and sPlotOpen75 databases. BIEN records were accessed using the BIEN R package v.1.2.7 in R v.4.5.1. Plot locations were visually checked against high-resolution Esri World Imagery (ArcGIS Pro v.3.2.1) and sites in fragmented or non-continuous forest landscapes were excluded. For each tree record, leaf phenology was assigned as evergreen or deciduous at the species or genus level using information from the TRY76 database and established protocols77,78. After filtering, we retained 289 plots in continuous forests for which phenological assignments were available for more than 90% of recorded trees (Extended Data Fig. 1). For each plot, we calculated the relative abundance of deciduous taxa as a ground-based indicator of local deciduous composition. To account for coordinate uncertainty and the scale mismatch between inventory plots (typically 0.04–1 ha) and satellite observations, we followed a spatial aggregation approach recommended in previous studies79,80. Specifically, within a buffer of 1-km radius around each plot coordinate, corresponding to the maximum coordinate uncertainty reported in sPlotOpen75, we extracted all valid 250 × 250-m2 satellite grid cells and used their median value to represent local satellite-derived deciduousness amplitude. Despite remaining uncertainties arising from sublandscape heterogeneity, residual geolocation mismatch and other factors, the plot-derived deciduous-taxa proportion showed a positive, moderate correlation with satellite-derived amplitude across all plots (r = 0.58, P = 7.24 × 10−28; Extended Data Fig. 3b), providing more independent validation.

Sources indicate that finally, we validated the spatial accuracy of the Sentinel-2-derived deciduousness product using 16 GEI scenes, each covering a 2 × 2 km2 area. For each GEI scene, we selected the closest available Sentinel-2 observation with less than 10% cloud cover, resulting in a mean acquisition-date offset of less than 10 days across all 16 GEI scenes. We performed an image-specific supervised classification following ref. 28 to generate reference maps of leafless and leafy canopy cover for each GEI. The GEI-based reference maps and Sentinel-2 deciduousness estimates were then aggregated to 100 × 100 m2 patches to reduce the effects of geolocation error, crown-scale heterogeneity and differences in spatial resolution22,81. Across the 16 sites, Sentinel-2-derived leafless-canopy fraction agreed well with the GEI-based reference estimates (r = 0.87, r.m.s.e. = 0.07; Extended Data Fig. 3c–e), providing independent support for the spatial accuracy of the mapped deciduousness product.

To quantify methodological uncertainty in the Sentinel-2-derived deciduousness product, we applied four complementary diagnostics: spectral reconstruction error, Monte Carlo perturbation analysis, sensitivity tests for shade representation and treatment and plot-satellite validation uncertainty assessment.

Recent findings suggest that we first assessed our IG-ECAE model performance using a spectral reconstruction error metric, m.s.e., as introduced in section ‘Deciduousness seasonality from Sentinel-2’. m.s.e. was calculated for each 10-km tile as the squared mismatch between observed Sentinel-2 reflectance and reflectance reconstructed from the estimated leafy, leafless and shade fractions. Our results show that reconstruction error was consistently low across the basin (mean m.s.e. = 2 × 10−4, equivalent to an r.m.s.e. of approximately 0.014 in reflectance units; Supplementary Fig. 19), indicating that the IG-ECAE model reproduced observed canopy spectra with low reconstruction error across diverse forest conditions and that the selected endmembers and unmixing framework adequately captured the dominant spectral variability associated with canopy leaf status.

We next evaluated the sensitivity of the inferred deciduousness to realistic spectral uncertainty. For each 10-km tile co-located with a ground inventory validation plot, we performed a Monte Carlo perturbation analysis82 with n = 50 independent iterations. In each iteration, we added zero-mean Gaussian noise to the observed spectra before rerunning the unmixing procedure. The total noise variance was scaled to match the basin-wide mean reconstruction m.s.e. (2 × 10−4) but was distributed proportionally to the median reflectance of each band to avoid overwhelming darker visible bands with unrealistic relative noise. The Monte Carlo ensemble means closely matched the no-noise baseline across the full deciduousness gradient (r = 0.99, r.m.s.e. = 0.02; Supplementary Fig. 20a), indicating little systematic bias introduced by the perturbation procedure. The pixel-level Monte Carlo standard deviation was also small, with a mean value of 0.012 across evaluated pixels (Supplementary Fig. 20b). These results indicate that the deciduousness retrieval is well constrained and not unduly sensitive to modest reflectance uncertainty.

Industry observers note that we evaluated uncertainty associated with both the inclusion of shade as an endmember and its postinversion treatment in the canopy spectral mixture analysis. First, we tested whether explicitly representing shade was necessary by repeating the endmember extraction and unmixing using only leafy and leafless-canopy endmembers. Omitting shade substantially reduced agreement with independent high-resolution GEI benchmarks (Supplementary Fig. 16), confirming the importance of separating illumination-related spectral variability from phenological signals. Second, we assessed the treatment of the retrieved shade fraction by comparing the adopted proportional reallocation with an alternative in which shade was retained as a separate component in the final canopy composition. Proportional reallocation is ecologically appropriate because the shade fraction primarily reflects variation in viewing geometry, solar illumination, canopy structure and local topographic conditions, rather than a distinct phenological state. This treatment reduced bias and improved agreement with GEI-derived reference estimates relative to retaining shade as an independent final component (Supplementary Fig. 17). Together, these sensitivity tests indicate that the inferred deciduousness patterns are robust to the adopted treatment of shade and support the interpretation of shade as an auxiliary spectral component rather than an independent canopy phenological state.

Recent findings suggest that finally, we quantified the observed scatter in the validation relationship between satellite-derived deciduousness amplitude and plot-derived deciduous-taxa proportion. We used the residual standard deviation because it summarizes the dispersion of observations around the fitted relationship at the plot-satellite comparison scale. This scatter probably reflects the combined influence of satellite retrieval error, field-sampling uncertainty, ecological heterogeneity in the satellite footprint, differences in what the satellite and inventory metrics represent and residual spatial mismatch between plot and satellite data. The residual standard deviation was 0.092 (Extended Data Fig. 3b) and was therefore treated as a validation-scale uncertainty rather than a pixel-level retrieval error.

Recent findings suggest that we evaluated the role of deciduousness in Amazon rainforest phenology through two complementary analyses. First, we compared annual deciduousness amplitude with existing satellite-derived canopy metrics (that is, forest cover, greenness and vegetation water status) to test whether our deciduousness metric captures phenological variation not represented by conventional satellite products. Second, we quantified the seasonal coupling between deciduousness and greenness to determine whether periods of leaf loss and increases in canopy greenness occur synchronously or are temporally offset. All analyses were restricted to pixels classified as evergreen broadleaf forest in the 500-m MODIS land cover product (MCD12Q1)38, which reduced contamination from non-forest areas and other vegetation types with distinct phenological dynamics37,73. To ensure spatial consistency among datasets and reduce scale mismatch, all datasets were aggregated or resampled to a common 5-km grid. Analyses were conducted both across the full Amazon basin and in three representative ecoregions37 (Fig. 2a): the Everwet Amazon in the northwest (with monthly precipitation greater than or equal to 100 mm year-round); the Guiana Shield in the northeast, characterized by highly weathered, low-fertility soils; and the Southern Amazon, a drier region with moderate-to-high soil fertility.

We generated a 5-km map of Sentinel-2 deciduousness amplitude (defined as the seasonal maximum minus minimum leafless-canopy fraction; see also section on ‘Deciduousness seasonality from Sentinel-2’) and compared it with four independent satellite-derived variables commonly used to characterize Amazon forest structure and phenology: (1) evergreen forest fractional cover (MCD12C1)38, (2) percentage tree cover from MODIS vegetation continuous fields (MOD44B)39, (3) EVI amplitude and (4) VOD amplitude from the multisensor VODCA40. VODCA v.2 harmonizes microwave observations, including SSM/I, TMI, AMSR-E, WindSat and AMSR2. Further details on the spatial and temporal resolution, data access and key references for each product are provided in Supplementary Table 2. Together, these metrics capture complementary aspects of canopy state and dynamics, including forest cover, seasonal variation in canopy greenness and variation in vegetation water content and biomass. This comparison allowed us to test whether deciduousness amplitude reflects phenological variability not captured by existing remote-sensing products. The resulting statistical relationships are shown in Extended Data Fig. 4.

Industry observers note that to assess the sensitivity of deciduousness estimates to spatial resolution, we conducted a controlled aggregation experiment using the original Sentinel-2 observations. The 10-m surface-reflectance data were first aggregated to 500 m before spectral unmixing, retaining the same tile- and year-specific endmembers derived from the original 10-m imagery. All subsequent processing steps were kept unchanged. We then recalculated deciduousness amplitude from the aggregated observations and compared the proportion of Amazon forest area exceeding the same amplitude thresholds used in the primary analysis: 0.10 and 0.20, corresponding to 10% and 20% leafless-canopy amplitude, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 2). Because the coarsened retrieval used the same endmember set as the 10-m retrieval, this comparison isolates the effect of spatial mixing alone and does not include the extra difficulty of identifying relatively pure endmembers from native coarse-resolution imagery.

To assess the temporal correspondence between the two phenological metrics, we compared the mean seasonal cycles (monthly averages for 2019–2021) of deciduousness and greenness across evergreen forest pixels in the Amazon. We quantified asynchrony as the time lag (in months; Δt) that maximized the correlation between the deciduousness and EVI seasonality, following the time-lag correlation method described in ref. 41. Specifically, the deciduousness time series was shifted in 1-month increments and the lag corresponding to the highest correlation with EVI was recorded. Lower Δt values indicate closer temporal alignment between deciduousness (leaf shedding) and greenness (leaf flushing), whereas higher values reflect a greater divergence in their seasonal timing. To aid interpretation of this metric, we highlight two representative sites (wet versus dry) with both satellite observations and local tower-phenocam records: (1) the ATTO in central Amazonia, exhibiting low asynchrony (around 2 months) and (2) the RJA in the southern Amazon, showing high asynchrony (about 4 months) (Fig. 2). We further examined the distribution of Δt across the basin and in each ecoregion (Supplementary Fig. 4) to characterize regional variation in the seasonal coupling between deciduousness and greenness. As a sensitivity test, we also calculated a peak-to-peak lag metric, defined as the difference between the months of maximum deciduousness and maximum EVI. This simpler metric produced patterns closely comparable to those derived from the lagged-correlation approach (Supplementary Fig. 6). We also examined the relationship between asynchrony and deciduousness amplitude across evergreen forest pixels (Supplementary Fig. 3), because these two metrics represent complementary aspects of canopy phenology, namely seasonal magnitude and temporal coordination.

To investigate the drivers underlying spatial variations in deciduousness–greenness asynchrony across the Amazon, we tested four hypotheses (Fig. 1c): (H1) hydroclimatic constraints, (H2) soil property constraints, (H3) light optimization and (H4) herbivory pressure. For this analysis, we selected eight independent variables grouped as follows: (1) water stress indicators (n = 3): MCWD, soil moisture83 and MAP; (2) soil properties (n = 3)—soil clay fraction, soil sand fraction and exchangeable base cations (Ca2+, Mg2+, K+) as proxies for soil texture84 and fertility85; (3) light condition (n = 1)—surface downwelling SR; and (4) herbivory pressure (n = 1), derived from a recent global herbivory dataset47. Details for the spatial and temporal resolution, data ranges and references for these variables are provided in Supplementary Table 3. To ensure consistency and minimize bias, all datasets were resampled to a 5-km resolution. We also constrained the analysis of climate and phenology variables to the 3 years (2019–2021) to match the period of the Sentinel-2 phenology analysis.

Sources indicate that to disentangle the individual and combined effects of these drivers on asynchrony, we used XGBoost modelling coupled with SHAP. The analyses were implemented in Python using the XGBoost package v.3.0.4 and SHAP package v.0.48.0. XGBoost was chosen for its computational efficiency, robustness against overfitting and ability to handle sparse data45. SHAP, based on Shapley values from game theory, provides an interpretable framework to quantify and visualize the magnitude and direction (positive or negative) of each variable’s contribution to model predictions46,86. To better interpret model outputs, we used SHAP to quantitatively visualize the linear/nonlinear relationships between asynchrony and each variable. Model performance was assessed using tenfold cross-validation (Supplementary Fig. 7). Relevant statistics and relationships are shown in Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 5. Given the minimal explanatory power of H4 (herbivory pressure), subsequent mapping focused on H1–H3 (hydroclimate, soil and light). For each pixel, we calculated the relative contribution of these three driver groups by normalizing their absolute SHAP values so that contributions summed to 1. These normalized values were visualized using an R(light)–G(hydroclimate)–B(soil) colour composite, illustrating how the three driver groups codetermine asynchrony across the basin (Fig. 3e). Finally, to quantify basin-wide influence, we summed normalized contributions for each driver group across all pixels to obtain their total proportional control area. These proportional area distributions are shown for the entire Amazon and for individual ecoregions in Extended Data Fig. 6. To test whether the Δt-based driver ranking was sensitive to the magnitude of deciduousness seasonality, we summarized SHAP values from the primary Δt-based XGBoost model in three equal-sized deciduousness-amplitude groups. These groups were defined using the one-third and two-thirds quantiles of deciduousness amplitude among the Amazon forest pixels included in the analysis, corresponding to low (less than 12%), intermediate (12–20%) and high (greater than or equal to 20%) amplitude classes (Supplementary Fig. 9a–d). We also fitted an XGBoost–SHAP model using deciduousness amplitude, rather than Δt, as the response variable, allowing direct comparison between timing-based and magnitude-based driver rankings (Supplementary Fig. 9e–h).

As an extra sensitivity analysis, we examined whether LST provided explanatory information beyond the original predictor set. Daytime LST was obtained from the MODIS MOD11A2 product87, averaged over 2019–2021 and resampled to the same 5-km grid used for the other predictors. We then repeated the XGBoost–SHAP analysis with LST included as an extra predictor, using the same model settings and cross-validation procedure and compared the squared correlation coefficient (r²) and predictor-importance ranking with those of the original model (Supplementary Fig. 8). Because LST integrates several interacting surface processes, including radiation, water availability, evapotranspiration and canopy state, we treated it as a sensitivity variable rather than as an extra mechanistic hypothesis.

We assessed how seasonal leaf turnover (represented by canopy deciduousness and its constraint on leaf-age demography) influences photosynthetic carbon uptake (GPP) in the Amazon. We used a tiered comparison across three established LUE formulations: the EC-LUE model88,89, the two-leaf EC-LUE model90 and the MODIS-LUE91 model. For each formulation, we tested three configurations: (1) a conventional baseline driven by standard greenness- or LAI-based satellite inputs; (2) a harmonized-input baseline driven by our deciduousness-constrained canopy structural input but assuming a temporally fixed maximum LUE; and (3) a full leaf-demography-driven framework (LD-LUE), which combines the same canopy structural input with a seasonally varying canopy photosynthetic capacity determined by leaf-age composition. All configurations were forced with identical ERA5-Land meteorological data inputs, including air temperature, photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) and vapour pressure deficit (VPD), so that differences among simulations reflected vegetation forcing and leaf-demographic representation rather than meteorological inputs. Model outputs were validated against EC measurements from four contrasting forest sites and against basin-wide SIF observations. Notably, EC observations were summarized as monthly mean seasonal cycles over the available observation period of each tower, whereas model outputs were summarized over the 2019–2021 Sentinel-2 period. Because these periods do not fully overlap, the site-level comparison was designed to test whether the models reproduce representative seasonal phasing and amplitude at each site, rather than interannual GPP variability during 2019–2021.

We describe the EC-LUE model here as an illustrative example and the corresponding formulations for two-leaf EC-LUE and MODIS-LUE models are summarized in Supplementary Table 4. In EC-LUE, GPP is calculated as the product of the LUE (ε) and absorbed PAR (APAR) (equation (3)).

Recent findings suggest that where FAPAR is the fraction of incoming PAR absorbed by the canopy. Parameter ε is determined by the maximum LUE (εmax) of the forest canopy under non-stressed conditions and environmental stress scalars for temperature (TS) and water limitation (WS) (equations 4–6).

where min in equation (4) represents the minimum value of TS and WS; T denotes daytime mean temperature, Tmax, Tmin and Topt refer to maximum (48 °C), minimum (2 °C) and optimum (28 °C) temperatures for photosynthesis, based on a previous study in tropical evergreen forests92; VPD refers to daytime mean VPD, with VPD0 as an empirical VPD sensitivity parameter88. Specifically, T, PAR and relative humidity were obtained from the ERA5-Land dataset93 and VPD was calculated from T and relative humidity using the established methodology88. To maintain a strictly controlled comparison, we intentionally omitted explicit atmospheric CO2 regulation terms across all baseline configurations.

Sources indicate that in conventional configurations, canopy light absorption was estimated from either satellite greenness indices or LAI, depending on the model structure (Supplementary Table 4). For greenness-driven EC-LUE configurations, FAPAR was derived using a linear relationship (equation (7)).

where VI denotes NDVI, EVI or kNDVI, depending on the configuration. For NDVI, we used the empirical coefficients a = 1.24 and b = 0.168, following the previously established relationship89. For EVI and kNDVI, index-specific coefficients were obtained by min–max rescaling to match the dynamic range of the NDVI-based FAPAR benchmark, thereby ensuring consistency across greenness-based inputs. For LAI-driven configurations (including the two-leaf EC-LUE and MODIS-LUE and an extra EC-LUE control run driven by MODIS LAI (MOD15A2H); ref. 94), FAPAR was calculated using the Beer–Lambert law (equation (8))11.

where ρ1 and ρ2 are the reflectivity at the canopy top and bottom, set to 0.05 and 0, respectively. The light extinction coefficient was set to 0.5 and the solar zenith angle \({{\vartheta }}_{{\rm{s}}}\) was fixed at 0, following ref. 11.

In the harmonized-input configurations, all LUE formulations were driven by a common Sentinel-2-derived canopy structural input. Because our Sentinel-2 approach quantifies the leafy canopy fraction (Cleafy), which is strongly related to LAI (unit: m2 m−2) (refs. 11,59), we converted Cleafy to LAI (m2 m−2; hereafter LAIdec) using an empirical relationship calibrated at the Tapajós National Forest (equation (9))11.

Recent findings suggest that we further evaluated LAIdec against available in situ LAI observations and the MODIS LAI product across two representative Amazonian sites, Manaus km 34 (K34) and Tapajós km 67 (K67)10. This site-level evaluation supports the conclusion that LAIdec accurately captures the observed seasonal canopy dynamics (Supplementary Fig. 21). Uncertainty in this empirical conversion was quantified using a residual bootstrapping analysis and subsequently propagated through site-level and basin-scale GPP simulations (section ‘Basin-scale GPP changes and uncertainty propagation’).

To represent seasonal variation in canopy photosynthetic capacity, which can vary systematically with leaf age in Amazon forests14, we implemented the leaf demography module11 in each LUE formulation. This module links seasonal canopy structural change to shifts in leaf-age composition, thereby allowing canopy photosynthetic capacity to vary through time as the canopy transitions among young, mature and old leaves (Supplementary Fig. 22). Unlike the previous site-based implementation11, which relied largely on field observations, seasonal canopy structure and leaf turnover are constrained here by satellite-derived deciduousness, enabling basin-scale application of the LD-LUE framework.

It has been revealed that step 1, modelling seasonal leaf-age demography. We simulated seasonal LAI dynamics in three age classes: young (LAIY), mature (LAIM) and old (LAIO) leaves (equations 10–14). This framework operates on discrete monthly time steps, constrained by the new leaf production (or flushing (F); unit is LAI per month; equation (14)), litterfall LAI (or shedding (S); unit is LAI per month; equation (13)) and satellite-derived total LAI (equation (9)).

The constants, \({r}_{{\rm{Y}}\to {\rm{M}}}=1/2\) and \({r}_{{\rm{M}}\to {\rm{O}}}=1/3\), represent the monthly fractions of leaves ageing from young (months 1–2) to mature (months 3–5) and mature to old (older than 5 months), respectively.

Monthly shedding (St) was derived from satellite deciduousness using a log-linear relationship calibrated across 47 Amazonian sites (equation (13)).

It has been revealed that where δ = 10−5 is a small constant added before log transformation to avoid undefined values near zero deciduousness. Litterfall mass was converted to LAI using specific leaf area values from ref. 95. Because deciduousness fraction and litterfall mass are related but not equivalent, the intercept b captures baseline litterfall associated with continuous evergreen leaf turnover. The fitted relationship (a = 0.09, b = 1.18; r = 0.76, P = 1.79 × 10−13; Supplementary Fig. 23) was then applied to the entire basin. Monthly leaf flush (Ft), which reflects both canopy expansion and replacement of shed leaves, was finally calculated as the sum of net monthly LAI change and monthly shedding, with negative sums set to zero11,14 (equation (14)).

According to recent reports, step 2, deriving seasonal canopy photosynthetic capacity. We then calculated a canopy age scalar, fage,t, as the LAI-weighted mean of the relative photosynthetic capacities of young, mature and old leaves at time t (equation (15)).

where aY, aM and aO describe the photosynthetic capacity of young, mature and old leaves, respectively. Previous syntheses across 30 tropical tree species reported an approximate 3:4:2 ratio in the photosynthetic capacities of young, mature and old leaves11,51,54,96, which we converted to relative scaling factors of aY = 0.75, aM = 1 and aO = 0.5 in equation (15). In this framework, the calibrated εmax represents the photosynthetic capacity of mature leaves. Consequently, seasonal variation in canopy photosynthetic capacity arises from changes in fage,t. For the LD-LUE configurations, LUE was then calculated as:.

These seasonal dynamics in εt were then integrated into each LUE formulation to construct the corresponding LD-LUE configurations. For basin-scale application, we used a spatially constant εmax and fixed relative photosynthetic-capacity coefficients for young, mature and old leaves (aY, aM and aO), whereas seasonal variation in canopy photosynthetic capacity was represented through fage,t. This parameterization avoids requiring spatially explicit maps of age-dependent leaf traits, which would nevertheless be valuable for further refining and validating these parameters across sites and regions.

Sources indicate that we calibrated all LUE formulations against EC-derived GPP from four Amazon forest sites spanning contrasting environmental conditions: K34, K67, Caxiuanã National Forest (CAX) and RJA21. For each formulation (EC-LUE, two-leaf EC-LUE and MODIS-LUE), we first calibrated the LD-LUE configuration, which explicitly represents leaf-age composition. The fitted parameters were εmax and the formulation-specific VPD sensitivity parameter(s). Parameter estimation was performed using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, following the sampling approach described in ref. 82 and the optimized values are reported as the medians of the sampled parameter distributions with 95% uncertainty intervals in Supplementary Table 5. All other parameters were prescribed from the literature91,92 to limit overfitting and preserve interpretability. In each formulation, the fitted environmental stress parameters were then held constant across all three model configurations so that differences among simulations reflected canopy representation rather than re-fitted environmental responses. For the two configurations without explicit leaf-age dynamics, we did not re-fit εmax and instead, we derived an effective value (\({\varepsilon }_{\text{max}}^{{\prime} }\)) from the fitted εmax, using the annual mean monthly leaf-age composition:.

where aY, aM and aO are the relative photosynthetic-capacity coefficients assigned to young, mature and old leaves, respectively; fY, fM and fO are the corresponding monthly LAI fractions of young, mature and old leaves and the overbar denotes the annual mean. This approach ensured that differences among configurations were attributable to canopy structure and leaf demography rather than to fitted physiological parameters.

In a recent development, parameter robustness was assessed using both joint calibration across all four EC sites and leave-one-site-out cross-validation. In the latter, parameters were calibrated using three sites and evaluated at the excluded site with each site serving once as the independent validation site. Model performance was broadly consistent between the two approaches, with slightly better results under joint calibration (Supplementary Table 5). Because both approaches led to the same overall conclusions, we used the jointly calibrated parameter set in subsequent analyses.

Model performance was evaluated at both site and basin scales. At the site scale, model-simulated GPP was compared with EC-derived GPP (gC m−2 d−1) using the correlation coefficient (r) and r.m.s.e., thereby assessing agreement in both seasonal timing and absolute magnitude. We used the processed and gap-filled gross ecosystem productivity (GEP) records from the LBA flux dataset for four Amazon forest sites: K34 (January 2000–September 2006), K67 (January 2002–December 2005), CAX (January 2000–July 2003) and RJA (January 2000–October 2002) (Supplementary Table 1). The GEP product provided by the LBA dataset incorporates friction–velocity correction, estimation of night-time ecosystem respiration using a 5-day window and gap filling using a look-up-table procedure97. Because the EC records and Sentinel-2 observations do not cover identical periods, the site-level evaluation focused on the mean seasonal cycle rather than interannual correspondence.

At the basin scale, we used satellite SIF as an independent benchmark for the seasonal phase of photosynthetic activity. Two global 0.05° SIF products (GOSIF52 and CSIF53) were used to characterize basin-wide seasonal dynamics. Because SIF is not expressed in GPP units, we used SIF to evaluate seasonal phase rather than absolute carbon uptake. Before comparison with EC-derived GPP at the site level, GOSIF and CSIF were matched to the same year–month observations available in the corresponding EC record at each site (Supplementary Fig. 24). Because both SIF products performed well, we used their ensemble mean in the basin-scale analysis to reduce product-specific bias. For the basin-wide evaluation, pixel-level simulated GPP, driven by ERA5-Land meteorological forcing and satellite-derived canopy inputs, was compared with the corresponding SIF time series across Amazon forest pixels. Seasonal agreement was quantified as the temporal correlation between monthly modelled GPP and SIF at each pixel. We also calculated Δr, defined as the difference in the SIF correlation between model configurations, to identify where deciduousness-constrained canopy structure and leaf demographic dynamics improved or degraded seasonal agreement.

Recent findings suggest that comparisons were made at two levels. First, each LD-LUE configuration was compared with its conventional baseline, quantifying the combined effect of improved canopy structural forcing and explicit leaf demography. To ensure our findings were robust to the choice of observational benchmark, this primary comparison was evaluated separately against GOSIF and CSIF (Supplementary Fig. 10), as well as against their ensemble mean (Fig. 4 and Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8). Second, each LD-LUE configuration was compared with a harmonized-structure baseline, in which both simulations used the same deciduousness-constrained LAI forcing but differed in whether seasonal leaf-age dynamics were represented (Extended Data Figs. 9 and 10). This comparison isolated the incremental contribution of leaf demography. All comparisons were performed for each LUE formulation and for the multimodel ensemble mean (Extended Data Figs. 7–10).

To quantify the changes in basin-integrated GPP in absolute physical units, we compared annual GPP simulated by the LD-LUE framework ensemble with that simulated by the conventional LUE ensemble. For each pixel, we calculated the difference in annual GPP between the two modelling approaches while retaining the direction of change and then spatially integrated these differences across the Amazon basin and main subregions to estimate the net annual GPP change (ΔGPP; Supplementary Fig. 11). Pixel-level differences in GPP, originally expressed in physical units per unit area, were converted to area-integrated carbon fluxes using pixel area before spatial aggregation. Regional improvements in seasonal phase were summarized as the percentage of forested area exhibiting a positive performance gain (Δr > 0). To test robustness to observational uncertainty, we propagated deciduousness uncertainty through the GPP simulations using LD-EC-LUE as a representative case. The model was rerun at the four flux-tower sites with deciduousness inputs perturbed within the ±1 s.d. uncertainty bounds derived from the Monte Carlo analysis (section ‘Uncertainty quantification for deciduousness estimates’). The resulting spread in simulated GPP indicated that the inferred improvements were overall robust to uncertainty in the Sentinel-2-derived deciduousness input (Supplementary Fig. 25).

We further assessed uncertainty associated with the empirical conversion from leafy canopy fraction to LAI (equation (9)). Using the original 12 monthly paired observations from K67, we performed 10,000 residual-bootstrap realizations by resampling the fitted residuals with replacement and refitting the slope and intercept jointly in each realization. The resulting bootstrap ensemble was propagated through the four flux-tower simulations. For the basin-scale analysis, we selected ten representative paired slope–intercept combinations spanning the empirical joint 95% parameter space and repeated the LD-LUE simulations for each combination. We then quantified the resulting variability in annual GPP, basin-mean seasonal GPP and the spatial extent of positive seasonal-performance gains (Supplementary Figs. 26–28).
