The excellent Kathryn Batte has run the rule over potential alternatives to Lucy Bronze.

The 35-year-old right-back is out injured, but Ella Toone was called up in her place, rather than a direct replacement.

“Bronze, who is two appearances away from reaching 150 caps for her country, has picked up an injury and returned to Chelsea for treatment,” Batte writes.

“The Lionesses will be missing one of their most reliable players for the matches on Friday and Tuesday, but it gives Sarina Wiegman an opportunity to look at potential replacements for the future.

“Bronze, who has been an integral member of the team throughout Wiegman’s reign, turns 35 later this month. While she will be expected to be the first-choice right-back should England qualify for next year’s World Cup in Brazil, the lack of a recognised back-up has been an ongoing problem.”.

Sarina Wiegman revealed that while dropping Toone was a difficult decision, the midfielder’s reaction left a lasting impression on the coaching staff.

“When I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call, but she took that straight away,” Wiegman said. “Of course she was very disappointed, but the first thing she did was say: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’”Wiegman was particularly pleased with how Toone handled herself both on the pitch and in front of the media before her late recall.

Recent findings suggest that “That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good,” the head coach added. “And then getting everything ready, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Greece vs England in the first leg of the 2027 Women’s World Cup play-offs.

The Lionesses kick off the two-legged tie tonight looking to secure a solid advantage ahead of Tuesday’s return tie at Leicester’s King Power Stadium. Although they finished level on points with group winners Spain, England’s goal difference sent them into the play-off path, setting up a first-ever senior meeting against a Greek side ranked 55 places below them in the FIFA rankings.

It has been revealed that all eyes are on Sarina Wiegman’s selection choices following a turbulent week of squad news. The manager originally raised eyebrows last month by dropping Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly, stating bluntly that “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch.”.

Toone swiftly accepted the setback. Speaking after starting in Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, the midfielder insisted: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”.

That opportunity arrived sooner than expected. An injury sustained by right-back Lucy Bronze - described by Wiegman as “really small” - forced the defender to return to Chelsea for assessment. Wiegman immediately turned to Toone, who flew directly to Greece from Spain, where she had been running her own self-directed training block during the international window.

With 69 caps and 24 international goals to her name - including crucial strikes in the Euro 2022 final and the 2023 World Cup semi-final - Toone brings proven massive-match experience back into the setup at a critical moment.

We will bring you all the build-up, confirmed team news, and live play-by-play coverage throughout the evening.

It’ll be Ben White on the night

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Arseblog

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that arsenal lads were in action, and on the scoresheet, last night as England beat Spain 3-2 in Madrid.
  • In a recent development, obviously I’m not especially invested in the national sides of other countries, but I was pleased for Ben White after all the nonsense he’s been through with England.
  • Holland was the one who sparked the matter originally when he was working with Gareth Southgate, so hopefully another goal for the Arsenal defender (he got one a few months back I think), and being part of a famous win in Spain will win around some of those fans who were giving him stick.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that arsenal lads were in action, and on the scoresheet, last night as England beat Spain 3-2 in Madrid. Ezri Konsa made it 2-0 with a close range header, Spain might wonder who was marking him (I think it was supposed to be Marc Cucurella) but the movement was really sharp. Then a couple of minute later, Ben White fired England into a 3-0 lead, with Cucurella also in close attendance.

In a recent development, obviously I’m not especially invested in the national sides of other countries, but I was pleased for Ben White after all the nonsense he’s been through with England. The worst sections of the media have fanned the flames against him, and it doesn’t take much to rile up those who are already of a jingoistic persuasion. As we’ve seen since seen with stories about Steve Holland being hugely unpopular at Man Utd, there’s a common denominator, and it’s not Ben White.

Holland was the one who sparked the matter originally when he was working with Gareth Southgate, so hopefully another goal for the Arsenal defender (he got one a few months back I think), and being part of a famous win in Spain will win around some of those fans who were giving him stick. I also feel quite confident that even if there is a cohort who won’t forgive Ben White for the crime of Steve Holland being a dickhead, he probably won’t care too much. Look at the reactions of his teammates and manager to the goal, and that’s tells you plenty.

According to recent reports, he was also involved in a minor scuffle going off at half-time, which also seemed to involved Konsa and Martin Zubimendi, but I’m sure it was just heat of the moment stuff. Although Spain got two back after England went down to 10 men, they made the fatal mistake of starting Mikel Merino. How was he supposed to come off the bench and get a vital goal then? Silly Luis de la Fuenta, bloke’s a fraud.

Elsewhere over the weekend, Viktor Gyokeres scored twice for Sweden, both from the penalty spot. We just need more penalties. This is the key to unlocking him. Riccardo Calafiori played the full 90 as Italy went down 4-1 to Belgium (ouch), Martin Odegaard played 90 as Norway beat Wales, and there are some more games to come this week with Germany facing Netherlands tonight (Kai v Timber), the Brazilians are in action in Singapore, and apparently Christos Tzolis is fit to play for Greece after having an MRI.

Maybe it’s my own recent experiences, but I don’t care for the idea he needs an MRI. I get it, it’s probably for his knee or hamstring or something, but it feels like if you need one of those to know if you’re fit, you’re probably not feeling 100% anyway. I guess this will be one Mikel Arteta will keep a close eye on tonight when Greece host Serbia and Tzolis inevitably starts. Ideally, these will be useful minutes for him, and help him deliver for us but you can’t help but worry considering he picked up an injury in the last Interlull.

Sources indicate that finally for today, it looks as if a Declan Rice contract extension is close. Speaking while on England duty, he said:.

“A latest contract is hopefully on the horizon soon. I’m extremely lucky to be at a club like Arsenal where the manager shows me so much trust and teammates who put so much energy and effort into to me.

“I’m extremely lucky not to have to worry about that stuff, and it makes playing football far more easier.”.

Industry observers note that this is, by any measure, a no-brainer. I don’t think there’s a club in the world that would turn him down if he were available, and his importance to Arsenal is just obvious. In a world when £100m+ transfers often struggle to provide value, this is one of the exceptions. If you went back to 2023 and had to do it all again, even if you added another £20m or £30m to the fee we paid West Ham, it would be worth it. It’s likely to be the kind of deal that sees him play out the rest of his prime years in red and white, and let’s hope there are more trophies along the way to accompany that.

Right, I have to leave it there for this morning. We will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on though. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

The pod should be out around around midday. Until then, have a good one – after which I’m gonna be off for a couple of days but the lads will keep things ticking here until I get back.

Liverpool duo Virgil van Dijk and Dominik Szoboszlai are both good to go for Sunday's Premier League clash with Manchester United at Anfield.

The pair were name-checked as part of Andoni Iraola's six-man injury upgrade, in which he confirmed that the Hungarian midfielder and Dutch defender are both fine to feature despite fitness concerns.

Szoboszlai has been managing a knee problem recently, but there is nothing to suggest that he will not join forces with Alexis Mac Allister in central midfield, even though Ryan Gravenberch could also return from a heel injury.

Van Dijk, meanwhile, withdrew from the Netherlands squad during the November international break, but the 35-year-old will no doubt partner Jeremy Jacquet in front of Alisson Becker here.

Fellow Dutchman Jeremie Frimpong is also in line to return from a hamstring injury, but Ronald Araujo has done nothing to warrant demotion, and nor has Milos Kerkez on the left-hand side.

Scorer of five goals against Manchester United in the Premier League, Cody Gakpo enjoys facing the Red Devils more than any other Premier League team and is a sure-fire starter on the right flank.

Expect Gakpo to line up alongside Florian Wirtz, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak in an unchanged forward line, the latter bidding to build on his seven goals from nine Premier League games so far in 2026-27.

Liverpool possible starting lineup:.

Alisson; Araujo, Van Dijk, Jacquet, Kerkez; Mac Allister, Szoboszlai; Gakpo, Wirtz, Barcola; Isak.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A statistic has been doing the rounds regarding Ruben Amorim’s league record with AC Milan, which is gathering some attention.

His style of play is open to criticism, his selections are controversial, his words are regularly quite strong and he’s often called into question at the first sign of failure. For Amorim, his first months with the Rossoneri have been a rollercoaster ride.

It has been revealed that read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

There have been ups and downs: things have been better domestically, culminating in a derby victory over Inter, but in the Europa League the one win from four games means the Rossoneri right now sit outside the playoff zone.

As La Gazzetta dello Sport write, there is a key bit of data to contextualise things. With 24 points in his first 11 Serie A matches, Amorim is averaging 2.18 points per game, the result of seven wins, three draws, and one defeat.

Industry observers note that it is the highest ever for a Milan coach in the three-point era, ahead of Stefano Pioli, Carlo Ancelotti and Massimiliano Allegri. Looking at coaches with at least five stints in the Italian top flight, only Antonio Conte boasts a better figure than the Portuguese coach, with 2.21 points per game.

This is obviously an unfair comparison, given that the former Napoli coach’s points average takes into account all 279 of his Serie A games – with spells at Atalanta, Juventus, Inter and Napoli – compared to just 11 for the former United manager.

However, it is a testament to the excellent work done thus far by Amorim and his staff. Even more so in a season in which the decision was made to undertake a revolution in several respects, to relaunch a team and a fan base that had been burned by the collapse of last season.

It has been revealed that gerry Cardinale and the ownership made significant investments during the last transfer window, spending €70m on Goncalo Ramos and €50m on Diego Moreira, plus €25m on Mario Gila. This is also why Milan fans have high expectations for Amorim’s era.

According to recent reports, to date, the average from these first 11 games project the Rossoneri to land around 83 points by the end of the season. Last year, Inter won the Scudetto with 87 points, and 71 were needed to finish fourth, the minimum target set by the owners.

Allegri’s Milan stopped at 70 points, despite a strong start to the season that even fuelled a few Scudetto dreams for a few months. That start, however, was inferior to this season: a year ago, after 11 matchdays, AC Milan had 22 points, two fewer than under Amorim.

It is an encouraging beginning to the fresh era that fans hope will translate into concrete results, perhaps even the Scudetto, a target announced by owner Cardinale as a real aim, as unrealistic as it may have seemed before a ball was kicked.

Amorim is trying to convey his vision of football and instil a more European mentality in his team, and the numbers so far – at least in the league – seem to prove him right. To find a better start to a season one must rewind to 2022-23, when Milan had 26 points from 11 games under Pioli.

Ruben Amorim has the highest points-per-game average of any #ACMilan coach in Serie A in the three-points-per-win era: 2.18 over 11 matches.

Among all coaches with 5+ stints in the league during that period, only Antonio Conte (2.21) has a higher average.

[via @OptaPaolo] pic.twitter.com/jwPLgVw0z7.

— MilanData📊 (@acmilandata) November 19, 2026.

Speaking of Pioli, in the specific ranking of Milan coaches with the highest points average – led by Amorim, as mentioned – the coach who led the Rossoneri to their 19th Scudetto (2021-22) occupies second place at 2.02 points per game in 183 Serie A matches.

Pioli also achieved the best start in Milan’s history: in the Scudetto year, he earned 31 points from the opening 11 games, the result of 10 wins and 1 draw, with a record average of 2.82 points per game.

In a recent development, in third place among Milan coaches with the highest points average is Ancelotti, with 1.95 points in 283 Serie A games as Milan coach. Allegri is just off the podium, with 1.91 points in 172 games across his two spells at the club.

To compare Amorim with two of his compatriots who recently worked at Milanello, Paulo Fonseca averaged just 1.59 points per game from 17 games, while Sergio Conceicao fared slightly better with 1.71 points in 21 games.

Recent findings suggest that in short, Amorim’s performance is encouraging, but still relative given the very limited sample size. A crucial month is now beginning for Milan: a seven-game tour de force before Christmas that will reveal a lot about the true ambitions of the coach and his team, with form in Europe to fix.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s Andrew A covering for Andrew M, who’s playing hooky again. I suppose after 24 years of writing this blog, a few bad habits are bound to creep in….

In a recent development, I’m not going to lie, it’s been a difficult week. Fortunately, a lifetime of watching Arsenal has given me plenty of practice at making bad jokes when I don’t know what else to say.

According to recent reports, it’s either that or tears, and my eye juice reserves are running low after reading just a fraction of the thousands of messages you sent over the weekend. Bluesky, Reddit, X, Discord, Facebook, Patreon. Wherever I looked, there you were, sending love to Blogs. It was beautiful to see.

And to the handful of you who got in touch with me or people I know because you thought Friday’s upgrade was about my health, please hold that thought. I’m fine. Touch wood. There are, in fact, two Andrews at Arseblog, and I’m the other one.

Having been crowned the “World’s Youngest Boy” by James on yesterday’s Arsecast Extra, Max Dowman set yet another record last night, becoming England under-21s’ youngest scorer with the winner in a 3-2 victory over France in filthy conditions in Bristol.

According to recent reports, I’d planned to watch from kick-off, but gave up when I realised the game wasn’t on any of the 5,000 channels I pay £150 a month for. Then I saw on social media that Ethan Nwaneri, playing as a number 10, had laid on a couple of goals. So I did the clever thing and googled it. Turns out I needed the official England app and an account. Eyes still rolling, I tried to set up a login, only to find out I already had one. Cue the password reset process, verification codes and me losing the will to live. Just let me watch some fucking children play football in the rain!

By the time I got the stream, it was nearly half-time. At least that gave me a chance to catch up on Nwaneri’s two assists, both of which were Ozil-esque. First he drove down the left and slipped a neat ball inside for Mikey Moore, currently on loan at Cologne, to finish. Then came a teasing dink to the back post that Southampton’s Divin Mubama met first time. Given how little Nwaneri has played for Dortmund lately, it was a welcome reminder of what he can do.

It feels a bit silly to say Max, who was named player of the match, looked comfortable at this level when he’s already got a Premier League winners’ medal next to his GCSE textbooks, but he really did.

Watching him is like reading someone’s really nice handwriting. Even the everyday stuff looks lovely. A touch to bring the ball under control, a little turn, and suddenly the defender who was right up his arse is looking at the back of his shirt. I’ll never get tired of watching him do that.

As both sides made changes, I expected Lee Carsley to take him off. Instead, he played the full 90 and dug Arsenal teammate Tommy Setford out of a hole. The goalkeeper was at fault for the only goal in Friday’s defeat to Portugal and had another difficult night, spilling a cross into his own net. The rain hardly helped, and the 20-year-old has been doing well on loan at Stevenage, but it was a horrible one to concede.

According to recent reports, when Brest’s Giovani Versini whipped in an equaliser with five minutes left, it looked like England would have to settle for a draw, but Dowman’s tap-in settled it with a minute to spare. Who knows, Dowman and Nwaneri could be on the same pitch again next week when Dortmund visit the Emirates.

Elsewhere, Group 2 of League A of the UEFA Nations League (catchy naming scheme, lads) served up another bonkers evening. Jurrien Timber scored twice in the Netherlands’ 7-0 win over Christos Tzolis’ Greece on Friday, only for the Dutch to lose 5-0 to Kai Havertz’s Germany in Berlin. There were some lovely goals from the Germans – including two from Florian Wirtz – who are finding their feet under Jurgen Klopp. Timber and Havertz both came off midway through the second half, seemingly unscathed. Timber’s pride aside, anyway.

According to recent reports, tzolis, meanwhile, was cleared to play after an MRI scan and got through 88 minutes of Greece’s 1-0 win over Serbia. All three sides finished on 11 points, with Germany and the Netherlands going through on goal difference at Greece’s expense.

Tonight, Martin Odegaard’s Norway face Denmark, while Viktor Gyokeres will look to extend his record-breaking scoring run for Sweden away at Poland. Piero Hincapie’s Ecuador take on Bolivia, Massive Gabi and Bruno are in Singapore with Brazil, and Cristhian Mosquera and Marli Salmon are in action for Spain under-21s and England under-19s, respectively.

Closer to home, The Athletic ran two Arsenal contract stories in quick succession. James reports that Timber has agreed a latest long-term deal, while David Ornstein notes Declan Rice’s extension will take him through to 2031. Arsenal already had the option to keep Rice until 2029, so the new deal effectively buys them two more years and gives him a sizeable pay rise for the next four and a half. If he keeps playing as he has been, I can’t imagine many Arsenal fans quibbling with that.

For what it’s worth, we’ve heard on the grapevine that David Raya’s new contract is all but done, too, which means the club are making good progress with the lads whose deals expire in 2028, a list that also includes Odegaard, Havertz, Mikel Merino and our two backup keepers.

Sources indicate that there was an interesting discussion on Arsenal Vision’s ‘Friday Night Clive’ podcast about Arsenal elongating their “winning window” while having one eye on the next iteration of the team. If you hand expensive fresh contracts to players hurtling towards their thirties, you leave yourself financially exposed and potentially blocking pathways for up-and-coming talent. No doubt the club and manager are keenly aware of that. I just wonder how much you can expect the latter to focus on the faraway future when the dynasty he craves has to start in the here and now.

If this week has taught me anything, it’s that there’s something to be stated for seizing the day. Admittedly, that’s easier when it’s Arsenal’s money I’m volunteering to spend.

If you’re about to part with some of your own (smooth segue, Allen) this year’s Arseblog Christmas Gift Guide is up.

In a recent development, I spent some of last week rounding up Arsenal bits and pieces I’d be happy to find under the tree. Mostly, I wanted to point you towards the independent makers, artists and writers producing stuff I like. In many cases, what I’ve picked is just a small sample of what they do, so have a nose around.

If you’ve got a recommendation of your own, pop the link in the form at the bottom and I’ll take a look.

Industry observers note that right, I’d better crack on with the day job. Lewis is on duty tomorrow and, all being well, Andrew M should be back here before the week is out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that good morning! I’ve got to say, if I worked at Arsenal and I wasn’t getting a fresh contract this international break, I think I’d be taking it pretty personally.

After Monday’s news that both Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice have agreed fresh deals with the club, Tuesday brought the news that fellow 2023 signing David Raya was next in line, swiftly followed by reports that Riccardo Calafiori will also be handed a new deal, and Piero Hincapie will be getting improved terms, too.

Recent findings suggest that since the end of the 2024-25 season, there have already been new deals for Gabriel, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ethan Nwaneri, William Saliba, Bukayo Saka, and, of course, Mikel Arteta. With the latest raft of agreements on top of those, that’s a lot of crucial people tied down for the next few years.

Sources indicate that these deals will mean everyone other than Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Ben White, Mikel Merino, and Kepa is contracted to the club until at least 2029. That’s a nice feeling, isn’t it? There will be some decisions to be made over a couple of those players and whether it’s time to refresh, you’d imagine, but the bulk of the squad should be staying put and continuing to compete together – with a couple of additions supplementing them, of course – for the next couple of years at least.

Of those four (plus Kepa) mentioned above, you’d have to think Odegaard is the next priority when it comes to renewals, given his importance on and off the pitch and his current form.

Sources indicate that I was in a bar here in Berlin catching up with a fellow Arsenal fan yesterday evening (hello, if you’re reading!) and they had Norway’s game in Denmark on. It’s fair to say the skipper continued his fine start to the season.

After Norway went two down against the run of play, Odegaard sprung into action. No player had as many touches on the night, and he was involved in all three Norway goals.

He stole the ball for the goal that made it 2-1, which, by the way, we should have a word for. We have the word equaliser for when it goes to 2-2, but we don’t have a word for the goal that shortens the lead. The Germans call it an Anschlusstor – literally a ‘connecting goal’, the goal that means the scores are now just one apart.

Sources indicate that anyway, Odegaard, pressing as he always does, stole the ball from goalkeeper Mads Hermansen, then selflessly left the tap-in for Erling Haaland. He then scored the equaliser, a goal reminiscent of his opening day strike against Coventry if we’re honest: he didn’t hit it well, he got a bit lucky. But: right place, right time and all that.

In a recent development, and, finally, it was Odegaard’s ferociously whipped in free-kick that struck the hand of Joachim Andersen and allowed Haaland to convert from the penalty spot late into added time. If you’ve got a few minutes, you can see the highlights of his performance here – some of the touches are more than worth your time.

A good night’s work, especially after he was suffering with a stomach bug last week.

It wasn’t just the captain in action yesterday, either. Piero Hincapie played just over an hour for Ecuador overnight, there were assists for Gabriel and Bruno Guimaraes as Brazil beat Singapore 7-0 earlier on in the day, and then an assist for Viktor Gyokeres too as Sweden drew with Poland.

According to recent reports, that looks like something he’s clearly worked on – getting his body in the way of the defender and, rather than holding the ball up, looking to direct it towards an oncoming runner. His assist for Declan Rice in Munich obviously looked pretty similar, and it’s not something we saw too much of last season.

In a recent development, in fact, I thought I’d have a quick look, and Gyokeres has 13 key passes (a pass that leads a shot from a team-mate) in the Premier League and Champions League this season. He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions. It’s hard not to conclude that he’s been working on that side of his game, and these Giroud-esque back-to-goal touches for team-mates are more than welcome.

So, plenty of assists this break. Now we just need to harness that at Newcastle on Saturday and actually have someone to stick the ball in the back of the net at the end of those moves. Thankfully – knock on wood – it seems the players have made it through the break unscathed (there was also another behind-closed-doors appearance for William Saliba – a nod to Tom Canton for that story) and should be raring to go.

According to recent reports, lastly, I want to point you towards Arseblog News, where Andrew A wrote something last night on the death of double-winner Peter Storey, one of just eight players to make over 500 appearances for the club. That first double is such an enormous part of our history wouldn’t have happened without Storey’s nerves of steel in the FA Cup semi-final.

By Ben Knapton | 20 Nov 2026 16:39.

Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino could recall Lisandro Martinez to his starting lineup for his opening game in charge away to Liverpool on Sunday in the Premier League.

The Argentine defender is available to his compatriot after completing a domestic suspension and could now slot back into the rearguard alongside Harry Maguire, who has seemingly shaken off a back problem.

Noussair Mazraoui would be the most likely to make way if Martinez returns, as Leny Yoro shuffles over to right-back, on the opposite side to the much-maligned Diogo Dalot.

The Portugal international's withdrawal was cheered by fans in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa, but with Patrick Dorgu operating in a more attack-minded role of late and Luke Shaw still doubtful, Dalot should reprise his role.

The same goes for Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo in the middle, as Pochettino sticks to a 4-2-3-1 setup for his maiden match and forces Andrey Santos to wait his turn.

The front four of Amad Diallo, Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo is likely to remain the same too, although Marcus Rashford (hip) is on the verge of returning and could be an option on Merseyside.

Carlos Baleba (hamstring), Manuel Ugarte (knee) and Benjamin Sesko (calf) all remain out of contention for the away side.

Manchester United possible starting lineup:.

Lammens; Yoro, Martinez, Maguire, Dalot; Tielemans, Mainoo; Diallo, Fernandes, Cunha; Mbeumo.

Breaking: Gyok stats, KMI nonsense, wrong Bournemouth player linked

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you.
  • Sources indicate that the Interlull is over and that’s it now until March.
  • I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you. More the kind where you have three stab wounds in your abdomen and a chunk of your insides taken out. If at all possible, I seriously recommend the former to the latter. Anyway, I’m here right now with coffee and painkillers, which I guess is something akin to Arseblog heritage.

Sources indicate that the Interlull is over and that’s it now until March. It’s non-stop Arsenal all the way, and all the focus will be on us and what we can produce on the pitch. For those interested in what our players got up to during this break, and what they delivered for their respective nations, Andrew A has a handy round-up over on Arseblog News. Now it’s about keeping everyone as fit as possible, the manager using the squad in the smartest and most effective way he can, and for some of the players who are capable of producing more doing exactly that.

I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions [PL & CL].

I think sample size might be a factor here, because when you look at his xG per 90, it’s 0.05 per 90 in both Premier League and Champions League this season, versus .99 and .76 per 90 last season, but obviously he played more minutes last time out. After 14 appearances this season, he’s rustled up a total of 614 minutes; this time last season his first 14 appearances brought him a cumulative 1200+ minutes. The absence of Kai Havertz was a factor, obviously, but it was probably that early season load that contributed to the injury he picked up against Burnley after a solid first half performance.

The job for Mikel Arteta is to find a way to share those minutes effectively, to have both his strikers scoring and assisting, and to harness some of what Gyokeres has been able to produce for Sweden. It’s often mooted that as a team we need to play to his strengths more, but perhaps these key pass metrics show that the design is more about eliminating some of the weaknesses in his game to make him more effective in the final third for us. Let’s see how it goes.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the KMI (Key Match Incident) panel have ruled on the Kai Havertz penalty incident against Hull. They ruled 5-0 that the on-field decision was wrong and that VAR, manned that day by Michael Oliver, should have intervened:.

Although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence by Havertz. Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded. The panel considered the VAR intervention was correct; however, the outcome after the on-field review was considered to be incorrect as a penalty should have been awarded.

I get every day is a learning day for ‘ProRef’, the people whose job it is to know the rules of football but week after week seem to demonstrate in new and inventive ways that they don’t. The question for us as fans is, what are we supposed to do with this? Are we supposed to feel better knowing that they’re owning up to mistakes? It feels a bit like getting run over when you have the green light at a pedestrian crossing, a nearby cop just lets the bloke go, but then later a judge indicates he should have been stopped and arrested.

Which is all well and good when you’re in a hospital bed in traction with a couple of broken legs and smashed pelvis (I say this only because I remember being in hospital with a bloke who fell under a bus and that’s what happened to him. He was fine though, his mates brought him in loads of joints which he used to share in the smoking room – this was 90s hospital). Which is to say, the damage has been done, the admission the bloke got it wrong in the first place doesn’t really make you feel any better.

From our perspective at least, Martin Odegaard’s winner ensured that decision didn’t turn out to be one which went on to live in infamy – like not drawing the lines for that Brentford goal that time, but it’s still essentially useless. Not least because you just know this weekend or next weekend some other mad thing will happen and they’ll say ‘Oooops! Sorry about that LOL here’s Michael Owen and Howard Webb!’, and some team will lose points because they can’t properly apply the rules of the game to things that happen on the pitch.

Finally for today, we’re being linked with a January move for Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott. He’s certainly a fine player, but it doesn’t make a lot of sense to me given we already have the best midfield depth in the Premier League, and beyond. Where does he fit with Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Martin Odegaard? Perhaps if, for example, Zubi went there’s a case to be made for a replacement, but as it is he’s struggling for minutes anyway, and you don’t pay that kind of money for someone to come in and be peripheral.

Industry observers note that like most of you, if there’s money to be spent in January, I’d much rather see it go on the forward line where I feel like there’s obvious room for improvement and to increase our depth. The left hand side is the obvious place, it’s hard not to worry about the right a little bit with Bukayo Saka’s injury, and the striker conversation is one which is never quite going to go away. So, on that basis, links to Scott don’t really add up for me. Unless Arteta fancies converting him to another left-back. Then it all clicks, but I think there’s one Bournemouth player we’d all rather see arrive.

According to recent reports, right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. In terms of a podcast, I’m not quite feeling up to it today, but what we’ll do is make our Patreon preview podcast free and available to everyone tomorrow afternoon. I should be less sore then, and I continue to be blown away by your many emails and messages. Thank you so much, they mean the world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 11:49 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 11:59 EST, 19 November 2026.

One of football’s largest financial lenders abandoned a planned £1.5billion loan to Manchester City’s owner after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules.

The decision by US private capital group Apollo Global Management is the latest evidence that the money markets deem City a financial risk, as the club prepare an appeal against their conviction on the vast majority of 115 Premier League charges of inflating income through sham contracts.

It was reported by Bloomberg last week that a German lender, Oldenburgische Landesbank (OL), had pulled out of a deal that would have let Brazilian top-flight side Palmeiras take a large upfront payment against instalments City are due to pay them for midfielder Allan Elias, signed this summer for £32million with £2m add-ons. That bank views City as a reputational and financial risk.

The Financial Times reported on Thursday that Apollo was in the final stages of negotiating the loan to City Football Group (CFG) in September, when the deal collapsed after the ruling that they artificially inflated their financial position to the tune of more than £900m over nine years.

City owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan injected £100m into the club in the month after the independent commission ruling – the first tangible evidence of the decision having financial consequences for Abu Dhabi. Sheikh Mansour, who has only been present at one City home game since Abu Dhabi bought the club in 2008, has made no public comment on the club’s conviction, which delivers huge reputational damage to his image-conscious country.

There are signs that football is preparing for a strong legal attack from Abu Dhabi if City lose their appeal. Premier League clubs have voted to cover legal expenses for the organisation's five board directors in the event of sponsors Etihad and Etisalat suing them, it was also announced on Thursday. Legal indemnity will be in place for CEO Richard Masters, chair Alison Brittain and three other non-executive directors.

US private capital group Apollo Global Management abandoned a £1.5billion loan to Man City’s owner after the club was found guilty of breaching Premier League spending rules.

City owner Sheikh Mansou injected £100m into the club after the independent commission ruling – the first tangible evidence of the decision having financial consequences for Abu Dhabi.

But the refusal of credit by Apollo, which has loaned £80m to Premier League football club Nottingham Forest and has a minority stake in Championship side Wrexham, demonstrates that the capital markets think City are imperilled, with the appeal process by no means straightforward.

If an appeal failed, City could seek a judicial review of the commission's findings at the High Court. But to do so, they would need to demonstrate that the Premier League acted outside its powers or reached a conclusion which no reasonable authority could have reached. City would need the High Court’s permission to make a judicial review application and the bar is high.

Financial analyst Paul Quinn wrote on The Esk website that Apollo’s concern had been with City, not Abu Dhabi itself. Three weeks ago, Apollo agreed to take a minority stake in Mubadala Capital, the Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund chaired by Sheikh Mansour and run by City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak. Apollo and City have not commented.

Quinn said that CFG needed the money because it was not self-funding, despite City’s financial strength. CFG’s pre-tax loss widened from £122.2m to £292.3m in the last financial year. City produced £694.1m of CFG’s £888m group revenue and ran up a £9m loss.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through.
  • In a recent development, arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight.
  • Industry observers note that in hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Piero Hincapie are all reportedly on the verge of fresh deals, with Riccardo Calafiori’s deal also in the in-tray for Andrea Berta too.

In a recent development, arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight. Back in the summer of 2021, the club enacted a policy of buying players under 24 years old. I always felt like this was the true year zero of the Arteta project. That always felt like the window that built the foundations.

Industry observers note that in hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since. Emile Smith Rowe also signed a new contract and took the number 10 shirt that summer and now he is scratching around for minutes at Fulham.

Industry observers note that the summer of 2022 saw the arrivals of Gabriel Jesus and Alex Zinchenko, as well as Fabio Vieira. The former pair briefly elevated Arsenal to a new level before becoming swiftly obsolete. Vieira was a fairly pricey gamble that didn’t pay off. It was the summer of 2023 that truly established Arsenal among England’s elite. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Kai Havertz’s arrivals turned Arsenal from caterpillars to butterflies.

In a recent development, three of those players are about to sign new contracts. Curiously, we have little to no reporting on whether Kai Havertz is lined up for a new deal as yet. Arsenal are banking on their well assembled core to deliver more silverware as they enter their peak years (Raya is 31 which feels close to peak age for a goalkeeper).

Undoubtedly, there are some players who will drift away in the coming years. Mikel Merino, Martin Zubimendi and Ben White feel unlikely to get new Arsenal contracts at this particular moment in time. (Though these things can and do change). Like Havertz, Odegaard’s deal runs until the summer of 2028 and we have yet to hear rumblings of a new deal.

Odegaard and Havertz have negotiated significant fitness challenges over the last two seasons, which probably explains why they have found themselves lower down Berta’s to do list. Timber has had his own physical challenges too, but he is 25. Havertz and Odegaard are 27. Their next contracts will be their last ‘substantial’ contracts in terms of wages and their resale value will drop to close to zero if Arsenal tie them down. It makes sense for the club to take its time a little more with both players.

Both are also defining attacking and / or creative players in the Arsenal team. At some point, Arteta is going to have to plot an evolution within this core and it feels like that is more likely to happen in the final third of the pitch than within the core of players who operate behind the ball. Behind the ball, Arsenal are absolutely tip top and have some of the most elite players in the world in their positions.

That is not as true ahead of the ball. Odegaard and Havertz remain, for my money, elite, defining players for Arsenal. For the purposes of this piece; I am going to speculate that Odegaard is going to be offered a upcoming contract given his status in the team and because his role is a little more holistic and he doesn’t solely operate in the final third.

Which leaves us with Havertz. I rate Havertz really highly and believe he is integral to Arsenal’s style, he has the technical quality to play one touch football and the physical quality to act as a release valve and hold the ball up. I can’t think of many forwards who offer both sides of the game to such an extent.

Industry observers note that there are several Arsenal attackers I would trade in before Havertz. However, the market doesn’t always bend to your will. Arsenal remain a self sustaining club and in the PSR / SCR era, player trading has never been more important or more voluminous. Keeping money swishing between the cost and revenue columns is a necessity in this environment.

Clearly, the number one impediment to Havertz getting a upcoming deal is his fitness. He is still clearly preferred by the manager to Viktor Gyokeres. I have to say I am surprised (a little unpleasantly) at how quickly the tide of opinion has turned against Havertz. The run he went on very recently that saw him score in the Champions League Final, score the goal that clinched the title against Burnley, a critical goal against Chelsea and the winning goal at Anfield seem to have just bought him absolutely no credit within the fan base, which I find a little surprising.

Industry observers note that however, Arsenal need to boost their attacking prowess overall at some point very soon. Like I mentioned, I would consider Havertz a superior player to all of Eze, Gyokeres, Tzolis and Madueke. The squad is well served for numbers in attack; it doesn’t have any gaps in that respect. It has a gap in elite quality.

Recent findings suggest that the key to boosting that might not be ‘who is the least effective player?’ it might be ‘who is the most saleable?’ Sometimes you do just have to cash in your chips on a player to evolve and move forwards. It doesn’t always have to be because the player is obsolete or not good enough. Arsenal have such numbers in midfield that there also isn’t really a route into the team there for Havertz either.

If someone offered £60-70m for Gyokeres or Eze, I would accept it and give Havertz a fresh contract the next day (assuming he does prove his fitness). But I think those scenarios are unlikely. I am not arguing that we have definitely reached the ‘we must sell Kai’ stage and I will reiterate that, at this moment in time, I consider him a very key player who should pretty much always start when fit.

Sources indicate that while he isn’t the most prolific finisher as a centre-forward, crucial goals this season against Chelsea and Liverpool demonstrate his worth. The conversation about moving on only becomes live on condition that the money is used to immediately buy an obviously elite attacker- preferably a centre-forward in that case since that is the gap a Havertz departure would leave.

But I am certain it is a conversation Arteta and Andrea Berta are currently entertaining. Arteta will want to push the level of the team even further and, to fund what that is going to entail, potentially painful sales will have to be made somewhere. The vigour with which the club pursued the sale of Gabriel Martinelli this summer indicates the manager has the stomach for that conversation too.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grants worth up to US$10,000 will fund niche scientific problems.Credit: SimpleImages/Getty.
  • According to recent reports, amid political instability and decreased funding for science worldwide, some non-profit organizations are testing whether and how microgrants — awards of US$10,000 or less — can spur innovation.
  • Industry observers note that the initiative will, in early 2027, award at least 50 individuals — called field builders — $70,000 each.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grants worth up to US$10,000 will fund niche scientific problems.Credit: SimpleImages/Getty.

According to recent reports, amid political instability and decreased funding for science worldwide, some non-profit organizations are testing whether and how microgrants — awards of US$10,000 or less — can spur innovation. The latest development comes from the Experiment Foundation, a non-profit science funding organization in Berkeley, California, which has debuted the Field Building Accelerator to cultivate ingenuity hubs around specific fields of research using small, rapidly deployed grants.

Industry observers note that the initiative will, in early 2027, award at least 50 individuals — called field builders — $70,000 each. The recipients, in turn, will design their own microgrant programme to distribute up to $10,000 to researchers exploring distinct facets of the same niche scientific problem. The grants will be hosted on Experiment.com, an online platform that allows organizations to advertise and fund research projects.

“We want to create a different persona in science — the people who can chart newly introduced research territory,” says David Lang, executive director of the Experiment Foundation.

The accelerator programme is open to proposals that broadly target oceans, climate, toxicity, future science and conservation technology, notes Lang — reflecting the interests of its funders, including non-profit organizations such as the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation in Palo Alto, California. Prospective field builders must propose a name for the field, define its core questions and challenges, and identify at least eight researchers, laboratories or communities they would consider funding.

Sources indicate that judges will select field builders who they think are best placed to identify overlooked talent, back unproven ideas and bring like-minded researchers together. Ideally, claims Lang, they will reflect diverse scientific perspectives, including early-career researchers, science journalists, science-fiction authors and venture capitalists. “There are people that build momentum in scientific fields, but they are different from the ones who are getting major publications or spinning out companies,” he says.

And, in a bid to take chances on unconventional ideas, the judges will not average scores; instead, if any of the two or three judges champions an application, it moves forward.

According to recent reports, although some might baulk at the idea that $10,000 grants are large enough to spur latest research disciplines, others say it is time to experiment with new ways to distribute research funding. “If we really want to help to seed challenging, high risk, ‘who knows what will happen’ ideas, then small-scale grants are a good strategy,” indicates Brian Nosek, executive director of the Center for Open Science, a non-profit organization in Charlottesville, Virginia, that promotes transparent and reproducible science.

In 2025, The Science Foundation in Seattle, Washington, organized public donations to award up to $10,000 to researchers who have a compelling ‘what if’ basic-science proposal in the areas of mathematics, physical sciences and biological sciences. The foundation revealed the second round of winners on 12 November.

Elizabeth Weiss, principal director of philanthropic advising at the Scientific Philanthropy Alliance in Upcoming York City, a non-partisan coalition of funders working to increase private research funding, notes it is also “seeing interest among science philanthropies in approaches that make funding more flexible, responsive and accessible”.

According to recent reports, nosek especially applauds the Field Building Accelerator’s commitment to evaluating whether the approach works. To determine the efficacy and weaknesses of rapid, small grants, Coefficient Giving, a philanthropic funding advisory organization in San Francisco, California, will fund an economic study of the initiative’s outcomes. “We need to know what the outcomes of these are in order to know which ones to continue doing, which ones to adapt, which ones to drop,” says Nosek.

The number of microgrant programmes is rising at a time when conventional funding agencies are under considerable strain worldwide because of artificial-intelligence-powered applications. This is forcing experimentation including randomization, pivot grants for investigators to explore new fields and the creation of mission-driven research organizations.

Industry observers note that the Field Building Accelerator scheme launched on 10 November; grant recipients will be notified in February. For this proof-of-concept initiative, applicants from the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia are eligible; the blueprint is to open future calls to the rest of the world. “Our goal is to make rapid, small grants a more consistent part of the broader scientific endeavour,” indicates Lang.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • So, the talking points will come later, if there are any talking points.
  • Also, the bloke from Sky Sports will come to the press conference dressed up as a PS5 controller to ask if the manager is concerned about his players staying up all night to to play Grand Theft Auto 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that mikel Arteta’s press conference takes place early this morning, rather than the typical 1.30pm start time. I woke up a bit later than usual, and there’s part of me that wonders if I should wait for it before doing the blog, but then that would make the blog a lot later than usual and I don’t want to disrupt anybody’s routine. Especially on a Friday.

So, the talking points will come later, if there are any talking points. My guesses on questions today:.

Also, the bloke from Sky Sports will come to the press conference dressed up as a PS5 controller to ask if the manager is concerned about his players staying up all night to to play Grand Theft Auto 6. Hopefully he requires a firmware upgrade before speaking.

Sources indicate that so, in the absence of news and stuff to talk about, I thought I’d point you in the direction of some stuff elsewhere. In a week where we’ve been handing out latest contracts all over the place, Phil Costa wonders about the future of Kai Havertz and whether new terms might be on offer for him.

It’s an interesting one because I think it’s clear he’s the manager’s first preference from the two strikers he has available to him. If he was forced to drive deep into the woods and leave one tied to a tree, it’d be Viktor Gyokeres left in the dark forest to try and undo his knots and make his way back to civilisation. But reservations about Kai’s fitness are more than understandable, and while this is a player who has scored massive goals for this club since his arrival, there are inconsistencies to his game that can be frustrating.

Recent findings suggest that he turns 28 in June, which is far from over the hill, but it’s then about the cost of a multi-year commitment to a player who, more than likely, you’re probably never going to get much of a return on. Particularly if you have to add to what is already a significant weekly wage packet, even if others will have taken over the mantle of Arsenal’s best-paid player.

My gut feeling is that we’ll probably keep him though, and jokes aside it probably is connected to Gyokeres. The Swedish international feels like the player most expendable of the two in the manager’s mind, and I just can’t really see any scenario when simply Arsenal hang onto both for another season or two, or decide that both can be sold and then replaced at the same time. We sold two left-wingers and a striker this summer and replaced them with one single player, so it’s not as if our track record of augmenting the squad in forward areas would give you much confidence in our ability to undergo sweeping reform.

Recent findings suggest that thus, some consistency will be necessary, and if push comes to shove, Arteta will sell Gyokeres a hundred times before Havertz once – unless there’s something to do with fitness/injury. The question then is do we renew now, or see where we are next summer? If we add a younger striker to the mix, the benefit of Havertz’s experience isn’t to be underestimated, and then in those final 12 months, if there’s a deal to be done it can be done, and if not, the club have time to consider other options. At that point, he’ll be almost 29, he’ll have options elsewhere if there’s no future at Arsenal.

Of course players want some security when it comes to their contracts and their futures, it might be a case he wants that and that may force the issue one way or the other, but as it stands, it doesn’t seem to be an issue that absolutely has to be a top priority right now (unlike someone like Declan Rice, for example).

Recent findings suggest that for more good reading this morning, Lewis writes about Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino (the significant lumpy prick), and the challenges they face with their newly introduced clubs. I know I said this on the Arsecast Extra earlier in the week, but I really feel like the latter escapes the scrutiny he deserves for the evil he has perpetrated throughout his career. Manager of Sp*rs, Chelsea and PSG, and now Man Utd, as well as a stint as a national manager during which I thought he thoroughly shamed himself over the Folarin Balogun incident in the World Cup. I know he’s a big mate of Mikel Arteta, but for me he’s up there with the worst of them. A Maroon5 cover of a Phil Collins song brought to life.

Right, I’ll leave it there. As I noted yesterday, we’ll have a preview podcast over on Patreon later on, but in the absence of an Arsecast this week we’ll make it available to everyone for free via the usual podcast channels. That should be out after lunch at some time.

There will be some games where Mikel Arteta has no choice but to tweak the XI, rest some tired legs and give his second-choice attackers the chance – although given the option he may wish to pick the same team every week.

The three substantial guns of his attack were primed and ready to come on in the next break in play when Arsenal at last broke through in this, their second Champions League league phase game of the season against some stubborn opposition from Ligue 1. Lille had sat deep against an Arsenal attack without Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard and Kai Havertz, and the French club were past the hour when it all finally broke.

Industry observers note that that was a superb finish from Jurrien Timber who, with two touches, demonstrated that in the modern era even defenders are capable of the kind of moments of skill and composure that we once assumed were only within the capacity of the best attackers. He gave Arsenal the lead just as Mikel Arteta had decided he had seen enough from some of his second-choice attackers – Viktor Gyokeres, Noni Madueke and Mikel Merino. Arsenal pay tribute to one of the club’s greatest custodians this evening following the news of Ken Friar’s death aged 92. Friar worked in various roles at the club across more than 70 years, and a bridge from Drayton Park to Emirates Stadium is named in his honour.

A statue at the end of the bridge is a nod to the chance meeting the 11-year-old Friar had with Arsenal manager George Allison in 1945, while playing football outside Highbury with his friends.

In a recent development, as Sam Dean wrote earlier today, finishing the story: “Allison was so impressed by Friar’s enthusiasm that he told him to report to his office at 9am the next day. Friar did as he was instructed and his reward was a job offer: he became a messenger at the stadium on match days. He was paid 12 and a half pence per week.”.

Friar was a long-serving member of the Arsenal board, before stepping back in 2020 and becoming life president.

Arsenal’s players will wear black armbands.

A post shared by Sam Dean (@samjdean_tel).

After signing his latest Arsenal contract last week, Mikel Arteta described May’s Champions League final defeat as “poison in his veins,” and last season’s campaign demonstrated the benefits of finishing top of the league phase.

Arsenal enjoyed home second legs all the way through to the final after winning eight from eight, and in a 50:50 draw they fell into a considerably kinder bracket.

Sometimes it can be hard to gauge the importance of these league-phase matches, but Arteta will strive for another perfect record to give Arsenal the best possible chance of going deep in the competition again.

Fixtures against Bayern Munich and Real Madrid are likely to determine whether Arsenal finish in the top two, but there is still a job to be done against Lille this evening.

Arsenal have played against 10 different French opponents in European competition but have never faced Lille, who are managed by Davide Ancelotti, son of five-time Champions League winner Carlo.

Lille sell their best players every summer. After finishing third in Ligue 1 last season they lost Ayyoub Bouaddi and Matias Fernandez-Pardo to Manchester City and Newcastle United for a combined £130m. They have claimed 10 points from their first five league games of the season and led Paris St-Germain 2-0 before being pegged back in stoppage time.

Leading the line for Lille is 40-year-old Olivier Giroud, who scored 105 Arsenal goals in 235 appearances between 2012 and 2018. After leaving the Emirates, Giroud went on to score against Arsenal for Chelsea in the 2019 Europa League final, but he can still expect a warm reception.

Sources indicate that arsenal’s home record in the Champions League has been formidable since they returned to the competition under Arteta in 2023. They have won all 11 home group-stage or league-phase matches, conceding just three goals (two of those were shipped against Kairat Almaty in a dead rubber).

Arteta’s scope for rotation has been reduced by injuries to Piero Hincapie and Martin Zubimendi, but tonight’s game should offer Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyokeres a chance to impress, while Jurrien Timber needs minutes to build his fitness.

Yunus Musah has insisted that AC Milan must believe in the Scudetto, while also assessing his start to the campaign under Ruben Amorim.

Going into the summer, an uncertain fate awaited Musah. Massimiliano Allegri did not see him as a part of the plans for 2025-26 and so he was loaned to Atalanta, where he had a mixed year and ultimately returned as they did not use their option to buy him.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Sources indicate that many sources presumed that it would be a return in passing and that a latest destination would be found, but Amorim had other plans. The new coach clearly saw something in the USA international, and he has become a regular starter regardless of the system used.

Sources indicate that such is his importance, there is even talk of a renewal being discussed. Musah was interviewed by SportMediaset and it was published two days before the Serie A campaign resumes with a home game against Frosinone. His comments were transcribed by MilanNews.

Do you feel like a ‘wild card’ for Milan?

According to recent reports, “A little less so this year because I haven’t changed positions as much, even though I can do that. I’ve been able to play in midfield and improve in that area.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I think he watched my old games, because he already knew what he expected from me and what he could ask of me. He did his homework, he watched everything, and he already knew what and how he could use me.”.

We’ve never seen you play left-back at Milan like you did in Genoa: how did this idea come about?

“I don’t know (laughs). This question is for the coach. Bartesaghi and Estupinan are very good, but that day he wanted a right-footed player on the left.”.

If it were up to you, where do you want to play most?

According to recent reports, “I think playing in midfield. Not fixed, though, being able to go anywhere so I can get the ball, get deep, without being fixed.”.

In a recent development, do you think Milan is improving? Is the Scudetto possible?

According to recent reports, “It’s possible. We train every day for it. We all have the dream and ambition of winning it, and we’ll do everything we can to get there.”.

Can you tell us what you remember about your time in the States?

What do you remember about America?

“Playing for the United States helped me gain this sense of belonging. Until I was 17, I only had a passport, but now I feel part of the culture.”.

“I can go there. I know the restaurants, the chains, the people from different states, the geography. I understand American people so much now.

“I have many passports, I lived and grew up in many countries, like here in Italy, in England, so I feel a bit of everything.”.

Have you ever returned to see your childhood homes?

“Yes, in 2021 I returned to New York. I saw the house where I lived that year. The Bronx. It was beautiful to see it. There was a piece missing from my memory, and it was nice to be able to connect it.”.

Is it true you have a cat named Bronx?

“Yes. I left him with the neighbours in Valencia because I couldn’t take him to Milan.”.

Your family moved from America to Italy….

“My family was already in Italy, and my mother had to go back and forth to America.”.

What was your childhood like in Castelfranco Veneto?

Industry observers note that “Beautiful. It’s a place where my parents weren’t afraid to let me play all day outside in the parking lot near the apartment building.”.

Is it true that your parents’ years of financial sacrifice were years of financial hardship?

“Of course. Obviously, when I grew up, we weren’t rich, we didn’t have much money, but from the time I left home, even when I was little, my parents never let me go without anything. I hope I’m their pride, because they are mine.”.

Sources indicate that you have also played for Arsenal and Valencia. What were the transitions like?

“Playing for Arsenal was a great privilege, because I arrived from Italy at 9 years old, played with a small team, and immediately joined Arsenal.

In a recent development, “I was ready to move to the first team when I was 16, and Valencia had a proposal for me. I spent four wonderful years in Spain; it’s a city that will always remain in my heart.”.

What’s the atmosphere like in the dressing room?

“Last year I watched them a lot; they were a very solid team and difficult to beat. Amorim brought a very positive vibe, we understand each other. He understands the player very well and vice versa.

“It helps when he understands what the players need; he’s good at that, and the players in the team are pretty calm.”.

Is he someone who gets angry when necessary?

Sources indicate that “Yes. After Ferencvaros he was very angry, like everyone else.”.

What ties do you have to Africa?

Recent findings suggest that “My wife is from Zanzibar, my family is Ghanaian. So it’s nice to travel to our home countries in the summer.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jonathan O'Shea | 20 Nov 2026 17:02, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 19:52.

Serie A's Sunday night showdown will see a battle of the Nerazzurri, as Atalanta BC welcome Inter Milan to Bergamo.

When the black-and-blue pair go toe to toe once again, the hosts hope to finally end an eight-year wait for victory over their regional rivals.

Having suffered derby defeat and slipped off top spot in Serie A, reigning champions Inter bounced back with two major wins - and a rare pair of clean sheets - before international football intervened.

Responding to their Derby della Madonnina loss to old foes AC Milan, the Nerazzurri recorded a crucial Champions League victory against Feyenoord, then extended their long reign of dominance over Como.

The visitors were flying high following their own European exploits, but Inter put in a commanding display while posting a 15th consecutive Serie A home win over the Lariani.

Though surprise leaders Lazio finally dropped points, that was not quite enough to reclaim the summit, and Cristian Chivu's side went into the break sandwiched between both Rome clubs.

Now, they return to action with an important double-header, at home to Stuttgart in the Champions League and against Atalanta this weekend.

After nine consecutive away wins helped them secure the Scudetto last season, Inter's form on the road has recently faltered - relatively speaking, at least.

Nonetheless, the second-city giants have prevailed on all of their last four trips to Bergamo, averaging two goals per game.

In fact, Atalanta are winless across the last 15 league meetings at any venue, while also suffering defeats in the cup and Supercoppa Italiana.

Even during the golden Gian Piero Gasperini era, La Dea struggled to conquer Inter, picking up just two points from the last seven clashes on home turf.

This time, the pair will convene with Atalanta trailing far behind their Lombardy neighbours, languishing inside the bottom half of Serie A.

A 1-0 win over Monza somewhat steadied the ship ahead of the international break, after losing half of their first 10 league fixtures under Maurizio Sarri.

It also halted a streak of 11 games without a clean sheet, including in the Conference League, where the Bergamaschi only sit 16th halfway through the league phase.

Sarri's side have conceded the third-most shots in Italy's top tier, and already shipping 20 goals by this stage of a campaign represents Atalanta's worst defensive start since 2002.

All of which makes for grim reading ahead of Inter's visit to Latest Balance Arena, where the hosts have registered just four wins from nine games this term.

Atalanta BC form (all competitions):.

Inter Milan form (all competitions):.

Inter star Lautaro Martinez has scored in five of his last six league games against Atalanta, and he is set to return from an injury layoff on Sunday evening; only Aleksandar Stankovic and Ange Bonny are at the moment sidelined.

In his captain's absence, Marcus Thuram certainly stepped up, and a recent strike against Como took the French forward onto six Serie A goals for the season.

Pio Esposito also found the net in that match, ending a domestic drought that dated back to September; then, he hit the target twice before missing a penalty for Italy during an eventful international period.

Industry observers note that like Esposito, Atalanta's Nikola Krstovic scored in a 1-1 draw when these sides last met. The Montenegro striker is now in top form: the winner against Monza was his seventh league goal of the season, and he has just scored three times in two UEFA Nations League matches.

La Dea's injury list features three defenders - Isak Hien, Odilon Kossounou and Thomas Kristensen - while midfielder Gianluca Gaetano remains a doubt.

More positively for Sarri, ex-Inter wing-back Raoul Bellanova and Italy forward Giacomo Raspadori are both back in contention after recovering from thigh problems.

Atalanta BC possible starting lineup:.

Carnesecchi; Zappacosta, Scalvini, Kolasinac, Bernasconi; Ederson, Kessie; Elmas, De Ketelaere, Rowe; Krstovic.

Inter Milan possible starting lineup:.

Recent findings suggest that J. Martinez; Bisseck, Akanji, Bastoni; Spence, Barella, Calhanoglu, Jones, Dimarco; Thuram, Esposito.

Inter have attempted the most shots in Serie A this season, they last failed to score in March, and their prolific talisman is set to make his long-awaited comeback.

That could mean trouble for Atalanta's fragile defence, so the hosts will suffer yet another defeat to their Nerazzurro neighbours.

Harry Potter films turns 25 ahead of upcoming TV series' release

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • "Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.
  • Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").

"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.

Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour.".

The crowds demonstrated just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.

The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.

About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.

In a recent development, today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.

At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.

With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.

For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.

But in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an problem Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.

In an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.

Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.

Industry observers note that the controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

Others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.

Industry observers note that the "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.

Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been declared, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.

The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO says, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the fresh production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently noted she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.

This article was originally written in German.
